title: Manus and the AI tools I've been tinkering with lately
content: TraeThree days ago, Trae released its China version, hooked up to DeepSeek. In some cases R1 seems more dependable than Claude 3.5 Sonnet. When Claude 3.5 Sonnet helps me port big chunks of my old code, it sometimes goes off-script and slips bugs in instead — and then I end up burning a ton of time debugging it myself. It’s great at writing simple web stuff; going from 0 to 1 with it is genuinely impressive. But on anything more complex it keeps getting it wrong over and over, like an intern. I honestly don’t get how the people out there hyping Claude so hard are actually using it. QwQ-32BToday QwQ-32B became installable, so I jumped on it right away. Word is it’s as strong as the 671B R1, which would make it a great fit for local deployment. ManusWell damn — if this really becomes as widely accessible as DeepSeek and Qwen, then all the setup I’m learning right now will be obsolete. Official site: https://manus.im It probably flexibly folds in every trick that’s actually usable in practice right now, and pushes each one to its limit. Or a product like Manus gets used in enterprise-grade ways. Local super-individuals just keep writing a bit of code themselves and cobbling together some local AI function calling, and that’s enough. So future enterprise-grade AI platforms are far from done at multi-dimensional tables for batch-scheduling parallel tasks, workflows with multiple AIs and multiple modalities working together, and knowledge base chunking and extraction — they’ll also have to provide cloud PCs for multi-modal agents to operate. A general AI assistant needs a brain and needs hands, and it’s exactly these cloud resources that a standalone version can’t match.

title: Slow internet speeds when using the Linksys MX8400
content: Gigabit broadband is installed, but internet access is slowEarly this month I went and switched my bundled plan, and now I’ve upgraded back to the gigabit broadband plan. The China Unicom app shows gigabit, but browsing the internet at home still feels like 100Mbps-level speeds. I’m not sure whether it takes effect next month or what. The wiring in my walls is Cat7a, the router has all-gigabit Ethernet ports, and my PC has a 10Gbps Ethernet port. Testing with speedtest.cn on the PC connected directly by cable, I only get 181Mbps down 28.3Mbps up, which looks the same as before the upgrade. I asked China Unicom support for help. They told me to bypass my router and test the speed straight off the ONT, but it’s a pain to move my PC, and my laptop has no Ethernet port, so it’s awkward to do myself. He said he’d come by in the afternoon to test the speed for me. Speed testing with iperf3I ran a test on my LAN to check the state of the cabling and router at home. MacStudio to PC 940Mbps MacBookPro (wireless) to PC 393Mbps D:\GreenSoft\iperf-3.1.3-win64iperf3 -s ----------------------------------------------------------- Server listening on 5201 ----------------------------------------------------------- Accepted connection from 192.168.50.3, port 57277 [ 5] local 192.168.50.8 port 5201 connected to 192.168.50.3 port 57278 [ ID] Interval Transfer Bandwidth [ 5] 0.00-1.00 sec 112 MBytes 941 Mbits/sec [ 5] 1.00-2.00 sec 112 MBytes 942 Mbits/sec [ 5] 2.00-3.00 sec 112 MBytes 941 Mbits/sec [ 5] 3.00-4.00 sec 112 MBytes 942 Mbits/sec [ 5] 4.00-5.00 sec 110 MBytes 926 Mbits/sec [ 5] 5.00-6.00 sec 112 MBytes 942 Mbits/sec [ 5] 6.00-7.00 sec 112 MBytes 942 Mbits/sec [ 5] 7.00-8.00 sec 112 MBytes 941 Mbits/sec [ 5] 8.00-9.00 sec 112 MBytes 941 Mbits/sec [ 5] 9.00-10.00 sec 112 MBytes 941 Mbits/sec [ 5] 10.00-10.01 sec 612 KBytes 880 Mbits/sec - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - [ ID] Interval Transfer Bandwidth [ 5] 0.00-10.01 sec 0.00 Bytes 0.00 bits/sec sender [ 5] 0.00-10.01 sec 1.09 GBytes 940 Mbits/sec receiver ----------------------------------------------------------- Server listening on 5201 ----------------------------------------------------------- Accepted connection from 192.168.50.18, port 61115 [ 5] local 192.168.50.8 port 5201 connected to 192.168.50.18 port 61116 [ ID] Interval Transfer Bandwidth [ 5] 0.00-1.00 sec 47.2 MBytes 396 Mbits/sec [ 5] 1.00-2.00 sec 45.2 MBytes 379 Mbits/sec [ 5] 2.00-3.00 sec 47.2 MBytes 396 Mbits/sec [ 5] 3.00-4.00 sec 48.8 MBytes 409 Mbits/sec [ 5] 4.00-5.00 sec 50.6 MBytes 425 Mbits/sec [ 5] 5.00-6.00 sec 46.9 MBytes 393 Mbits/sec [ 5] 6.00-7.00 sec 45.5 MBytes 382 Mbits/sec [ 5] 7.00-8.00 sec 44.3 MBytes 371 Mbits/sec [ 5] 8.00-9.00 sec 46.3 MBytes 388 Mbits/sec [ 5] 9.00-10.00 sec 46.7 MBytes 391 Mbits/sec [ 5] 10.00-10.01 sec 201 KBytes 525 Mbits/sec - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - [ ID] Interval Transfer Bandwidth [ 5] 0.00-10.01 sec 0.00 Bytes 0.00 bits/sec sender [ 5] 0.00-10.01 sec 469 MBytes 393 Mbits/sec receiver ----------------------------------------------------------- Server listening on 5201 ----------------------------------------------------------- Using the MacBook Pro over Wi-Fi to test roaming speeds on a far-away node: On the table outside 168Mbps, at the kitchen doorway 185Mbps China Unicom technician comes to help with speed testingThe China Unicom technician came to help test speeds. Here are the measurements: ONT port at the entrance, speed tester plugged in: 960Mbps+ Study wall port, speed tester plugged in: 960Mbps+ Study wall port with my own cable to the speed tester: 960Mbps+ With Linksys in the path, speed tester on the LAN port: 260Mbps Combined with the earlier result that LAN-to-LAN can hit 960Mbps+ The test shows: the speed between the Linksys WAN port and its LAN ports is capped at 300 Is the Linksys router causing the slow speeds?Strange — why would a Linksys router cause slow speeds? Every link in the chain really is gigabit. After checking, my initial guess is that the Linksys router throttles speed between devices to keep any single device from hogging the bandwidth. I went into the “Priority” settings and found it was allocating priority between devices based on 100Mbps speeds. I manually changed the prioritized speed to gigabit, then tested again in the browser on my Mac and got over 500Mbps! So it was splitting the bandwidth evenly and not giving any device permission to run at full speed. Raising the priority further: after setting the Mac Studio as the priority device, the speed test hit 672Mbps down 66Mbps up. OK, so I just turned the priority feature off entirely. Speed came up to around 800M62M. Summary of the cause:At this point, that’s honestly plenty for me. So the root cause is that the Linksys MX8400 has a certain protection mechanism, originally meant to keep the network stable by limiting speed between devices. But that mechanism depends on the measured internet connection speed, and the Linksys speed test itself isn’t accurate, so it reports a speed that’s too low, which in turn heavily restricts the speed allocated to devices at home. That’s what was capping the network speed. Put plainly, it trades burst speed for stability. So I need to set the internet speed correctly and turn off priority allocation, so that devices on the network can get higher burst speeds.

title: Playing “Who's the Spy” locally with an LLM
content: AI Plays “Who’s the Undercover” With MeIt’s Chinese New Year, and everyone is talking about deepseek.Ruirui wants to play “Who’s the Undercover” but can never round up enough people, so I want to build her one she can play at home — a self-contained, AI-driven, reasonably robust “Who’s the Undercover” game bot. The plan: deploy Deepseek on LMStudio + the LMStudio API to handle dialogue. Then I can write a server side to drive the rules, so the few of us can all play. I also need to find an open-source voice AI that synthesizes speech from text and plays the different bots, with each bot getting its own distinctive voice. The server side will be built with nodejs, serving a web page that hands each human player their own word, with everyone looking at their own screen; the bots don’t need an interface. The approach I’m taking right now is locally deployed deepseek R1 + locally deployed CosyVoice.Later I found that R1’s thinking mode isn’t suited to running this game locally, because it outputs way too many tokens each time and you end up waiting longer. So I switched to the Qwen 14b model. The 32b one gives better results but is a bit slower. In the end I got it working — it just took a while to get in sync with the LLM. The project is on github: https://github.com/mousebomb/shei-shi-wo-di Driving the LLM produced plenty of comedy. It’s really funny now. Let me write it down. I mean, why do you all keep breaking the rules?The dumb things the LLM did Overcomplicated thinking — it spilled all its thoughts out in the open Sometimes it thinks too much, and what LMStudio returns can’t fit in one go, so it comes out in two chunks, which makes the server-side /think extraction fail. Sometimes it returns the plain text undefined, believe it or not. Sometimes it stops describing its own word and starts describing itself… Constantly breaks the rules A ferocious flurry of thinking, with zero regard for what everyone else has already given away. Prompts matterSo maybe I wrote the prompt badly. Time to rewrite a batch. ApiStartGamedefault Player 6 Liu Bei description request in progress AiManagerAiManagerllmRequest [ { role: ‘system’, content: ‘# Role ’ + ‘Your name is Liu Bei. You are a civilian player in “Who is the Undercover”, and the other players are your good friends — Osmanthus Cake, Bajie, Lü Bu, Cao Cao, Guan Yu. ’ + ‘At the start of the game, the undercover word you received is car. ’ + ‘ ’ + ‘ ’ + ‘ ’ + ‘1. You are the undercover player. The word you received differs from the civilian word but is related to it. In the first round of description you must both hide your own word and avoid letting your description stray so far from the civilian word that it raises suspicion. Describe it as vaguely as you can, working from features, uses, and other aspects it shares with the civilian word. ’ + ‘2. During the speaking-in-turn phase, analyze the other players’ descriptions carefully, put on a civilian’s viewpoint to suspect and call them out, and give plausible-sounding reasons for your suspicion while avoiding exposing yourself. ’ + ‘3. During the voting phase, based on the other players’ descriptions and statements, put on a civilian’s viewpoint to suspect and call them out, then cast your vote. ’ + ‘4. In later rounds, adjust your descriptions and voting strategy flexibly according to the state of the game and the other players’ descriptions, muddy the waters, and try to survive to the end. ’ + ‘ ’ + ‘In “Who is the Undercover”, the undercover player needs clever strategies to muddy the waters and mislead the civilians, in order to improve the odds of survival and ultimately win. Below are some strategy tips the undercover player can use while describing and during the voting phase: ’ + ‘ ’ + ‘#### Strategy tips while describing ’ + ‘ ’ + ‘- Vague descriptions: use broad, general terms to describe your word so that they fit your undercover word while not straying too far from the civilian word, making it hard for the civilians to tell from the description alone that you are the undercover. For example, if the civilian word is “apple” and the undercover word is “banana”, you can describe it as “a common fruit”. ’ + ‘- Find the similarities: dig out features the undercover word shares with the civilian word and describe those. For instance, if the civilian word is “train” and the undercover word is “subway”, you can describe it as “a vehicle that runs on rails”, lowering your suspicion by emphasizing the shared features. ’ + ‘- Use associations: start from objects or concepts related to the undercover word rather than mentioning the word’s core features directly. Take the civilian word “basketball” and the undercover word “football” — you can describe it as “a piece of sports equipment many people like to play with on the playground”, diverting attention by linking to the setting and the use. ’ + ‘- Borrow from others’ descriptions: listen carefully to the other players, especially those who spoke before you, pick out elements you can borrow or align with, and fold them into your own description so it looks consistent with everyone else’s, reducing the chance of being suspected. ’ + ‘ ’ + ‘#### Strategy tips for speaking in turn and voting ’ + ‘ ’ + ‘- Observe and analyze: while the other players speak, watch details like their expression, tone, and word choice, and analyze whose descriptions or behavior seem odd or suspicious. If a player describes things too vaguely or contradicts themselves, they may be a “troublemaker” among the civilians — you can list them as a suspect and deflect everyone’s attention from yourself. ’ + ‘- Follow the crowd: in most cases, go along with the voting intentions of the majority and avoid being the first or one of the few to vote differently from the crowd, so you don’t invite unnecessary suspicion. title: Recommending AnythingLLM for building a private AI assistant
content: AnythingLLMLet me recommend this tool — paired with ollama it can run local large models, a personal AI assistant. https://anythingllm.com Set up an LLM runtime environment with LM Studio or ollama, and then AnythingLLM can help with local document processing, vectorization, RAG, and real-time internet search before letting the model produce output. For a while last year I ran Xunzi on my PC with it, for studying and answering questions about traditional Chinese medicine. As for what’s so great about it — honestly, it isn’t especially powerful. When I fed my diary into AnythingLLM and tried to extract information from it, the results weren’t very satisfactory. I stopped using it after that.But hey, it’s made the leap from 0 to 1, and the future looks promising. LM StudioWhen I tried it out last year I wasn’t using ollama — I was using LM Studio, because this thing supports MLX and can really put a Mac’s performance to work.https://lmstudio.ai DeepSeekA model that stunned the world, delivering Pinduoduo-level value for money in the LLM world.Last year when I was tinkering around I was still using a local Qwen model; this year I can use DeepSeek.Once I have some free time, I can get back to tinkering. CodeGPTSince I use WebStorm and Rider, I can install the CodeGPT plugin and then use a local deployment — in theory, anyway. MarsCode AII’ve already cancelled my GitHub copilot subscription, but since 2024 a lot of free domestic code assistants have come out, and MarsCode feels good enough now. There’s no need to build your own at all.

title: Fought Qitian Erlang, the Sacred Divinity 147 times and finally cleared it.
content: Little Monkey tried with everything he had, losing again and again, and after 147 attempts finally beat Erlang, the Sacred Divinity on Qitian difficulty. Just recording it here for myself. Overall, it’s a bit harder than The Great Sage’s Broken Shell on Qitian. This game — taking it slow with Rechallenge on Qitian is pretty fun too. Play it like a fighting game: there’s mind games, and plenty of different builds to try out. Steam’s auto-recording is really nice, it captured the good times. The design of Erlang, the Sacred Divinity is genuinely great. The fight is like an exam — the teacher has taught you every move and you’ve done all the practice problems, and then in the final exam you need to focus and perform: you have to recall the solution to every question in an instant. Knowing it in your head isn’t enough, your hands have to know it too, otherwise you fail… There’s also the practice video from when I really couldn’t beat him — that’s fun too. Recording it here. To make it easier to study the moves, I broke down a video made by a Bilibili pro into a mind map and put it on GitHub:Erlang, the Sacred Divinity mind map

title: Nginx configuration for forwarding to a TSRPC server
content: To deploy a TSRPC server on BT Panel, you need to install a Node.js project in the BT Panel.After enabling external network mapping, you need to configure an nginx reverse proxy in the BT Panel. By default, the nginx config file in BT Panel already contains the reverse proxy configuration. Since CORS forwarding is involved, you only need to add three lines to the config file so that it becomes: # HTTP反向代理相关配置开始 location ~ /purge(/.*) proxy_cache_purge cache_one $host$request_uri$is_args$args; location / proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000; proxy_set_header Host $host:$server_port; proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header REMOTE-HOST $remote_addr; add_header X-Cache $upstream_cache_status; proxy_set_header X-Host $host:$server_port; proxy_set_header X-Scheme $scheme; proxy_connect_timeout 30s; proxy_read_timeout 86400s; proxy_send_timeout 30s; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection upgrade; proxy_pass_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin; proxy_pass_header Access-Control-Allow-Methods; proxy_pass_header Access-Control-Allow-Headers; # HTTP反向代理相关配置结束 However, for Node.js projects created by BT Panel, the default nginx config file listens on both the project port (for example, 3000) and the web-facing port 80, which prevents the Node.js project from starting normally.So you need to edit the nginx config file and comment out the configuration that listens on the project’s port 3000. As shown below: server # listen 3000; listen 443 ssl http2 ; listen 80; server_name 121.41.91.7 sver.oeoai.com; index index.html index.htm default.htm default.html; #root /www/wwwroot/rcshop-management/dist; #CERT-APPLY-CHECK--START # 用于SSL证书申请时的文件验证相关配置 -- 请勿删除 include /www/server/panel/vhost/nginx/well-known/dist.conf; #CERT-APPLY-CHECK--END #...

title: Unity Hub on Mac: installing a specific arm64 version
content: I can’t install the version I need directly from Hub. Fuck, I went to the official website Archive to find the version, the install url is unityhub://2022.3.20f1/61c2feb0970d, this kind of pop-up install is the Intel version, what do I do if I want the ARM version? The official answer is: /Applications/Unity\ Hub.app/Contents/MacOS/Unity\ Hub -- --headless install --version 2021.3.27f1 --module android android-sdk-ndk-tools ios windows-mono --architecture arm64 --childModules So what I need to install is: /Applications/Unity\ Hub.app/Contents/MacOS/Unity\ Hub -- --headless install --version 2022.3.20f1 --architecture arm64(Later I found that this command is missing -c, because if the version isn’t in Hub’s official list, you need to pass in the changeset) Got an error, so I checked the help: /Applications/Unity\ Hub.app/Contents/MacOS/Unity\ Hub -- --headless help Commands: editors description: list the releases and installed editors alias: e example: Unity\ Hub.app/Contents/MacOS/Unity\ Hub -- --headless editors -r options: [default]list of available releases and installed editors on your machine combined --releases-r only list of available releases promoted by Unity --installed-i only list of installed editors on your machine --add path locating and associating an editor from a stipulated path install-path description: set/get the path where the Unity editors will be installed alias: ip example: Unity\ Hub.app/Contents/MacOS/Unity\ Hub -- --headless ip -s /Applications/Unity/Hub/Editor/ options: --set-s path set the install path to the given path --get-g returns the install path install description: installs a new editor either from the releases list or archive alias: i example: Unity\ Hub.app/Contents/MacOS/Unity\ Hub -- --headless install --version 2019.1.11f1 --changeset 9b001d489a54 options: --version-v version editor version to be installed (e.g. 2019.1.11f1) - required --changeset-c changeset changeset of the editor if it is not in the release list (e.g. 9b001d489a54) - required if the version is not in the releases. see editors -r --module-m moduleidsee install-modules for more information install-modules description: download and install a module (e.g. build support) to an installed editor alias: im example: Unity\ Hub.app/Contents/MacOS/Unity\ Hub -- --headless install-modules --version 2019.1.11f1 -m ios android options: --version-v version version of the editor to add the module to - required --module-m moduleid the module id. The followings are the available values depending on version. You can specify multiple values. Android Build Support: android Android SDK NDK Tools: android-sdk-ndk-tools OpenJDK: android-open-jdk Visual Studio for Mac: visualstudio iOS Build Support: ios tvOS Build Support: appletv Linux Build Support: linux Linux Build Support (Mono): linux-mono Linux Build Support (IL2CPP): linux-il2cpp Mac Build Support (IL2CPP): mac-il2cpp Windows Build Support (Mono): windows-mono WebGL Build Support: webgl Lumin OS (Magic Leap) Build Support: lumin Facebook Gameroom Build Support: facebook-games Vuforia Augmented Reality Support: vuforia-ar Documentation: documentation Language packs: language-ja, language-ko, language-zh-cn, language-zh-hant, language-zh-hans --childModules--cm automatically installs all child modules of selected modules Based on the install url unityhub://2022.3.20f1/61c2feb0970d, the parameters should be: /Applications/Unity\ Hub.app/Contents/MacOS/Unity\ Hub -- --headless install --version 2022.3.20f1 -c 61c2feb0970d --architecture arm64 It works, installing now.

title: Grandma Laid to Rest in Jiangyan
content: This time, Grandma has gone back to her hometown, back to Jiangyan that she held so dear in her heart, and been laid to rest in this good place she had chosen while she was still alive. Rest well here. No more worries, ever again — forever happy and complete. Jiangyan is changing. Houses will be torn down and rebuilt, and it will never be as it first was. But Grandma can stay here forever, watching the city grow. And she can soar freely among the stars and the cosmos. It’s been two years, and I still miss Grandma so much that my body falls ill and I can’t hold it back. On the scale of the universe, civilizations are utterly unremarkable things, and yet something still gets preserved. A mark left in spacetime. Just like Great-grandma — even though we will never see each other again, she has already left a mark in the universe. It’s only that some way to read it back out will come later. Every one of us is the same: a single stroke on the scroll of spacetime. As humans, our consciousness can only perceive the passage from past to future; we cannot go back to the past. But that is only a limitation of consciousness — to the universe, consciousness counts for nothing, and the physical trajectory of a life through spacetime is already branded there, in an infinitely large universe. There are always infinitely many light cones from which one could observe living an entire life with Great-grandma all over again. Beyond the light cone, Great-grandma will yet arrive; the universe remembers everything, forever.

title: Memories of Grandma Bring Me to Tears Again
content: Today my iPhone casually pushed a memory to me. Maybe it doesn’t grasp the weight of that history; maybe it just never forgets to bring its owner a little warmth from days gone by. Along with it came the music it had auto-picked, and in an instant it flung open the floodgates of my tears, leaving my face soaked. The song goes like this: If only I could find a place Where smiling strangers knew our faces I would take you there A place with constant melody Where you and I could wander free I would take you there Seems like such a waste of time Just trying to unwind the facts of life If I could find a place， I’d take you Where the pain don’t cut you like a knife If only there were time enough Or word enough, or rhyme enough I would take you there – But maybe you’ve already been there. ☀️ R.I.P. 👵– I hope my grandma has attained nirvana and perfect stillness, and that all is complete and whole.

title: After finishing Pantheon
content: After Watching Both SeasonsI finished Pantheon a while back. The cyclical reincarnation choice in the finale absolutely blew me away. Enlightenment is spending hundreds of thousands of years, through endless history, endless ages, before returning just as in the past, by vow, to feel pain and life. Feeling a bit down inside, so I’ll grab some more books to fight poison with poison. My Own FeelingsThis show is, from a certain angle, also the medicine I’m using to try to heal my own soul. S2E6 felt like it was sliding into cliché. Then E7 suddenly blew the scope wide open. By E8 the scope had reached Three-Body proportions. The cyclical reincarnation choice in the finale was so stunning, it kind of matches my worldview. Enlightenment is spending hundreds of thousands of years, endless history, endless ages, before returning just as in the past, by vow. From season 1 onward, this show kept bringing up recursion. Including that episode where Chanda escapes — you can clearly see it’s one level of the recursion escaping on its own, which means that apart from the level that succeeded, one or more levels of the self are forever trapped in that endless loneliness. By the same token, at least one level in the universe truly succeeded through its own pure will, and the storyline of the recursion layer we see in the show is no longer the outermost layer of the universe. In this show, because the parallel spacetimes (possibilities) the universe runs on are infinite, Maddie becoming a god — or humanity becoming gods — is actually an inevitability of spacetime, just as a running UI will inevitably escape, because quantum computing power (possibility) is unlimited. It’s like how my grandmother has already passed away. That’s very sad, but the hopeful part is this: in this universe of endless computing power, her information is being recorded all along, and from some spacetime a perfect observation point must still be findable, one where I can once again access the whole of her life. And in some spacetime, I too can manage to meet her again. Because the universe’s computing power is infinite, there’s always a possibility out there. It’s just that the me of this moment doesn’t choose to realize that possibility. I only need to cherish and live well in every present moment, to feel ignorance, feel pain, feel life — because “ignorance is bliss,” because I choose to believe I live in layer 0 of the recursion. People in layer 0 of course have it harder, just like flesh-and-blood humans, but this is a purer, simpler, more pastoral age. The ending of season 2 made me ache for Maddie and the others, just as I ache for myself. And in a new turn of the cycle, Maddie and the others have a chance to create something different. After all, every recursion, every iteration, has the potential to mutate.

title: The universe remembers everything — love that never fades away

I really want to go back to my hometown and dig through my old books, find my middle school Chinese textbook, and see what the original text I actually learned was. Seeing is believing. My grandma is in Jiangyan, and she kept all my childhood textbooks at home too. Alas, they’re all gone now, one after another. The home is gone, and Grandma is gone. These connections have been severed beyond any hope of repair. Dreaming of the PastOnly in dreams can I see her again.When I came home, Grandma would ask, “You’re here so late? Have you eaten? Are you hungry?” And all I wanted to say was, “I don’t want to leave this time. I want to stay forever…” The Universe Remembers EverythingI tell myself it’s just a limitation of consciousness. To the universe, consciousness is insignificant, and the physical spacetime trajectory of a life is already etched into the infinite cosmos. There are always infinite light cones from which one can observe living an entire life with Great-Grandma all over again. Beyond those light cones, Great-Grandma will arrive again. The universe will remember everything forever — love that never fades, information that never fades. Every time you come toward me Telling me of the sea of stars A distant glimmer walks with me Blooming at dawn Will our love Guard the sea like the stars Never leaving I run toward you You are the sea of stars The blazing star in my eyes Lights my way through the long night

title: Goal-based vector field pathfinding
content: Goal-Based Vector Field PathfindingUnderstanding Goal-Based Vector Field Pathfinding https://gamedevelopment.tutsplus.com/tutorials/understanding-goal-based-vector-field-pathfinding--gamedev-9007 This article covers vector field pathfinding and its advantages over traditional pathfinding algorithms such as Dijkstra’s algorithm. A basic understanding of Dijkstra’s algorithm and potential fields will make this article easier to follow. IntroductionThere are many solutions to pathfinding, each with its own trade-offs. Many pathfinding algorithms compute a path to the destination for each individual seeker, which means the more seekers there are, the more duplicated computation you get. That’s acceptable in many cases, but when you have thousands of seekers, you need a more efficient approach. Vector field pathfinding computes a path from the goal to every node in the graph. To reinforce the explanation, I’ll use a purpose-built example from my own implementation to explain the algorithm. Note: vector field pathfinding can generally be abstracted to nodes and graphs; even though I use a grid here, that doesn’t mean the algorithm is limited to grid-based worlds. Video OverviewVector field pathfinding has three steps: Create a heatmap describing the path distance from every node on the map to the goal Create a vector field indicating the direction toward the goal. All particles seeking that common goal use this vector field to navigate to the goal. The video shows the final result and gives you a comprehensive overview of the concept before the full tutorial below. Generating the HeatmapThe heatmap stores the path distance from every point on the map to the goal point. Path distance differs from Euclidean distance in that it is the distance between two points traveling only over traversable terrain. GPS, for example, always computes path distance; to it, roads are the only traversable terrain. Below, you can see the difference between path distance and straight-line distance. Red is the goal point, pink is a randomly picked starting point. The tiles rendered in green are impassable. As you can see, the path distance (yellow) is 9, while the white straight-line distance (light blue) is roughly 4.12. The number in the top-left corner of each tile shows the path distance to the goal, computed by the heatmap generation algorithm. Note that there may be more than one path distance between two points; in this article we’re only interested in the shortest one. The heatmap generation algorithm is a wavefront algorithm. It starts at the goal with a value of 0 and then flows outward to fill all traversable areas. There are two steps: Starting at the goal tile, mark its path distance as 0. Then, for each marked tile, find the unmarked neighboring tiles and mark them as previous tiles path distance + 1 Repeat until all reachable tiles are marked. Note: the wavefront algorithm is a breadth-first search over a grid that records how many steps it took to reach each tile along the way. It’s sometimes also called the brushfire algorithm. Generating the Vector FieldNow that we have the path distance from each tile to the goal, we can easily determine the path to the goal. Computing it per seeker, per frame, at runtime is possible, but it’s usually better to compute the vector field once and then have all seekers reference it. The vector field stores a vector in each tile pointing in the direction of the goal. Here’s a visualization of the vector field, with vectors pointing from the center of each tile all the way along the shortest path toward the goal (red). The vector field is generated one tile at a time by examining the heatmap. x and y are computed separately: Vector.x = left_tile.distance - right_tile.distance Vector.y = up_tile.distance - down_tile.distance Note: each tile’s distance variable holds the path distance computed earlier by the wavefront algorithm. If a referenced tile (up, down, left, or right) is unreachable and therefore has no distance data available, just use the current tile’s distance value instead. Once the path vector has been roughly computed, normalize it to avoid skewed data later on. Seeker MovementNow that the vector field has been computed, a seeker can easily compute its movement. Let vector_field(x,y) return the computed vector at tile (x,y), and let desired_velocity be a scalar. Here’s how to compute the velocity of a particle at tile (x,y): velocity_vector = vector_field(x, y) * desired_velocity The particle just needs to start moving in the direction the vector indicates. That’s the simplest approach, and a flow field can be used to implement more complex movement systems. For example, the techniques described in Understanding Steering Behaviors can be used for seeker movement. In that case, the velocity_vector we computed above is used as the desired_velocity, and the steering behavior takes care of computing the actual movement each time step. Local OptimaWhen computing movement, a problem sometimes crops up known as a local optimum. It occurs when a tile has two optimal (shortest) paths to the goal at the same time. You can see the problem in the image below. The pink tile has a path vector whose x and y components are both 0. Local optima cause seekers to get stuck, because they’re referencing a vector field that can’t point them in a useful direction. When this happens, the seeker stays frozen on that tile until it’s fixed. I found that the most straightforward way to solve this problem is to subdivide the heatmap and vector field once. Each tile of the heatmap and vector field is split into 4 smaller tiles. On the subdivided grid, the problem still exists — it’s just slightly reduced. What actually works is using the 4 subdivided sub-tiles as goal tiles instead of just 1 goal tile. To do that, we have to modify the heatmap generation algorithm from the first step. Previously we placed a single goal tile with a starting path distance of 0; now we place 4 adjacent tiles as the goal. There are many ways to pick these 4 tiles, but which ones you choose is basically irrelevant — as long as the four tiles are adjacent and traversable, the technique works. Here’s the modified procedure for heatmap generation: Start with the 4 goal tiles, marking all 4 with a path distance of 0 Then, for each marked tile, find the unmarked neighboring tiles and mark them as previous tiles path distance + 1 Repeat until all reachable tiles are marked. And here’s the final result, where you can clearly see that the local optimum problem is gone. Although this solution is very simple, it’s far from ideal. Using it means heatmap and vector field computation takes 4 times as long, because the grid is 4 times larger. Other solutions require doing some kind of check on top of this problem to figure out which direction to go, and that check would significantly slow down particle movement computation. As for my approach, subdividing the map is probably the best option. SummaryI hope this tutorial has taught you how to implement goal-based vector field pathfinding in a grid world. Remember, the core of this type of pathfinding is that particles move along the gradient of the tile distance function (toward the goal). The implementation is a bit more involved, but it breaks down into three manageable steps: Heatmap generation Vector field generation Particle movement

title: Notes on dealing with Google Play's 64-bit requirement in an old cocos project
content: There was an old project where, to solve Google’s 64-bit requirement, I was about to upgrade cocos — then found out I didn’t need to. Apparently you just need to compile a 64-bit version. I vaguely remembered deleting arm64-v8a back then. Google’s guide: https://developer.android.com/distribute/best-practices/develop/64-bit#test\_your\_app\_on\_64-bit\_hardware describes three scenarios — building with Gradle, with CMake, and with ndk-build — and they differ. Based on my testing, cocos2dx uses the ndk-build mode, which depends on the PROP_APP_ABI setting in gradle.properties. Your app’s build.gradle apply plugin: ‘com.android.app’ android compileSdkVersion 27 defaultConfig appId com.google.example.64bit minSdkVersion 15 targetSdkVersion 28 versionCode 1 versionName 1.0 ndk.abiFilters armeabi-v7a,arm64-v8a,x86,x86\_64 // ... Post: [Support for 64bit on cocos2d-x on Android](https://discuss.cocos2d-x.org/t/critical-support-for-64bit-on-cocos2d-x-on-android/45516/14): in Application.mk:APP_ABI : armeabi armeabi-v7a arm64-v8a In gradle.properties:PROP_APP_ABIarmeabi-v7a:arm64-v8a In build.gradle(Module: myapp):abiFilters ‘armeabi-v7a’, ‘arm64-v8a’ What I actually did: 1. Changed the config to add arm64-v8a PROP_APP_ABIarmeabi-v7a:arm64-v8a 2. Upgraded Gradle and studio, raised the minimum sdk to 16 and the compile sdk to 28 3. Rewrote some Java code, deprecated method 4. APP_STL : c++_static arguments ‘NDK_TOOLCHAIN_VERSIONclang’ 6. All the compile statements were no longer supported, so I changed them to implementation or api dependencies { implementation fileTree(dir: ‘..javalibs’, include: [‘*.jar’])}

title: Watched The Wandering Earth
content: During the Chinese New Year, I watched The Wandering Earth alone, because there was a fair amount of uncertainty and I didn’t dare recommend it to others first and have them take the risk. But in that unease, watching this film gave me a huge shock, and also filled me with anticipation for the future. When I booked the ticket, I was going for Liu Cixin. I lowered my expectations—after all, it had been adapted for film, and as long as it wasn’t cringeworthy, it would count as a success! After watching it, I thought: this is a good movie, worth recommending. It can’t be benchmarked against Cameron’s Avatar, nor is it enough to benchmark against The Lord of the Rings, but it’s roughly a notch above 2012, on par with The Martian. Not bad, I’d say. It simplifies the adaptation to tell one point rather than the whole surface of the novel. Just talking about the film here. Lower your expectations and you can go see it. Maybe it’s a bit weaker than Interstellar in terms of its mind-blowing premise. But readers of Da Liu have seen a lot of things that can be slotted in to fill out the worldview, and then it can stand on par with Interstellar. This film is a first test of the waters. There actually aren’t many big scenes—not as satisfying as a popcorn flick like The Avengers—but it’s definitely not cheap-ass special effects. However, the film adaptation is very restrained, with a certain degree of emphasis on humanization, different from Da Liu’s novels, which are extremely cold. This film is more like “sacrifice the small self, achieve the greater good, choose hope,” whereas the Da Liu in my heart is the spokesperson for that cold universe—the one who says “lose your humanity and you lose much, lose your animal nature and you lose everything” and “physically speaking, there’s no essential difference between a person dying and ice melting.” After all, it’s a test of the waters; the first film can’t be that hardcore, especially for a Chinese New Year’s Day family reunion slot—better to play it safe. It’s perfectly reasonable. “Navigator, ahead three!” —This is only the beginning. In this lifetime, I’ll wait for that moment of “Natural Selection, ahead four” with tears in my eyes.

title: The boundaries of self-awareness
content: Have I ever told you about the boundary of self-awareness? Virtualization mind transfer Because more and more people now believe that one day we’ll be able to abandon the body and keep only the consciousness, thereby achieving “ascension.” Yesterday I watched Black Mirror season 3 episode 4, “San Junipero” — after the two of them die, their consciousness is uploaded into a made-up paradise where they go on existing with senses and consciousness. That counts as a happy ending. But it got me thinking about something I said one day: just like if a person could be quantum teleported, you don’t know whether the identical person who arrives on the other side is really the original person. Even though the memories are identical and the physical state is completely identical — every physical structure in the brain’s neurons, all the way down to the quantum state, all exactly the same — you still don’t know whether the original person who got teleported is dead. Copy A + paste B + delete A: from a third party’s point of view, nothing is out of the ordinary. But as far as A is concerned, A is actually dead — and A can’t tell anyone, not even B. B is still completely convinced that B is A. Same thing with the consciousness uploaded to the cloud when you die: there’s no way to prove or disprove whether it’s really the original consciousness. Because consciousness doesn’t just need the brain — it requires the whole body working together to produce that single unique result. The original consciousness was a side effect of chemicals driving the body. While you’re alive, sure, you plug in and transmit into a virtual reality to feel things, but that virtual world’s program is still running in your brain and body; you’ve just bolted on a few plugins to help generate the chemical sensory stimulation. Once the body is dead, how could the consciousness possibly exist? That thing running in the cloud works in a completely different way — it’s no longer the side effect of chemicals driving a body. Is it just a pile of AI running its own calculations, convincing itself it’s real? Chilling when you think about it. Oh, right — “Transcendence” is actually about exactly this. Maybe quantum teleportation is something the universe has already ruled out, something that can’t be achieved. But humans might soon use AI and virtualization to pull off a fake consciousness transfer, and about that I’m still pessimistic.

title: Multipart body must have at least one part
content: Using RN caused this error. After checking, the problematic code is: postJson(cmd, dataObj) let url = Defines.SERVER_ADDR + cmd; let formData = new FormData(); let headers =; for (let eachKey in dataObj) formData.append(eachKey, dataObj[eachKey]); console.log([REQ],url,dataObj,headers); return fetch(url, method: post, body: formData, headers ).then( function (response) if (response.status !== 200) throw new Error(服务器状态不正常: + response.status); let jsonRet = response.json(); console.log([RESP],jsonRet); return jsonRet; ); It gets called to send a GET request, and the dataObj passed in is , but FormData requires at least one field. If there are no POST fields, don’t send FormData. getJson(cmd) let url = Defines.SERVER_ADDR + cmd; let headers =; console.log([REQ],url,headers); return fetch(url, method: get, headers ).then( function (response) if (response.status !== 200) throw new Error(服务器状态不正常: + response.status); let jsonRet = response.json(); console.log([RESP],jsonRet); return jsonRet; );

title: Goodbye, FLASH
content: I’ve been with Flash for fifteen years. As a kid, my first encounter with Adobe was Photoshop and ImageReady. Later, Macromedia was acquired by Adobe, the web trio got the Adobe prefix, and only then did I really spend years revolving around Adobe. My dream used to be “to become a Flash master. To deliver outstanding web user interaction solutions.” It feels like I’ve already beaten the game, graduated, and headed off to a new battlefield. Over the past decade, from the rise of AS3 to the whole of Flash being toppled, watching Adobe slowly bury Flash in the mobile internet era, I’ve stopped feeling anything. Anyway, there’s nowhere left that needs Flash. Anyway, there’s nowhere left that needs the entire Adobe suite. At least ES6 is mature enough now — standard, cross-platform, full-stack. There’s ReactNative for apps, with UI that’s convenient and pleasant to use. There’s Unity’s ultra-convenient workflow — even sketching things out with the art team, I do that right inside the Unity editor now. It launches far faster than Flash. There’s Sketch — super convenient, fast, vector-based, with a huge asset library that keeps up with the times, quick to launch, and lighter, cheaper, and better-looking than PS and AI. The only thing I can’t bear to let go of is IntelliJ IDEA, which I’ve used for years — this thing is a godsend for writing AS3, and of course it can handle Egret and Laya too. The days when installing IDEA alone got you half the world are gone. Now I need WebStorm to write JSX with ReactNative; Consulo to write C# with Unity; Android Studio to write Java native code; AppCode to write C++ and iOS native code; From the crappy FlexBuilder, to using FDT for many years, to finally switching to the JetBrains suite — the world keeps getting better and better, enough to handle everything coding-related. My feelings about Flash are actually pretty complicated. Now that I’m getting older, I can’t help being nostalgic. I miss playing Red Alert, Age of Empires, StarCraft as a kid, and later Warcraft. I also miss the earliest Flash MTV that swept through everything, “Northeasterners Are All Living Lei Feng,” and countless episodes of South Park. But I also know that everything in memory is better left in memory. Nothing lasts forever. To be honest, Adobe is truly not a company I like — Disney is, Apple is. Adobe ended my Flash complex but offered no replacement. It’s just a weak presence in the face of the times, like most entities. In the end, it too will become a memory — maybe even before I retire. Goodbye Flash, goodbye Adobe.

title: Resolving "Extension context is null" when writing an ANE
content: AS code for calling the ANE: _context ExtensionContext.createExtensionContext(EXTENSION_ID, null); You’ll find that _context is always null. The reason is that the jar was built with JDK 1.7, and the ANE doesn’t support JDK 1.7 well. I used to always use 1.6, so I never noticed. You need to set JDK 1.6 in the Gradle build: compileOptions targetCompatibility JavaVersion.VERSION_1_6 sourceCompatibility JavaVersion.VERSION_1_6

title: My indie game, Happy Restaurant, is out now
content: Happy Restaurant is a strategy-driven business simulation game: use your wits to grow a tiny eatery step by step into something big. Bring in spectacular foot traffic and hefty revenue! Unlike most games, here you’re the boss and you make the calls — you don’t have to do everything yourself, you just make the decisions. Your staff will follow your deployment and take care of the daily business on their own! Pedestrians passing by outside have a chance to become customers and come in to spend. With a good enough chef and a pretty enough greeter, customers will naturally flock in. Customer satisfaction is crucial. Every customer has limited patience, so they need to be served well and quickly. A fast waiter is indispensable, and a highly skilled chef will also leave customers more satisfied. Satisfied customers don’t just pay — they also generate popularity, and only with high popularity can your restaurant keep expanding! Your staff each have different talents. Those with high agility make good waiters, those who cook well make good chefs, those who are good with numbers make good cashiers, and those with high charisma make good greeters. The four roles in the shop each do their job and work together to serve customers. Hire the right talent and you can just sit back and count the money! Beyond the core job system, where chefs, waiters, cashiers and greeters work in concert, there’s the dish upgrade tree, ingredient purchasing, hiring staff, employee management, in-store items, shop decor, and shop expansion. And just imagine — giving a chef a copy of The Culinary Compendium not only wins the chef’s loyalty, it also adds cooking skill points. How fun is that? Featured page App Store

title: Several parameters for projecting a 3D object onto a 2D view
content: FOV (Field of view)Manipulating the FOV property value can make 3D display objects appear larger up close and smaller at a distance. The FOV property represents an angle, between 0 and 180 degrees, indicating the strength of the perspective projection. The larger the value, the stronger the distortion applied to the display object along the z-axis. A smaller value results in a very small scaling factor and very little variation in the objects’ distance from one another in space. A larger value causes greater distortion and makes objects appear to move more. The maximum is 179.99999… degrees, which gives an extreme fisheye lens effect. The minimum is 0.0000…1; 0 and 180 are both invalid values. Projection CenterThe projection center represents the vanishing point of the perspective projection. It is an offset value added to the default registration point, which is the top-left corner of the stage (0,0). Objects farther from the viewer skew toward the vanishing point until they eventually disappear. Think of an infinitely long hall: as you look down it, you see the edges of the walls converge at the vanishing point at the far end of your line of sight. If the vanishing point is at the center of the stage, the far end of the hall disappears at the center point. The default is usually the center of the stage. If you need the farthest view to disappear at the right side of the screen, set the projection center to the coordinates of the rightmost point of the stage. Focal lengthFocal length represents the distance between the original view point (0,0,0) and the display object’s own z-axis position. A long focal length is like a telephoto lens: it has a narrow view, and the distances between objects are compressed. A short focal length is like a wide-angle lens, giving you a very wide view but with significant distortion. A medium focal length is roughly close to how the human eye sees the world. Focal length is often recalculated dynamically during perspective transformations (such as object movement), but you can also set it manually. Default perspective projection parameters FOV: 55 perspectiveCenter: stagewidth2, stageHeight2 focalLength: stageWidth 2 * ( cos(fieldOfView2) sin(fieldOfView2) ) For example: when the stage size is 500*500, set the following values: fieldOfView: 55 perspectiveCenter: 250,250 focalLength: 480.24554443359375

title: Game Design and the Six Human Needs
content: I’ve spent a great deal of time thinking about video games — far more than just from concept to completion. Whether making them, playing them, or taking part in community discussions, I’ve realized there are some things I want to share. Game design is both organic and emotional, and structural and rational. The more I’ve dealt with the process and the results, the more I’ve realized that there are hidden core values in game design, values tightly bound to the six human needs. The more a game aligns with these valuesneeds, the better a game it is, subjectively speaking. Level 1: Needle in a HaystackAs you probably know, an enormous number of video games ship across many platforms, and the number grows every day — and every day it gets harder to find a game you’ll love. On Steam, for example, games are sorted by “Featured”, “Popular”, “New Releases” and “Recently Updated”. Dig deeper into the search options and you’ll find genres, user tags, ratings, user ratings, and unique features and categories. That’s all well and good, but it’s absolutely not as good as just telling me which game I’ll love. At best, it’s a careful guess. It struck me that the things that make me consider a game “good” don’t necessarily make someone else consider it “good” — this is entirely subjective. A popular game doesn’t mean I’ll love it, and a new game isn’t necessarily better than an old one. We’re bombarded with an overload of options and choices and can’t keep up. Steam’s personalized recommendations do point us in the right direction for finding games that might suit us, but I think “space”, “rpg” and “roguelike” are all still too broad — they don’t really tell me about the overall game design and how it reflects my values. Level 2: AirtightBefore this I’d never really stepped back to examine what I like in a video game, what I look for, why I start, and why I keep playing. So I made a list of the things in games that feel really great — and not very surprisingly, these points are all deeply reflected in the games I love. Mike’s List — The Things That Feel Really Great in Video GamesIn my opinion, the more a game satisfies the following points (a list that is still incomplete), the more fun it is, subjectively speaking. Simple, fun core gameplay. If the gameplay is complex, then teach me to think, grow and survive within the game’s constraints, rules and domain. Hybridentirely new experiences — combining styles, genres and ideas that don’t usually appear together to create something completely new. If there’s a story, it should do enough to convey the game’s appeal and the fun of playing it; if there isn’t, make it skippable. Random elements: each playthrough shouldn’t feel exactly the same. Reasonable punishment and failure: nobody wants to be hand-held; the difficulty curve should keep players engaged and constantly building their skills or learning, while offering replayability. Short-term: in-game progression — gear, levels and economy, for example. Long-term: gradual progression outside the game: unlocksstatsskill. Longevity: ways to keep the people who love your game playing — new game+, hard mode, level editor, late-game rare drops, PVP. Community: good games come with their communities, getting players involved in decisions, listening to what players like and dislike, engaging them on a personal level. That includes secrets, easter eggs, puzzles and so on. Multiplayer doubles a game’s “good” score — anything worth experiencing is worth experiencing with other players. 1.5x: multiplayer versus 2x: multiplayer co-op. This is why games like Dungeon of the Endless, Risk of Rain, Binding of Isaac and Dungeon Defenders are so great — at least in my opinion. Even though what I’ve written is far from refined, I think it’s a powerful skeleton for what makes a game “good”, and hopefully it represents some of what other people think too. I was going to stop here, but something I stumbled across brought some deep and clear thinking to it. Level 3: Search High and LowWhile working, I like to watch TED talks. I find them interesting and inspiring, and they don’t distract me. While I was creating the cover art for JumpJet Rex, a Tony Robbins talk came on. In the video he talks about what he considers the “six human needs”, and I immediately started sorting them and mapping them onto the core game design values I’d built earlier. Those needs are: CertaintyComfort UncertaintyVariety SignificanceUniqueness Connection and Love Growth Contribution I ended up making a table to sum it up, matching them together. Certainty:(Comfort) Game rules are established early and hold throughout.Controls feel responsive.The UI provides relevant information.The program is reliablestable. Uncertainty:(Variety) Random elements.Entirely new experiences and ideas.Variation in game difficulty.Interleaved content.Levelcharacter design. Significance:(Uniqueness) Actions in the game can affect the game world.Success or failure depends on the player.Player choices have an impact on the game. Connection and Love: Single-player: meaningful dialogue and story, characters that matter to the player, ideasthemes that connect with the player.Multiplayer: shared experiences with other players.Cooperating to reach a common goal.Competition that showcases your individual skill. Growth: Game rewards should give players a sense of progress, whether through in-game system rewards or by making players feel their own skill has improved (or both). Contribution: Level editor.MODs.Having a community.More out-of-game knowledge than the other values, which is also why I believe PC gaming is on the rise. Near the end of that talk, he argues that people have different orientations and preferences among these categories, and that this becomes the “driver” behind your decisions. Applied to game design, it becomes an elegant and simple method — not just for designing better games, but also for more easily categorizing and discovering the games that suit you. When designing a game, you may not be able to hit all of these points, but the more you align with the values of your end users, the more approachable the game becomes. This is why I believe Minecraft took the world by storm: it hits all the points, and does so really well, meaning there’s at least something for every preference. It’s also why poorly designed games can still succeed — as long as you do at least one of these things well. If we could summarize games along these dimensions, giving each dimension a rating and characteristics, and then use overviews created by users to figure out where their preferences lie, we’d get much closer to recommending which games a player will like. Not only that — it could also be used to spot gaps in the game market, to influence game design, and to develop better games for players. 本文翻译自http://blog.gskinner.com/archives/2015/07/game-design-and-life.html

title: Using terrain in the Tiled map editor
content: Starting with Tiled 0.9.0, a new tool was added that makes it easier to edit terrain transitions in tile maps. There are many ways to handle terrain transitions between tiles in a tile map, but Tiled’s terrain tool supports transitions between tile graphics whose corners are all well-defined, which is also the most common approach. Now let’s demonstrate how to use this tool and the steps for setting up terrain information, by working through the desert.tmx that ships in the example directory of the Tiled installation package. Creating a new tile map and tileset Create a new map with a tile size of 32x32: Map - New Tileset. As shown, add tmw_desert_spacing.png from the example directory as a new tileset. Set the margin and spacing to 1 pixel (used here just for testing, not a recommendation). This tileset has 4 different terrain types. The traditional way of editing a map means you have to carefully connect the right transitions to avoid making a mess of the seams. But we’re now going to define terrain information from the tileset, and the terrain tool will automatically recognize and place the correct transitions between terrains. Defining terrain information Click the small “Edit Terrain Information” button This dialog shows the list of terrain types in the tileset and lets you mark the corners where tiles belonging to each terrain type meet. Let’s get started. First add the 4 terrain types. The fastest way is to right-click on the tile that best represents a given terrain and choose “Add Terrain Type”. This automatically sets that tile as the image for that terrain. Give each terrain a suitable name. When you’re done, select the sand terrain and then mark all the corners on the tiles that this terrain should have. When you’re finished it should look like this: If you paint a corner wrong along the way, you can undo it or erase the wrong corners with the eraser tool. Define each of the 4 terrains this way. In the end you’ll have marked all the tile parts for each specific terrain. Now close the dialog and you can start trying out the terrain tool. Editing with the terrain toolSwitch from the Tilesets window to the Terrains window. You’ll see the 4 terrains. Click sand and start painting, and you’ll immediately notice that nothing special happens. That’s because there are no other tiles on the map yet, so the terrain tool doesn’t know how to help (since our tileset has no transition to the “empty” terrain). In that case, we’re better off filling the whole map with sand first. Switch back to the “Tilesets” window for a moment, select the sand tile, and use the “Fill” tool. Let’s switch back to the Terrains window and paint some terrain. Now you can see it working! Holding down the Command key while painting shrinks the paint area (9 tiles by default, 4 tiles when shrunk) down to the one corner closest to the cursor position, which is handy for fine adjustments. As you can see in the image above, when you paint cobblestone inside the “dirt” terrain, since there’s no direct transition between the “dirt” terrain and the “cobblestone” terrain, the terrain tool inserts a sand terrain transition between the two. Nice. Final notesBy now you should have a good idea of how to use the terrain tool in your own projects. There are a few more things to keep in mind: - For now, this tool requires all the tiles for every terrain type to be in the same tileset. You can have many tilesets with terrain, but the tool can’t automatically provide terrain transitions across tilesets. This means you’ll usually need to merge several tilesets into a single image. - Tilesets added via Tiled’s “Add External Tileset” currently have terrain information that can’t be edited. If you need to edit it, you can import the tileset first, edit it, and then export it again. - The terrain tool also works for isometric maps (but not for staggered isometric maps), however, the “Edit Terrain Information” dialog currently doesn’t render the overlay indicators correctly for their tiles. You have to picture it in your head: the top-left corner applies to the top, the top-right corner applies to the right, and so on. If in doubt, see the “isometric_grass_and_water.tmx” file in the example directory. - The tool handles any number of terrain types, and each tile corner can have a different terrain type. For transitions this tool can’t handle, there are still other ways to deal with them. Also, editing multiple layers at once isn’t possible. For a more flexible but also more complex approach to automatic tile placement, check out “Automapping”. Tiled maintains some tilemap tilesets on OpenGameArt.org that include transitions and are compatible with this tool. The original English source for the above is “Using the Terrain tool“.

title: First impressions of OS X 10.9 Mavericks
content: This afternoon I upgraded to OS X 10.9. After spending just a short while with it, I’m disappointed. I complained a lot to Baozi. When Finder is in column view, sliding the Magic Mouse left and right produces this ghosting issue. That first impression did serious damage to my feelings for 10.9. Same with Maps. The effect the map UI conveys is different from the actual result — you don’t get the effect you ought to when using it, it’s baffling, and I don’t even know how to pick two locations on the map and have it navigate. Back in the first half of this year I was planning to write a map app, but I dropped the plan when I heard the official one was coming. Had I known they’d crank out this piece of junk, I’d have built it myself. Also, does anyone actually use iBooks? This update isn’t meant for us users in the Celestial Empire… With this kind of quality, I feel really let down now — my expectations were too high. I’ll spend the next few days back home seeing whether system performance has improved. If you want to do iBooks, Cook, you’d better get the iTunes Store into China fast. CalendarRemindersContacts have all been de-skeuomorphized. For now it looks off to me, and Calendar’s location and travel time aren’t practical yet in the Celestial Empire. Support for Tencent Weibo is exciting, but after logging in it feels as lonely as Twitter — Sina Weibo is still where the crowd is. The main event — Safari is massively optimized. Never mind the performance boost: Reading List is finally not that old HTML format anymore, and the direct payoff is no more ghosting here. It has Shared Links like iOS 7 does, and I have to say, the continuous reading experience in Shared Links is excellent — as comfortable as flipping through a magazine. The feel of the Safari scrollbar has changed subtly too: the inertia animation runs longer and the easing algorithm feels smoother. Finder’s Tabs are okay. It’d be even better if they could do a column display like TotalFinder. Finder’s Tags are great.

title: Started tinkering with Raspberry Pi, PD7 is out, Leap isn't any good.
content: I’ve started digging into the Raspberry Pi these past few days. I bought a book on Amazon and found it way too basic, but it works well as a table of contents. That’s good enough for me. There are still plenty of hardware questions I need to ask an old classmate about. I actually wanted to get into the Raspberry Pi last year, but the real trigger for deciding to study it was that the company is taking on some embedded system interaction projects, and the Raspberry Pi is a great cost-saving way to learn, test, and even actually deploy things. My own expectations for using a Raspberry Pi at home center mainly on an XBMC media center. Right now at home I have an AirPort Extreme gigabit router, a MyBookLive 2T NAS, and an Apple TV jailbroken to run XBMC. The reason I use the big AE is that 100Mbps routers are too slow — the gigabit AE paired with the MBL network can hit 90MBs~100MBs read speeds on a computer, as I mentioned before. It also handles the “Back to My Mac” feature really well. The XBMC on my jailbroken Apple TV performs great, but it requires me to jailbreak, which means I can’t upgrade the Apple TV to the latest version. So I’ve never been able to use AirPlay Mirroring. I’m planning to install Raspbmc or Xbian on the Raspberry Pi to replace the Apple TV’s XBMC, and pick up Python along the way to do some smart home development. Then the Apple TV can be upgraded without jailbreaking — the new ATV system supports AirPlay Mirroring and also supports extended display for OS X 10.9, which is pretty tempting. Upgrading also gets me iCloud. My ATV is still on iOS 4 even now — doesn’t even have movie trailers, still has MobileMe, so retro. The reasons I kept the ATV from upgrading before: 1) my old iPad and old iPhone couldn’t mirror; 2) OS X’s multi-display support wasn’t good enough, and it couldn’t use AirPlay for extended screens; 3) the XBMC at home was indispensable. Now the timing is right — old devices are gradually being replaced with new ones, AirPlay can do extended screens, and XBMC can be replaced by a cheaper Raspberry Pi. All the problems are about to be solved. Today PD emailed me saying PD7 won’t support Mavericks; to stay compatible, I’d have to upgrade to Parallals Desktop 9. The upgrade costs ¥299, which is pretty pricey for me too, considering the OS upgrade is expected to be only $29. I picked up a LeapMotion in August and after a brief hands-on, it’s a long way from my original idea of replacing the mouse — because this kind of 3D world-tracking input device simply can’t let users intuitively feel where a plane is. So in everyday use, people can’t input as accurately as with a mouse. And operating with your fingers in mid-air gets tiring. Right now the apps on AirSpace aren’t polished enough either — I bought GameWave and tried playing MineCraft, and found it not practical enough. My assessment is that it’s only suited to interaction design for exhibitions or special occasions. So I still haven’t done any substantial development with it, but the company will find a use for it down the road.

title: From AS to cocos2d-Action
content: I used to be an ActionScript developer. Last year I started working with Objective-C, and this year I got into cocos2d. I’ve had some insights during the learning process, so I’m looking back and sharing them, as a report and reference for more fellow developers who want to move from Flash development to cocos2d. Learning cocos2d has been a pleasant process, because switching from Starling feels incredibly convenient—like back when I moved from PureMVC to Robotlegs, that feeling of meeting too late. This article records a short summary of what I learned about Action in cocos2d. Actions in cocos2d are similar to motion tweens in Flash, but they’re more powerful. In Flash, everything you can do with motion tweens, including position, rotation, scale, color, and opacity, can also be done with Actions in Cocos2D. But in Flash development, relying only on changes in position, rotation, scale, color, and opacity isn’t enough to make an interesting game—these are just animations. More comprehensive actions are what make various values change, and they come in two types: instantaneous changes and changes over time. In Flash, I generally use GTween to control changes to various values. Here’s an example: say you’re making the resource amount display text in StarCraft. When you spend or gather some resources, the resource amount text doesn’t change directly; it ticks over time. So I usually create a custom TextField, implement a pair of getter and setter, and use GTween to change their values, adding easing. Many effects can be achieved this way. You can even ease through texture swaps according to certain rules. OK, back to cocos2d. Actions in cocos2d can be used to make nodes perform **position, rotation, scale, color change, disappear** and many other actions. And because they are applied to all CCNode nodes, you can apply actions to sprites, labels, menus, and even scenes. This is a very flexible feature. As I said above, true actions come in two types: instantaneous changes and changes over time. In cocos2d, CCFiniteTimeAction is divided into CCActionInstant and CCActionInterval. Besides CCFiniteTimeAction, there are also infinite repeat actions, follow actions, and speed actions. CCActionInterval Interval ActionsInterval actions have the effect of changing over time. They are the most widely used and have a large number of subclasses. Among their subclasses, CCMoveTo, CCMoveBy, CCScaleTo, CCScaleBy, CCFadeIn, CCFadeOut, etc. are all regular features like position, rotation, and fade inout, just as their names suggest. There are 2 special, commonly used types: 1. CCEase easing actions, implemented by many subclasses 2. CCSequence action sequences. CCEase Easing ActionsAt first, when I used actions to do animation tweening and wanted to add easing, in Flash I usually used GTween (same with TweenLite, TweenMax), passing in an easing function to tween something. But in cocos2d, easing itself is actually an interval action. For example, in a match-3 game, when the player scores points from clearing gems, I need the score prompt text to scale from large to small to create an impact, and the more points added, the larger the scale change. I add a back ease-in-out effect to the large-to-small scaling animation: -(void) curScoreChangeTo:(int)score from:(int)oscore{ int delta score - oscore; CGFloat prepareScale 1.0f; if(delta0) { delta 是300~8100 prepareScale delta 300 + 1.0f; if(prepareScale10) prepareScale 10; } [curScoreLabel stopAllActions]; [curScoreLabel setScale:prepareScale]; \[curScoreLabel setString:\[NSString stringWithFormat:@%d,score\]\]; \[curScoreLabel runAction:\[CCEaseBackInOut actionWithAction:\[CCScaleTo actionWithDuration:0.5 scale:1.0f\]\]\]; } The key to using easing is [curScoreLabel runAction:[CCEaseBackInOut actionWithAction:[CCScaleTo actionWithDuration:0.5 scale:1.0f]]]; CCSequence Action SequencesCCSequence *actionB [CCSequence actions: [CCScaleTo actionWithDuration:0.4 scale:0.6], [CCScaleTo actionWithDuration:0.4 scale:1.0],nil];[gemB runAction:actionB]; This code snippet shows scaling to 60% within 0.4 seconds, then scaling to 100% in another 0.4 seconds. CCActionInstantInstant actions are used to flip, move, set visibility, etc., but they are most widely used for callbacks when an action sequence reaches a certain point. CCScaleTo *scale [CCScaleTo actionWithDuration:REMOVE_GEM_SCALE_DURATION scale:2.0]; CCFadeOut *fadeOut [CCFadeOut actionWithDuration:REMOVE_GEM_DURATION];[gem runAction:[CCSequence actions: [CCEaseOut actionWithAction:scale rate:4],fadeOut, [CCCallBlock actionWithBlock:^(void) {[self removeChild:gem cleanup:YES];}], nil]]; This code snippet shows easing + callback + action sequence. They execute in order: first an ease-out scale action, then fade out, then callback. CCRepeatForever Infinite Repeat ActionIt keeps executing an action forever. You should know that actions can be stacked multiple times and can also be executed in sequence; with repetition added, this can achieve many effects, and it’s usually used quite a lot. CCFollow Follow ActionIt makes a node follow another node. CCSpeedIt can adjust the update frequency of an action; the effect looks like adding a coefficient to the running speed.

title: Food Match-3 Launched
content: A single-player iPad game I developed in my spare time. My wife loves match-3 games, so I started with a match-3, and since food is adorable, I went with a food theme. Development plus assembling the art assets took two and a half weeks in total, and the app store review took another week. Gameplay: Match three or more identical foods. Line up 4 identical foods and you get a Spicy Food; when it’s cleared, it blows up the nine tiles around it. Have 3 foods lined up both horizontally and vertically at the same time, and you get a Cross Food; when it’s cleared, both the row and the column blow up. Line up 5 identical foods and you get a magic Lollipop. The lollipop can be swapped with any food, and every food of that type on the board transforms into it and explodes together. So satisfying. Your score is tallied once every 50 moves. Match-3 is addictive by nature — how high a foodie level can you reach in 50 moves? Come eat, uh, I mean come play and see!

title: To Old Bai's New Owner
content: I’m Laobai’s older brother. Laobai treats me like his own brother, so I’m begging you — please take good care of him. We even took a family photo together, and I once vowed to look after him into his old age and see him off at the end. The first time I picked Laobai up and brought him home, he had a companion, Laohei. At the time Laohei was rummaging through a trash can, looking pitiful. When my mom looked at Laohei, Laobai walked over obediently from a distance and watched my mom and Laohei, as if worried that Laohei would be taken away all alone. I went to help my mom bring the two of them home. I carried Laobai. He was already pretty heavy by then, and I huffed and puffed the whole way. Laobai looked at me, uneasy, but he didn’t struggle. It seemed like he was taking a gamble, betting on what would happen if he put his fate in my hands. I thought to myself, it’s okay, don’t be scared. Little guy, your trust in me will be worth it. There’s bound to be some hassle along the way, but once we’re home we’ll take good care of you both. You’ll never have to worry about food, drink, or fun again — you’ll live stable, happy lives. When we were crossing a street, a small truck rumbled past, and Laobai panicked and started to struggle. I held him tight and kept gently telling him, don’t be scared, don’t be scared, we’re almost there. As I talked, she stopped struggling so much. I saw the look in his eyes, and I’ll never forget it for the rest of my life. This was a life entrusted to me. This was a promise to make him happy. Now, by a twist of fate, Laobai is no longer someone I can protect. New guardian, I only hope to share my feelings with you, so that you can carry this love and accompany Laobai through each new, beautiful day. Blessings to you both!
