title: ANE for opening the native Maps app and navigating on iOS 6
content: cn.flashj.ane.ios.OpenMap is a native extension for iOS that does one very simple thing: jump to the system’s built-in Maps app and navigate to a place. It provides 2 methods: openMap.routeFromSourceToDest(source, dest); navigates from source to dest. openMap.routeToDest(dest); navigates from the current location to dest. The source and dest parameters are both cn.flashj.ane.ios.MapItemVO, a class with three fields: latitude, longitude, and place name. Example usage: package cn.flashj.OpenMapTest { import cn.flashj.ane.ios.MapItemVO; import cn.flashj.ane.ios.OpenMap; import flash.display.Sprite; import flash.events.Event; public class OpenMap_test extends Sprite { private var openMap : OpenMap; public function OpenMap_test() { addEventListener(flash.events.Event.ADDED_TO_STAGE, onStage); } private function onStage(event : Event) : void { openMap new OpenMap(); var source : MapItemVO new MapItemVO(34.2657088225793, 108.948158127014, ‘钟楼’); var dest : MapItemVO new MapItemVO(34.21253, 108.973968, ‘大唐芙蓉园2’); openMap.routeFromSourceToDest(source, dest); openMap.routeToDest(dest); trace(“Open”); } } } Download link: ANE and packaged test code download

title: Error when packaging Adobe AIR with an ANE from an external SDK
content: Symptoms: Our project needed the ANE QR code scanning feature. After writing it in XCode with ZBarSDK and publishing it as an ANE, packing it into an IPA with adt threw this error: Packaging failed! Packaging error message: Compilation failed while executing : ld64 Packaging output: ld: warning: ignoring file varfoldersl5kql7svqx5j93vwg65tj3pt_c0000gnT8e0d5504-ffea-41da-a45b-22cfe260a197libcn.flashj.ane.ios.QRScan.a, file was built for archive which is not the architecture being linked (armv7): varfoldersl5kql7svqx5j93vwg65tj3pt_c0000gnT8e0d5504-ffea-41da-a45b-22cfe260a197libcn.flashj.ane.ios.QRScan.a Undefined symbols for architecture armv7: “_QRScanExtInitializer”, referenced from: _g_com_adobe_air_fre_fmap in extensionglue.o (maybe you meant: _QRScanExtInitializer_name) “_QRScanExtFinalizer”, referenced from: _g_com_adobe_air_fre_fmap in extensionglue.o (maybe you meant: _QRScanExtFinalizer_name) ld: symbol(s) not found for architecture armv7 At first I thought some project setting in XCode was wrong, and suspected libiconv wasn’t added correctly under “Link Binary With Libraries”, but after checking carefully it was fine, and all the required source files were already included in the target. Eventually I found the solution: Any ANE developed with external libraries needs an XML file that declares the external libraries it uses, like my platformoptions.xml here: An optional description 2012 (optional) \-liconv And add -platformoptions platformoptions.xml to the adt packaging parameters. Add -platformoptions platformoptions.xml to the adt packaging parameters and you’re done. By the way, here’s a great tool that works wonders for writing ANEs for iOS: XCode-template-ane.It’s an XCode template — just set the path to the SWC with the interface you use to generate the ANE and the AIR SDK path, and all that’s left is writing OC code. It handles the adt packaging steps for you and generates the ANE automatically in one click.

title: Inspire people, don't judge or give advice
content: I remember someone once told me: when you keep a cat, you have to remember to discipline it. Don’t let it develop bad habits—if it does something bad, you have to hit it. Spoiling it and pampering it the way you do? If it ever gets lost or ends up with someone else, and that person can’t stand it, they’ll just beat it to death. By indulging it, you’re the one hurting it. At the time I thought: if I can keep this cat for its whole life and indulge it for its whole life, why would I let someone else take it in? Why would I let people hate it and torture it to death? It’s like how people live. Someone gets bitten by a snake once, and not only are they afraid of a rope for ten years, they also go around forcing everyone else to be as wary as they are. But these things are different for everyone to begin with. The world each person can explore is limited, and others may never run into the difficulties you’ve faced. Just tell people your own stories of experience—there’s no need to force them into becoming you. Whenever you spot shortcomings in someone else, look at yourself first. Because when people feel the pain, they’ll change on their own; if you still haven’t changed, it’s just that it doesn’t hurt enough yet. The person you truly need to care about is yourself! Let your heart dwell inside yourself. Inspire people—don’t give them advice. I’ve met truly wise people, and they don’t judge what you do, nor do they hand you a solution to your problem. They just tell you stories to inspire you. Because they understand that everyone’s life is created by themselves. Judgment carries subjective emotion and is bound to be unfair; advice comes with suggestion, and if people follow it blindly, their life is no longer fully their own—it turns into something like copying someone’s homework; inspiration awakens a person’s confidence and wisdom and helps them create a unique life. The richer your life experience, the more stories you have to inspire others with. Every one of us is like a frog at the bottom of a well, each seeing our own patch of sky through the mouth of the well. There’s wind and rain, thunder and lightning, clouds and clear skies; there are sun, moon, and stars, waxing and waning. When we share that patch of sky through conversation, we can piece together the skies we each see, to inspire more individuals—without forcing others to learn to adapt to your patch of sky.

title: Beat StarCraft II: Heart of the Swarm
content: I finished Heart of the Swarm. The Zerg always struck me as filthy, cruel, bloodthirsty, and heartless. This expansion, on top of showing their take on life — constant evolution — also lets a hint of warmth show through, like broodmother Zagara not seizing power after Narud wounded Kerrigan, but instead letting her rest. And there’s Kerrigan’s emotional journey. The ending leaves you sighing. The final battle on Korhal: husband and wife, of one mind, taking down Mengsk. Victorious, Kerrigan says goodbye to Raynor — in those few words, sighs and laments; what she wants to say rises to her throat and gets swallowed back down. That’s how it is. Fate plays tricks. Long before, back when she decided to take revenge on Mengsk, when she resolved to avenge Raynor, it was already destined that they could never go back. I still remember Kerrigan, having just rescued Raynor, telling him: “I love you. Always remember.” I still remember Raynor storming out the door, saying, “We’re through.” Better to forget each other in the wide world than to keep each other alive, gasping. That girl wearing the Zerg’s ugly shell returns to the sky like a fairy. The camera pushes in, soaring through the stars, and a voice speaks: “I see the true enemy now. It waits in the distant void. It has power beyond anything I can imagine. I gave everything to find it — my humanity, my identity, even… the man I love.”

title: The first instant of thought ≠ the first idea
content: Last night after finishing a phone call with my mom, combined with some of the wisdom Lukia had shared with me before, I had some insights. I wrote them down during the night and organized them this morning. The master says: Whether you’re chanting Buddha’s name or handling affairs, always use the first thought, not the second thought. The true first thought is not the first idea that pops into your head — that first idea is just the consciousness of human nature’s curiosity. Like how many children’s first thought upon seeing ice cream is “I want to eat it,” but eating it might give them a stomachache. The consequences aren’t necessarily something they can afford. The master explains: “More often than not, it’s greed, it’s delusion. Don’t get it wrong. The so-called first thought is seeing your original nature, it’s the outflow of your true mind, your original face. Thoughts of craving food, craving comfort all belong to the deluded mind, the greedy mind — not the true mind.” There is a big house. In the basement of the house lives a giant dragon. It is the owner of the house, but it has been sleeping all along. The house has many servants and stewards. Under the head steward’s leadership, everyone keeps repairing and expanding the house, living their lives in perfect order. The owner has been asleep the whole time — all matters big and small are handled by the steward. As time passes, the steward mistakes himself for the owner and forgets that the true owner is sleeping. The steward is like our consciousness; the dragon is the original face (or you could say, the soul). Many people practice spiritually precisely to awaken the dragon, to recover true insight — only then can the first thought emerge. What does this mean for ordinary people like me, walking through the mundane world, chasing enjoyment and the fruits of karma? The Bodhisattva fears the cause; the ordinary person fears the result. People who are wise and follow their inner voice have an advantage over us when facing choices. The power of the true inner self is immense — it transcends time and space, it is omniscient. That is what’s called true insight. A true inner choice is planting the cause that will never make you regret — a cause that will inevitably produce a result in the future, and that result is something you can fully accept and fully take responsibility for. If you can’t bear the result, then you’ve already planted the wrong cause — and what follows will prove it wasn’t following your heart. If after planting the cause you keep wavering, frequently regret it, or even change your mind, then you haven’t figured out what your heart truly needs. So for those of us whose wisdom hasn’t yet opened, how do we find the true inner choice? In all things, you must first be calm before you can find what your heart truly wants. There’s still much to cultivate in daily life. A simple rule: what your true inner self wants is always an inevitable result — it doesn’t have complicated butterfly effects. Anything else — the roundabout, the unpredictable — is driven by deluded thoughts. Sometimes deluded thoughts even blind us, making us believe that some small immediate gain is what our heart truly wants. I don’t use “deluded thoughts” as a pejorative — there’s no praise or blame, only cause and effect. Deluded thoughts arise as causes, and you get deluded results. It’s just as described above: when such results manifest, you may not be able to bear them, and they may only add to your troubles — though of course, they also accumulate experience and open up wisdom. Once you know the pain, you can learn to let go. I live in a world of deluded thoughts, where gain and loss are impermanent, where there is joy and sorrow. Sometimes I marvel at my good luck, sometimes I feel the times are against me. Various unexpected appearances of happy or sad results often arise, and I find it fantastical and wondrous. It’s actually just like playing an online game — after reading the walkthrough and understanding all its possibilities, knowing that everything boils down to the same principle, you can still go in and play. When you get good gear, you’re happy; when your dungeon run wipes, you get flamed. There’s joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness — but at every moment you know this is just illusory appearances brought about by a bunch of data in a game. The emotions that arise are all temporary and will quickly dissipate and vanish. These too are perfectly ordinary and no big deal. Being able to know this at every moment — that brings you closer to your true inner self. We need to explore the inner self and uncover wisdom. Being compassionate and treating others with respect will continuously enrich our life experience and increase our wisdom.

title: Private Notes released
content: My first personal app, Private Notes, is now live on the App Store. From the first version submission to approval, including one rejection along the way, it took 10 days in total. Private Notes is a password-protected memo app I built for my own needs at work and in daily life. Back when I was a kid, my teacher taught me what Chairman Mao once said: “A good memory is no match for a worn-out pen.” That line has stayed with me ever since, and over the years I’ve put it into practice — if it’s worth remembering, I write it down. Now we’re in the information age, and I’m a heavy user of electronic devices. Going out without my phone cuts my HP and my mood in half. My important information — website accounts, security questions — all lives in my phone’s notes app, carried with me everywhere. Even my bank card details, my phone number’s PUK code, the serial numbers and MAC addresses of all my devices — all of it depends on my phone to remember. But phones are easy for other people to grab and play with. With everything stored on the phone, private data is easy for others to see, so a lot of the time I don’t dare write it down at all… Rely on my brain instead? Then I’d turn into that guy who’s always forgetting his accounts, passwords, security questions — and that’s a whole lot of trouble… By the time I can’t even remember my security questions, there’s no one to turn to and nowhere to hide, just standing there alone, weeping in despair. It’s agonizing. This kind of trade-off shouldn’t be something people have to pay for — technology should solve it! Phone notes can help, but they can also leak your data. So all we need is to keep the data confidential. That’s why I wanted a password-protected memo app: something that can safely store the sensitive information you wouldn’t want in the built-in notes app — network passwords, bank cards, private URLs, private accounts. This data is stored on the iPhone only in encrypted form. Without the password, it can’t be viewed, so even if the phone is lost there’s no risk of a leak. Someone without the password for Private Notes could be handed my phone, crack it open, pull out the data file, and all they’d get is a pile of gibberish. All I have to do is remember the password for Private Notes itself — when I lend my phone to someone, as long as Private Notes isn’t unlocked, I’m fine. Lock the phone or go back to the home screen at any time, and Private Notes locks itself automatically. I solved my own problem, and I figure there must be other people in the world with the same need. I hope this little tool can make things easier for more people. Features: ★ Secure password protection with the AES encryption algorithm, encrypting all text — without the correct password, the plaintext can’t be decrypted. ★ A cross-platform WIFI access mode: when the phone is connected to WIFI you can turn this mode on manually, and a computer on the same local network or any device that can open a web page (phone, tablet, etc.) can view and edit notes (also requires the password). Close the app on the iPhone at any time and the data is safely locked away in the phone again. Pull up your records anytime at the office; take them with you anytime you leave. ★ Convenient and easy to use, clean and elegant, simple, with smooth operation. I recommend turning on your phone’s iCloud backup while using this app.

title: Loli Adventure project completed and published
content: Loli’s Adventure was the first mobile game project I saw through to completion as lead programmer. I learned a lot from it and got a feel for how it differs from browser games. The project was built with PHP (AMFPHP) + AIR (Starling plus traditional UI), and on the front end, Starling + traditional UI still runs into plenty of performance limits — from here on, I plan to drop traditional UI entirely for mobile games. This year is a breakout year for mobile platform products, and my interest is sky-high right now. A game built around KUSO fairy tales. It brings together three things: hero development, city building, and tower defense. Players build up their own virtual territory and raise cute fairy-tale heroes while following a lighthearted, fun story through the fairy-tale world, until they finally defeat a powerful demon. Game features: Feature 1: Dream world building — Loli’s Adventure has a simple yet fun city building system. It stands for a girl’s inner world, playful and full of dreamlike color. Players can not only construct all kinds of structures of the mind, but also harvest and grow them as time passes. It lets players enjoy the fun of raising and building. Feature 2: Hero development — Loli’s Adventure makes your fairy-tale hero dream come true. In the game you can get help from all sorts of fairy-tale characters and recruit them for your own use. Players can not only train and upgrade all kinds of fairy-tale heroes, but also mix and match lineups to forge a powerful dream legion. Feature 3: Classic tower defense mode — Loli’s Adventure‘s signature tower defense mode comes in two flavors: story and difficulty. In story mode, players travel through all kinds of KUSO fairy-tale worlds, fighting and growing alongside the protagonist; difficulty mode is tailor-made for hardcore players, letting them break their own limits and push to the extreme. Feature 4: Compendium mode — Loli’s Adventure has a rich story system. Every hero you collect and every enemy you defeat is displayed in the compendium. You can read fun little stories about the heroes, and get a deeper look at your enemies too. Feature 5: Strategy — The fairy-tale heroes in Loli’s Adventure each have their own attributes and skills. How you get through each stage comes down to how you raise and understand your heroes. Different terrain and enemies call for different combinations of heroes and skills. The path to victory lies in your clever brain — come give the challenge a try! Feature 8: Graphics — Loli’s Adventure uses 960×640 pixel, 1024-color graphics, with crisp HD image quality and a bold, lively, finely detailed art style. Six campaigns in a range of styles, three difficulty levels with four or five exquisitely crafted maps, hundreds of monsters with distinctive looks, and spectacular battle scenes with more than four hundred units on screen at once — tower defense fans won’t be able to stop playing! Loli fans won’t be able to resist! Let’s all join in!

title: FastApple's DNS conflicts with iTunes Connect
content: When using Xcode’s Archives panel to Distribute to iTunes Connect, I got this error: The certificate for this server is invalid. You might be connecting to a server that is pretending to be “contentdelivery.itunes.apple.com” which could put your confidential information at risk. Then I opened iTunes Connect in Safari and found that lots of images wouldn’t load and scripts wouldn’t run either. I captured the browser requests and found that a certificate for itc.mzstatic.com had a security problem and looked like a forgery. At first I thought it was because I’d bound some hosts entries, but after restoring DNS to the default it was fine — turns out it was FastApple’s DNS causing the problem. I’ve now switched to 114.114.114.114. BTW, on OSX, GameCenter failing to connect to the server is also DNS-related. I’d previously bound 127.0.0.1 ocsp.spo1.verisign.com and 127.0.0.1 crl.verisign.net in hosts — just remove them.

title: Unity3D loses textures when importing fbx
content: Question: When exporting FBX from 3dsMax for use in Unity, textures always get lost. Unity does automatically import materials when it imports the FBX, but the texture files all end up empty, so you have to go in and assign each texture one by one — a huge waste of time. Solution: In 3dsMax, give the model and its textures matching names, copy the texture files into the Unity project, and then import the FBX. That way the automatically created materials will find their corresponding textures.

title: Expected too much from the AirPort Extreme base station
content: When it came time to upgrade to a gigabit home router, I agonized for a long time between Cisco’s e4200 and Apple’s AirPort Extreme. In the end, Apple’s big January 6 sale made the decision for me, and I bought the big AE (MD031) on the spot. The big AE paired with a MyBookLive is great value for the money compared with a Time Capsule. The gigabit Ethernet port has genuinely been a huge win — I get up to 100MBs transferring files from the MBL, though wireless still feels a bit slow. And the one-click network extension you get from pairing the big AE and the little AE is genuinely handy. Signal coverage is okay, but signal stability disappointed me. The W941n I bought earlier (a bit over ¥200, probably cheaper now) paired with an AirPort Express one wall away (roughly 10 meters in a straight line) would only stutter occasionally on AirPlay. After switching to the big AE, AirPlaying from my iPhone to the little AE stutters so badly that the connection drops. The Apple TV one wall away (about 5 meters in a straight line) playing videos over 5GB with XBMC buffers far more often than before. I figured 5GHz would be smoother, but when I checked, the signal on 5GHz was already down to -80, and the rate was actually lower. In short, the wireless performance doesn’t even match a three-antenna router that costs a bit over ¥200. Weak wireless, and on the wired side it actually has one fewer port than the other guy’s. Apple, what am I supposed to do with you? Next time a friend wants to buy a gigabit router, I’ll absolutely recommend the e4200.

title: Jobs got on board too
content: The day after the iPhone 4S was released, Jobs let go and left Apple, left us — on the day after the iPhone 4S was released. The world was divided on the iPhone 4S, and in our somewhat restless country in particular, its industrial design drew no shortage of criticism. So today some people joke that “the iPhone 4S is what killed Jobs.” Of course we all know that can’t be true — it’s as absurd as saying the old man took a boat ticket to go play Dou Dizhu with Gates and Buffett. That said, there are two other theories: 1) “Jobs held on until today only to see the iPhone 4S launch”; 2) Jobs “was declared dead” today, having put it off for the sake of the iPhone 4S. Nobody in this vast world can rule out either possibility — but none of that matters now, because the departed are gone and all we can do is hold them in our hearts. As for the pressure Tim Cook was under when he took the stage yesterday, we only understood it today. As Apple’s top leader now, Cook clearly knew about Jobs’s critical condition — and the other Apple VPs had no reason not to know either. At yesterday’s event there was no Jobs, no redesigned iPhone 5 to carry the show, and a matter as weighty as Jobs’s failing health pressing on everyone’s mind — yet at 50 years old, Cook gave a performance that betrayed nothing. As Apple’s new CEO, appearing without Jobs, only he can truly understand how much pressure and how heavy a burden he carried through his debut keynote. Under those circumstances, Cook’s ease and composure really do deserve a fresh look from us. If iPhones are meant to be major generational updates in Apple’s roadmap, then we certainly can’t lay all our dissatisfaction at Cook’s feet. Here’s to Apple’s future — and to Cook and the Apple team. -http://www.macx.cn/forum.php?mod=viewthreadtid=2021439from=portal Yesterday I was still at home watching the keynote, and today old Steve has “boarded the ship.” It’s really hard to believe this is real. Apple and I really did meet too late Ever since I left my hometown, my grandmother has been living alone, with a desktop computer in the house. She kept telling me she wanted to learn how to use it. Once when I went home I gave her a quick walkthrough, but I realized that everything — from turning the computer on and off, to using the mouse and keyboard, to reading what’s on screen — was a huge hurdle for her. She always felt the text on screen was too small to make out, and reading it was a strain. She could never figure out what the scrollbar was, or how to use the mouse wheel. She couldn’t aim the mouse at all, and when she clicked, the cursor would drift… She couldn’t understand why a computer had so many menus and so many options. All she wanted was to go online and read a bit about medicine and culture lectures, or look up the definition of a word. That simple. Yet she had to deal with so many things she had no idea about… Because of all those obstacles, we all gave up. Last year Apple launched the iPad. I thought its simple UI would suit an elderly person, so I bought one on a whim to let my grandmother try. The result was excellent — even though there’s still plenty she doesn’t understand, she doesn’t need to. What she wants is very pure. Now she uses “iPad中文报刊” to read the newspaper every day, and apps like “蘑菇新闻” and “华尔街日报” to read aggregated forum news posts. She even knows some internet slang now. Of course, she also uses “iBooks” to read and “iPod” for music — but that’s extra. I’ve long believed that so-called magic is just the mirror image of technology. The iPad is so magical that my grandmother has become a netizen too. This is Apple’s magic, and that’s when I fell in love with Apple. Ironically, a year ago I was still fuming in my blog, complaining about Apple blocking Flash. A year later, I was completely won over. Looking at it from outside the bubble, Flash really does have all kinds of flaws and isn’t suited to being plastered everywhere on the web. And because of all sorts of UX issues, tablets are better served by apps redesigned from scratch than by direct ports (I won’t get into the specifics on a personal blog). Apple devices are like a set in a game Of course, every company’s products are more compatible and integrate more tightly with its own other products — but because Apple controls both software and hardware and its product line is small and refined, that integration is tighter still, like a set with more hidden stat bonuses. Owning just one device already makes you a set — the perfect marriage of software and hardware embodies that old maxim: “People who are really serious about software should make their own hardware.” And when you own several devices, the effect is even more striking. Starting from the iPad, within a year I followed the trail and picked up an iPhone, a MacBook Pro, a Time Capsule, an Airport Express, an Apple TV, and a Magic Mouse — every one of them impressive. With iCloud, everything becomes even more convenient. Technology is magic. Master magician Jobs is gone, just like when Dumbledore left — he had already foreseen what was to come, and calmly accepted his fate. Jobs is gone, and his spirit shouldn’t be inherited by Apple alone As for Apple’s future, I’m vaguely pessimistic. First, its soul has departed, so it will inevitably lose part of its character — though that could cut both ways, and might be a good sign for cracking the Chinese market. Second, the Chinese market: one look at the market data and Apple can be sure China is territory it must fight for — but I’m afraid it’ll end up like Google Search there: play nice, or get out. Third, history repeats itself: the grand chess game Microsoft has been playing is about to explode with Win8 — will the mobile market repeat the same mistakes all over again? Fourth, Apple’s core competitiveness lies in innovation, but how many times can a big company erupt? How many more “world-changing” innovations can Apple actually produce? As a consumer, I’m not worried about Apple falling. I’m worried about Apple slipping again while other vendors remain so underwhelming. And even if Apple merely maintains the status quo, it’ll still be a long while before anyone overtakes it. Many of my needs can only be met by Apple. Jobs is gone, and his spirit shouldn’t be inherited by Apple alone. Stay hungry, stay foolish. A word of encouragement for us all. On death On the subject of death, who has ever put it better than the man himself: Your time is limited, so don’t waste it living someone else’s life. Don’t be trapped by dogma — which is living with the results of other people’s thinking. Don’t let the noise of others’ opinions drown out your own inner voice. And most important, have the courage to follow your heart and intuition. They somehow already know what you truly want to become. Everything else is secondary.

title: The 8th Flash Developer Conference — "Mobile Development, Social Games and Light Online Games"
content: Time: Sunday, October 16, 2011 Location: Meeting Room 1, Jingyi Hotel, No. 9 Dazhongsi East Road, Haidian District, Beijing Online registration:http://wefdc8.51qiangzuo.com/ Conference page:http://www.wefdc.com/index.html Flash Developer Conference Weibo:http://weibo.com/wefdc I. title: It's now confirmed that Unity 3.5 will be able to publish swf
content: As previously announced, Unity projects will be publishable to Flash via Stage3D (FP11). Before long, Unity projects will run in browsers with FlashPlayer11 installed. The Unity team says it is bringing as many Unity features into Flash as possible, with the goal of making Unity the best tool for building 3D functionality for Flash Player. On the 27th of this month, Unity will hold a Flash Tech Day, which will get Flash developers up to speed on moving to Unity development, show and introduce the features Unity supports in the Flash environment, and provide a beginner-level overview. For some of the latest news, check out this introductory article: http://blogs.unity3d.com/2011/09/01/unity-and-flash-a-sneak-peek/. I’m not all that interested in Unity’s own features, but one item — that programs running inside FP can talk to AS code both inside and outside a Unity project — is great news as far as I’m concerned. title: Some random notes on AppleTV2G
content: 1. Even though the power cable is labeled 125V, it plugs straight into a Chinese outlet just fine. If your TV is an older model with no HDMI port — only AV composite, S-Video or VGA — you can pick up a Langqiang converter and use it with the Apple TV. I bought one: http://item.taobao.com/item.htm?id=8080216931 In XBMC, if you want to switch audio tracks, subtitles, etc. during playback, long-press the round center button on the Apple Remote and an options menu appears. Audio track and subtitle settings live under that speaker icon (same as on a computer). In the XBMC main menu, long-pressing the Menu button on the Remote over an item opens the context menu, just like right-clicking on a computer. Before I knew this, I was browsing my shares, typo’d an IP, and got stuck having to create a whole new connection — what a pain. Being able to open the context menu means you can just edit the existing connection. Update: 4. After a few days of use, I feel the Langqiang converter is only barely usable — it loses a lot of color. A good saddle needs a good horse; an old TV deserves to be retired. XBMC still isn’t stable enough, and there are plenty of rough edges (for example, during asynchronous operations it neither locks the UI nor shows a prompt, but it does make the app sluggish). To watch 720P over your home network, the router can’t be too crappy. I’ve now switched to a TP-link W941N (11n, 300Mbps) and the speed is decent. Unfortunately its Ethernet ports are only 100Mbps, so paired with a WD My Book Live it can’t reach full performance.

title: Here comes Little Flower
content: Went out for a walk this morning and ran into a kitten on the road that meowed at us. At that moment I wanted to say, let’s take it home — listen to how pitiful it sounds. We kept walking, got to the end of the road, turned around, and it was still there meowing. My mom said if we took it home, Grandma would start yelling. I said let’s take it home, it’s not like we can’t afford to feed it. Then we moved fast. Carried the cat all the way back. Watching it meow nonstop in my hands, I was dying of anxiety, so I sped up. I figured the cat must be uncomfortable being held in my hands, and I wanted to get home as fast as possible to feed it. Its texture is different from the two we already have — it’s fancier — so we named it Little Flower. Finally home. My mom gave Little Flower a bath while Old Bai watched from the side, tail fur all puffed out, in full battle-ready mode. It looked really nervous. Thankfully, after the bath, Old Bai and it spent ages greeting each other, sniffing each other several times too. Both were a bit scared, but at least they didn’t fight. Eventually they accepted each other — live and let live. Little Black was a different story. Little Black had been sleeping on top of the cabinet that morning, and woke up to a strange Little Flower. I thought Little Black would push it around, but who knew — Little Black was terrified of it. The moment it saw Little Flower it started yowling, which scared Little Flower into bolting, and Little Flower bolting scared Little Black even more. After that Little Black didn’t dare come out to eat. Little Flower ate a ton of cat food like a starving ghost reincarnated, which reminded me of how wind and Little Black acted when they first arrived. Little Flower barely knows the room, wandering everywhere, sniffing scents and feeling textures — a lot like wind when it first arrived. Actually, Little Flower is a size bigger than wind was back then. It also jumped up onto the bookshelf to lie down after a while, as if it were wind’s childhood. The funniest thing: it was bouncing around and suddenly bonked into the TV screen. Wahaha — just like wind used to. At first they can’t quite tell reflective surfaces and transparent ones apart from the real thing. Right now Little Flower has found an empty corner behind the computer to sleep in. Little Black finally dared come over and sneak a few peeks at it, then, finding no danger, went up to sleep on its own. Grandma was pretty happy to see Little Flower too. Actually, over the past two weeks, Grandma had run into this cat several times when she went out to buy the newspaper. Every time, it would yell at her too, but Grandma figured there were already two at home, and bringing a third would be a hassle, so she never picked it up. Today we brought it home, and when Grandma saw it she even said: “Oh, little cat, haven’t seen you in days!”

title: Compiling a Robotlegs project in Flash causes runtime errors
content: When compiling a project that uses robotleges in the Flash IDE, it always throws a null error at runtime (cannot access a null object…). Previously I had only ever compiled in FDT and never had this problem; puzzled, I compiled the DocumentClass with FDT, and surprisingly there was no problem at all. It only errors at runtime when compiled in the Flash IDE. I figured the cause might be a failed injection, because all the variables that errored were Inject variables. Ultimately, the cause was that the Flash compiler ignored the [Inject] metadata. Solution Method 1: Just check “Publish SWC” in the publish settings, and it will force the Flash compiler to make all metadata take effect. Method 2: Add the compiler arguments -keep-as3-metadata+=Inject -keep-as3-metadata+=PostConstruct. The reason this error doesn’t occur when compiling with FDT normally is that the robotlegs swc has already added the arguments. I prefer Method 1.

title: Cornered Beast
content: Half asleep, I heard a fly buzzing against the window glass, thumping into it again and again, trying to find a way out. It kept at it, failing and trying again across the wide pane, droning the whole time. Lying in bed, I turned my head to look, wanting to give it a hand — let it fly free, and let my ears have some peace. But the windows on either side were open. It kept exploring the glass that wasn’t open, never once flying toward the two open windows. Maybe it does have a sense of direction — I watched it run a random, exhaustive grid search for a “gap,” changing course whenever it bumped into the metal frame. Yet it stayed busy inside that single pane, unwilling to back up a little first and try the pane next door. If only it would step back when it hit the wall and then keep moving sideways a bit, it would already be outside. A lot of the time, it’s the same for us in startups. Failing and trying again, eyes locked on the light ahead — we’ll take the walls to the face on the way there, we’ll spend endless time exploring, we’ll endure the hardship, but we won’t step back and look for a new direction. Little do we realize: one step back and the sea and sky open wide. Let go of the tunnel vision, let go of the stubbornness, take one step back, and the whole situation looks different. Then pick up your original approach again, and you’ll reach the same destination just fine.

title: Severus Snape
content: The life of Snape. In his childhood, he was a scrawny boy with black hair that was too long and dirty, clothes that fit him poorly — jeans that were too short, a shirt that was some oddly styled smock, a tattered coat that was obviously an adult’s. His face was sallow, and he was short and frail. Just from appearances alone, he was not a likable child, and coupled with his cowardice, timidity, and oddity, even fewer people liked him. (—Of course, being unhealthy-looking and poorly dressed wasn’t his fault; it only showed that his misfortune began in childhood.) Since he was young, his parents’ endless quarrels were his nightmare, his shadow. This kind of quarreling generally leads to two outcomes: either the child grows up not believing in love and rejecting marriage, or he desperately craves love. Poor as he was, he was clearly the latter. Of his roughly forty years of life, nearly three-quarters were entangled in his love for Lily. In his heart, he believed pure wizard blood was noble, yet he himself was a half-blood of Muggle and wizard, which left him unable to find his place. Eventually, under extreme self-loathing, he adopted the seemingly arrogant way of calling himself the “Half-Blood Prince” to assert himself. He was extraordinarily gifted in Potions and had a deep interest in the Dark Arts, in which he was also quite accomplished. Voldemort was his idol, and this could be seen as his pursuit and commitment in his career. But because of this, he offended the woman he loved, causing her to break with him and ultimately turn to the Potter he hated most. From then on, he turned his grief into strength, wanting to accomplish something great, and so he devoted himself loyally to Voldemort to realize his ideals and ambitions. Therefore, when he heard Professor Trelawney’s prophecy about his idol, he immediately told his Lord Voldemort — never imagining that he would thereby lose the woman he loved forever, and afterward bear the shackles of his soul, spending his whole life in remorse and self-blame. Perhaps to atone, perhaps for revenge, he was forced to play the “villain,” to be a spy, and later even to kill Dumbledore, letting everyone misunderstand him. In his self-blame, he chose to unconditionally and forever protect Lily’s child — the boy with Lily’s eyes. Perhaps being able to look into Lily’s eyes was a kind of happiness for him, but those eyes were on his nightmare, “Potter,” tormenting him endlessly. Most outrageous of all (the conversation between Snape and Dumbledore) — “I spied for you, I lied for you, I put myself in mortal danger for you. Everything I did was to protect Lily Potter’s son. And now you tell me you’ve been raising him to slaughter him like a pig—“ In love, Snape had a secret crush on that little girl from the age of nine or ten. The two had originally become best friends (see Chapter 33, “The Prince’s Tale,” in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows —), but they diverged because of differences in friendships, careers, and their sense of right and wrong. In a moment of carelessness, Snape called Lily a “Mudblood,” and the heartbroken Lily realized the irreconcilable conflict between herself and her best friend, and chose to stand on the side of her own house. But no matter how Lily saw him, he regarded Lily as his true love. For Lily he betrayed his career and his beliefs; for her he endured humiliation, willingly bore infamy, and went almost his entire life misunderstood by everyone; for her he protected that detestable child, Potter. Snape shouted: “Expecto Patronum!” From the tip of his wand burst a silver doe. She landed on the office floor, bounded once across the office, and soared out of the window. Dumbledore watched her fly away, and as her silvery glow faded, he turned back to Snape, and his eyes were full of tears. Snape held Lily’s body and wept bitterly, with little Harry on the left. “After all this time?” “Always.” …… “Snape folded the page signed by Lily and tucked it into his robes, then tore the photograph he was holding in two, keeping the half with Lily’s smile and throwing the half with James and Harry back onto the floor beneath the cupboard…” (—a childish gesture) Even his last words before death turned out to be: look…at…me — only because of those eyes like Lily’s, fulfilling his “always,” forever. Even his death seemed utterly meaningless — Voldemort mistakenly believed that only by killing him could he truly use the Elder Wand — “The last trace of color drained from his face, and at the same time his black eyes widened abruptly. The snake’s fangs pierced his neck. He struggled in vain to break free of the magical cage around him, then his knees buckled and he fell to the floor.” — Dying so miserably, so silently?! “Besides blood, something else was leaking from Snape. Silvery-blue, neither gas nor liquid, it poured from his mouth, his ears, and his eyes” (tragic and heroic) With the last bit of strength before death, he left the truth behind. Those memories surged out from everywhere — not only because his life was ending, but also because this was the only chance in his entire life to speak the truth and his innermost feelings. - The above is excerpted from Baidu Baike I excerpt this article solely to commemorate the conclusion of many years of HP. Last night I went to see the final film. And so everything has come to a full stop, leaving behind the legend of Severus Snape.

title: The old era has already come to an end
content: Back in Shenzhen Alright, this is an addendum. Actually I got back to Shenzhen on July 13th. After I returned I met up with some people, and then started work on the 18th. But as I suspected, I’m not cut out for a long-term office job — after one week I switched back to developing from home, going into the office only when necessary and dropping in on clients now and then. Since coming back to Shenzhen my rhythm of life has become regular: three meals on time, in bed before 23:00 every night, up a little after 7 in the morning. These things matter. Yeah, not bad at all. Website restored A few days ago the site got hacked again here in China. This time it was a commercial attack. The funniest part: after this internet company in Guangzhou took down the server I was on, they sent me an email like a cat weeping over a mouse, telling me that under their recent “kind-hearted monitoring” they’d noticed my site had gone down — and they left their website and contact details in the email. Receiving that email out of the blue, I was so grateful I was speechless. All I can do is learn from certain masters and move out of China. Yesterday afternoon I bought a shared hosting plan. I’ve been busy ever since, restoring the site and restructuring it. mousebomb.org still has some compatibility issues that aren’t fully sorted out, and I can’t be bothered to fix them. This has moved up the timetable for my big overhaul of my personal site. I don’t want my personal site to be centered on Flash anymore. I won’t host it myself either — instead I’m just offering the source code for download. I’m happy today: even though I’ve torn down the Flash site I ran for years, I’ve given away all the source code. This year’s job changes and life changes have made Flash and technology stop being the focus for me; I’m facing a broader horizon, oriented around product. Breaking out of my intoxication with technology is what I’ve really gained these past few years. Three years in the workforce People usually write a pile of retrospectives and resolutions when the year turns over, but at year’s end I never feel as sentimental as they do. It seems my node for change is summer. Every summer is when I change the most. It started in the summer of ‘08, when I left school for a one-year internship. In the second half of ‘08 I went to Shanghai and joined Qoolu, met that group of outstanding young people, and worked with them on Undersea World. I left in the first half of ‘09. July ‘09: I joined a Flash animation company in Shenzhen and worked on Flash games for a long time. End of July ‘10: I left Shenzhen and went to Shanghai again, to co-develop a real-time strategy browser game — Kingdom Wars. July ‘11: back in Shenzhen again. Maybe I’ll take it easy for a while first. Then again, the world is full of sudden opportunities — what happens next, we’ll see. Come to think of it, jumping around like this also means there was something unsatisfying each time, right? That’s true. The specifics are hard to sum up in a few words — some were forces beyond my control, some pressure from circumstance. I won’t get into it today. Anyway, people move upward. Gains and losses, success and failure, are all a precious and interesting process. No matter where I go, what project I work on, whether I succeed or fail, I’m gaining XP and leveling up. I value every collaborator. Along the way I’ve treated everyone I’ve worked with as a close friend. Wherever people are, some form of collaboration can always continue. This post is really rambling — no central theme from start to finish; the words just flow wherever my mind goes. Now let me ramble about something else. My love affair with Flash Years ago — it must have been 2002 — I fell in love with Flash at first sight. From ‘04, when I got to school, I kept thinking up ways to tinker with this hot-tempered thing, dreaming of mastering it and becoming a Flasher, a Flash master. Seven years have passed since then. Though I did successfully save the continent of Azeroth… I’ve now achieved the dream I had back then, and I’ve done Flash development for years, making a living from it. My devotion to Flash once made me take it far too seriously, believing nothing in the world could be better. Although I also worked with plenty of other technologies, everything revolved around Flash. Now Apple has gradually changed my attitude toward Flash, and with new opportunities appearing, I’ve jumped out of the Flash-centered world. Once out, my heart feels hollow — a spiritual pillar of many years is collapsing. But that’s not so bad: an attitude of treating all technologies equally, and a new internal mechanism, will be rebuilt. At first I got into Flash just to make some flashy animations and websites for people to look at — you could say it was Flash for Flash’s sake. Once I’d achieved that, I became more and more calm about it. So, heh, I guess I’m past the stage of chasing visual effects. Now I look at the product. I focus on its completeness and usability, feature design, user experience and every other aspect. I admire Apple’s minimalist design: whatever the need, just the right amount is best — technology is secondary. The old era has come to an end Maybe you don’t get it, and that’s fine. Once a hobby rises to the level of belief, it stops making sense to anyone. After I stopped taking Flash so seriously, everything needed adjusting. And as the adjustment began, fragments of the old and new worlds overlapped and collided. In this recent collision and reflection, I’ve pinned down some goals that used to be vague, met new people and developed new desires, and most importantly, I’ve finally made up my mind about some big goals. Time to act — the real career begins. A new era is about to arrive.

title: Return to Shenzhen at the end of July
content: I’ll be heading back to Shenzhen at the end of July 2011. This time last year I was lamenting the lack of talent around me — having skills with no room to use them, having ideas with nobody to talk them over with. Then I set off, building projects I actually cared about alongside like-minded people in Shanghai. A year went by in a flash, and it’s blazing July again. Our project has gotten somewhere. Time for the leaves to return to their roots. I did once think about staying in Shanghai, but that was quickly ruled out as unrealistic. My mom has been traveling a lot this year: April and May in retreat, June touring China from north to south, and July off to another retreat… The pet shop downstairs has closed, so there’s nowhere to board our two cats, and we have to ask friends to come check on them. That situation made me realize something: it’s already hard enough to get the family together — why spread ourselves even thinner? If I were in Shanghai, pulling a salary far higher than in Shenzhen, I’d work myself to death all day, skip meals over a single bug, go out partying at night, stay up with friends until 3 a.m. because I couldn’t bear to sleep, exhausted day in and day out, running a physical deficit every single day… But if I work to stay alive, why would I kill myself for work? So right now, what I want isn’t to grind for money in this materialistic metropolis — it’s a stretch of stability. I want to go home and live with my family and my cats. A while back, while browsing online, I stumbled across a few incredibly talented people in the south: rich life experience, brilliant writing, plenty of work experience already while still in school, their own distinctive taste and sharp takes on things — and some of them are involved in public-interest work. And the kicker: they’re younger than me. The new wave pushes the old one along, and all at once I had that deflating feeling of looking up at something out of reach. I like to think I’m pretty unflappable these days, and that I’m genuinely good at certain things, but I’ve realized I still have to break out of my shell and get to know more badass people — that’s what makes life interesting, far more important than just raking in money in a restless industry. If I could get to know a lot of people who are both exceptionally capable and doing public-interest work, my life would only just be starting to be glorious. So awesome. I have to make the most of this move back and carve out more time to explore new circles.

title: Kingdom Wars Battle Demo
content: The two short videos below are match demos of Kingdom War, a game developed by a team of three. Technical skill isn’t the problem, and the core features are done — but the art assets aren’t ready, so the buildings, unit types and attack animations are all pretty thin, and the map was drawn on the fly. A front end with no artist really has it rough, doesn’t it?! Kingdom War supports up to 4v4 matches, with as many as 400 units brawling it out at once. There are two tactical approaches to choose from — tower defense and unit swarm — and players get to decide the tactical allocation among their allies, each person’s strategic role, and how to take on the enemy together. Every map has neutral buildings; capturing them gives one side an advantage…

title: Team Up for Rio Adventure
content: After finishing Angry Birds Rio, I was looking forward to the movie version. Last Monday I suggested to my friends that we go see it on Friday, opening day, and by Friday I’d gradually rounded up a group of 14. Quoting fenix: Tonight colleagues from four departments went together to see the premiere of Rio. It’s worth noting that this wasn’t a free perk from the company, but purely a self-funded outing by people in the industry. Company benefits should mean raising employees’ pay and creating better room for advancement; what employees need to do is create and keep up with the company’s pace of progress, and on that basis, everyone has to keep learning. I’m really glad so many people responded to my proposal. It turns out this film is great for relieving the pressure on our stressed-out dev team. Rio doesn’t preach any grand lessons or aim for deep meaning — it’s just a comedy out to make everyone laugh, and that’s enough. Recommend it for a group of friends or the whole family.

title: 2011.3.27 Tiandixing Beijing Stop
content: Latest Events2011 RIA Tian Di Xing Beijing City Elite Forum Event Time: 2011.3.27 Registration Period: 2011.3.7-2011.3.25 Event Scale: 300+ people Location: No. 33, North 4th Ring West Road, Zhongguancun, Beijing National Science Library, Chinese Academy of Sciences (Documentation and Information Center, Northwest Gate, 1st Floor Lecture Hall) Presentation TopicsFlash 3D API Related Topic IntroductionHow to use the awesome Molehill 3D in the new version of Flash Player! Besides 3D, can 2D rendering also benefit? This topic will walk you through the latest 3D API content, and there will be an awesome demo. Topological Map-Based Line-of-Sight Pathfinding Topic IntroductionPathfinding is one of the classic and interesting topics in game AI, and it holds a fairly important position in Flash game application development as well. Although the traditional A* pathfinding based on a 2D numeric matrix can basically meet our basic needs, there is a pathfinding approach based on topological data structures that can bring us more ideal path results and ideas. Let’s share its beauty together when the time comes. The Non-Mainstream Agile Development Model for Small Flash Game Projects Topic Introduction: How can a team divide work and collaborate to maximize efficiency? How do you avoid a nightmare of frequent bugs caused by changing requirements? Without an outstanding designer, how do you make the UI good? If front-end programmers are inexperienced, how do you avoid project delays? Why do product planners always cause trouble? Faced with so many intricate frameworks, how exactly should you choose? What kind of development approach can actually help a team avoid project risks? Drawing on many years of Flash project development experience, the author will discuss the way of agile development for Flash projects with everyone. Developing WebGame with the Flex Framework Topic Introduction:Break away from conventional thinking and adopt the Flex framework to develop games. Experience what it feels like to write games with mxml and how to use Flex’s ready-made frameworks to increase development efficiency, solve the performance and size issues brought by the Flex framework, and at the same time share some insights and experiences in game production. Special TopicEveryone Has Their Say — Whether to Use a FrameworkTopic IntroductionWhether to use a framework? Under what circumstances should a framework be used? Should you use a well-known third-party framework or a self-developed framework? It’s all up to you to speak. As long as you’re on site, you can speak freely.

title: A New Year
content: 2011.02.22: Another year has passed in the blink of an eye, and I realize it’s been a long time since I left any warm words here. In 2011, I hope to write more personal things here. Fair warning: from now on, if you don’t like it, don’t come in! As mentioned in the subtitle, let this blog return to its essence, its original intent. Looking back at last year, I feel more and more that this personal blog isn’t personal enough. So many truly personal things never got written here; instead I posted a few articles and videos that can’t withstand the test of time. I was afraid of everything—afraid that if I wrote something too simple, someone would look down on it; afraid that if I wrote something based on my own interpretation, someone with a different cultural background would take issue with it; afraid that if I wrote something slightly technical, people wouldn’t understand it. In the end, I became both afraid to write and disdainful of writing. These past couple of days, after going to Golden Beach to reflect on the old and learn the new, I realized—what was I even afraid of? It was really just a fixed, firmware-like pattern: everything I said and did was oriented toward pleasing others. In life I have very little self-confidence. Why don’t I have self-confidence? If a person could see their own qualities clearly enough, would they still lack confidence? I have a great deal of self-denial, and it’s like dark clouds blanketing the sky—it obscures so many wonderful qualities. When self-denial becomes more and more of a habit, you forget the good things that once were. If you’ve forgotten them yourself, others can see them even less. Wait—just a moment ago, I was still agonizing over every single word, terrified of typos, terrified of awkward sentences, terrified of being laughed at. In that one-third of a second of sudden inspiration, I became aware of it, and I’m now telling myself: “To hell with all this second-guessing, to hell with the onlookers. As long as I understand it, that’s enough. I don’t write this blog for anyone!” These are my words, this is my blog. This is not a tech blog. It doesn’t need the so-called rigor and objectivity that science and engineering demands. I don’t need to make things convenient for anyone, I don’t need to please anyone. I’m only responsible to myself, and onlookers should be responsible for themselves too. Okay, now let’s take another look: why did I develop this pattern of pleasing others when blogging? To explain it with the brain—part of the reason comes from work habits, because most of my mental energy goes into computer-related things. Work goes without saying—developing games and websites (interest-driven)—and even entertainment is in front of a computer: playing games, reading news. For me, development is also entertainment—I’ve loved planning since childhood, loved playing strategy and management games, and the joy I get from project development is as great as playing those games; and playing games and reading news are also deeply connected to work. So I no longer have any strict distinction between work and play. This makes me more and more of a homebody, and the events my brain processes become very limited. It’s easy to seek out and apply a unified, optimized, universal set of principles distilled from your areas of expertise to everything around you. That sounds convoluted—really it just means work and life are tightly intertwined, so your thinking becomes limited, and you often neglect your inner needs. When you need to assert yourself through words (writing a personal blog), you easily get led into a ditch by your brain’s suggestions (I’m still writing a tech blog, I need to be concise, well-reasoned, well-organized, easy to read, and so on). I’ve seen some blogs by my Haiwen classmates, and I admire the personal touch in their writing. Even when they repost articles, it represents the blogger’s own reflections on life, imprinted with their growth along the way. The brain computes fast, and typing always lags behind. Many thoughts flash by—it seems like I’ve opened them up, but I didn’t write them down. Opening them is enough; I can’t be bothered to write the rest. Now to summarize: This year, this personal blog will return to my own control, written for no one else. I give myself permission to cry when I want to cry and laugh when I want to laugh in this blog. Permission to write as long as I want. Permission to skip making images if I can’t be bothered. Warning: This is Mousebomb’s personal blog—computer games, movies, music, myself. Play but don’t lose your drive; the mystery of mysteries; enter without invitation at your own peril. Onlookers, take care of yourselves. I am not responsible for any reactions or consequences resulting from reading this blog.

title: Notes on compiling SWF with ant in FDT
content: This afternoon I ran into an issue where Chinese output from Ant in the console was fine, but the Chinese output from mxmlc was garbled. The cause was that flexTasks was using $FLEX\_HOME/ant/lib/flexTasks.jar from a different version of the SDK — switching to the matching one fixed it. For the mxmlc parameter documentation of the Ant tasks provided by the FLEX SDK, see http://livedocs.adobe.com/flex/3/html/help.html?content=compilers_13.html If you run Ant tasks in FDT and hit “Java heap space” while mxmlc is compiling a swf, the reason is that some of the swc files used as libraries are too large, or there are too many of them, so memory runs out and you need to give it more: in FDT go to window-preferences-java-installed jres- select the current entry and click edit, then set the default vm arguments, for example -Xms64m -Xmx512m.

title: AS3: Notes on Non-Alchemy Fast Memory Access
content: Honestly, my recent project has been getting more and more boring. The core work is basically done, and what’s left is almost all grunt work — nothing new or fun. Yesterday I finished The Settlers 7 and was just about to drift off to sleep, when I suddenly came across two pages that jolted me wide awake: http://www.buraks.com/azoth/ and http://philippe.elsass.me/2010/05/as3-fast-memory-access-without-alchemy/ , and just like that I was energized. Reading and writing ByteArrays in FlashPlayer always falls short when you’re up against certain extreme requirements. These past couple of days Xu Can got pushed into hunting for some unorthodox, unofficial workaround — and sure enough, he actually found one. I’d heard before that haXe is so fast because its author found the low-level interface FlashPlayer 10 provides for Alchemy, but for various reasons I never used haXe. Seeing these two pages showed me some new tricks — turns out the three of them are goods from the same circle. All three found the “back door” FlashPlayer 10 opened for Alchemy to squeeze out performance at a low level. Now that I’ve seen something new, it’d be a shame not to play around with it. I still don’t plan to use haXe — I want to depend on unofficial APIs as little as possible. Apparat is great and powerful, but it needs a runtime installed, and it’s a framework with tons of features; I don’t like using something where more than half the features go unused. Azoth is a small tool built specifically to give you a high-speed memory access API — compact, lightweight, single-purpose. That’s exactly the kind I like. It lets us use a ByteArray as a standalone block of memory. Download http://www.buraks.com/azoth/azoth104.zip, then use the fastmem class it provides to read and write data. Once you’ve written your code and compiled it to a SWF, run azoth.exe to inject it into the swf, and it becomes the optimized version. Without the injection, it’s obviously slower than the APIs Flash provides. Since I’m playing around anyway, I figured I’d go looking for trouble and run an experiment. Spurred on by Xu Can, I had a momentary burst of foolish enthusiasm today and tried using this high-speed memory access to optimize bitmap rendering. The basic idea: store all the BitmapData used for rendering as binary inside a single ByteArray, with each bitmap having a start memory address and a length; manually manage all the internal addresses of that ByteArray and maintain the image layering; in the end, the only thing output to the view is a single BitmapData — all in hopes that fast reads and writes would bring a performance boost. After trying it, the results weren’t impressive — even though memory reads and writes are faster, it moves the burden of implementing copypixel onto per-pixel processing. Copying a mere 300*300 image to another image requires computing 90000 * 2 memory addresses; bigger images mean even more address computation, and doing all that math at a high level is very time-consuming. And copypixel between images isn’t just plain value reads and writes — it also has to blend based on alpha, and the color math eats up more time. Flash’s own bitmapData copypixel takes only 4ms to process a 300*300 image 5 times, whereas running 180000 looped additions in Flash takes 7ms on my machine. So there you have it: throughput isn’t the problem — the amount of computation blows up. High-speed memory access isn’t meant for this kind of thing. I really was having a moment of foolish enthusiasm.

title: Notes on Hollowing Out the Black Shadows Over Unexplored Areas in Strategy Games
content: Carving a cutout (a circle or ellipse) out of a large dark shadow: once a sub-shape cache has been built, bitmap channel subtraction is cheaper than drawing a Shape with blend mode ERASE — but building that cache is costly, and the cost scales with the area of the region. So the two approaches each fit different cases. For large-area cutouts like drawing the border of a sphere of influence, blend-mode draw is probably the better choice.

title: Misc notes - jQueryMobile linked page not styled
content: Today I discovered that in jQueryMobile’s listview, to link to a page in the same directory with the mobile style applied, you must use .xxxx.html instead of xxxx.html. Otherwise, the target page’s data-role=header and other content get ignored (meaning that although it’s loaded asynchronously and has a transition, it becomes an HTML page without mobile styling). What a waste of time… Now with the alpha version, there’s still a long way to go in terms of platform compatibility.
