title: Problem: manually installing the Flash Player plugin in newer versions of Chrome doesn't work
content: Problem description: After switching systems, I found that I’d moved to the new Chrome 6. I wanted to use the debug version of the flashplayer plugin, so I installed “flashplayer 10.1 plugin debug” as usual. Once it was installed, I restarted Chrome and opened http://www.flashplayerversion.com/ and saw that the version was the latest one — but it wasn’t the debug version. That struck me as odd. Later I went into the Control Panel and uninstalled the flash plugin outright, but Chrome could still play flash! It turns out that both Chrome 5 and Chrome 6 ship with flashplayer built in, and it’s the latest version. That’s a good thing in itself, but for flash developers what’s needed is the debug build of fp, so you have to find a way to swap Chrome’s built-in fp for the debug version. Solution: In Chrome, type chrome:plugins in the address bar and you’ll see an entry — Shockwave Flash - Version: 10,1,53,64 Description: Shockwave Flash 10.1 r53 Location: C:\Users\Administrator\AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\Application\6.0.453.1\gcswf32.dll That’s the built-in flashplayer. Disable it. Then just install “flashplayer 10.1 plugin debug” as usual. Once it’s installed, you’ll see an entry in chrome:plugins — Shockwave Flash - Version: 10,1,53,64 Description: Shockwave Flash 10.1 r53 Location: C:\Windows\system32\Macromed\Flash\NPSWF32.dll

title: The Project type has to be set.
content: Problem description: After switching to FDT4 M3, I pointed the workspace straight back at its old location, and of course a fair number of errors showed up that needed fixing. One of them, though, kept telling me “The Project type has to be set.” in the SDK settings (FDT compiler) — yet there’s nowhere in that screen to change the so-called “Project type”. Solution: Select the project, right-click - Flash Project - Set project type… set it, hit OK, and you’re good.

title: The 21st summer...
content: They say Aquarius is extremely calm, extremely rational. But somehow, come summer, I turn sentimental. Maybe only warm sunshine and scorching heat can melt a heart of cold, glassy stuff. Only when summer arrives each year do I suddenly feel like a living creature. Every year, my personal emotional eruptions happen in this blazing summer — the days when school lets out for vacation. Lately I’ve been feeling down, tinged with a faint sadness. I’ve realized I’ve wasted so much of my youth and accomplished nothing. Right now my biggest wish on the work front is to build an interesting game product. I’ve never liked being bound by the things around me, ever since my school days as a kid. I could be home all alone, keeping company with my computer day and night, sowing seeds of words in my notebook — anything but submitting to the spoon-fed education at school. All through college I did a lot of social practice every year, piling up plenty of flash development experience, all by my own effort. — Speaking of which, the sad part is that my one and only fabricated social practice (giving a policy presentation at some hospital) earned me an “Outstanding Social Practice**“, while every bit of my real social practice (the IT stuff, flash websites, etc.) was completely ignored by the school authorities. This kind of topsy-turvy irony happened again and again on campus. After seeing it so often, I’ve grown detached and calm. Everyone else is drunk and I alone am sober — you guys can go screw yourselves. If only I could have run into a group of like-minded people at school and formed a team — how happy that would have been. But in that restless campus, every club tied to arts or tech made me feel that meeting them was worse than never meeting them at all. Birds of a feather really do flock together, and every time I was left alone staring up at the sky. Fighting alone — is that my fate, kid? My last internship before graduation, from the second half of ‘08 to the first half of ‘09, brought me briefly together with a group of idealistic young IT people in Shanghai. After a few months on the job, I noticed that because the company’s human resources were so weak, a big chunk of my time was being wasted on back-end development. That wasn’t my personal direction, so I chose to leave early. Living under someone else’s roof, it’s hard to find a wise lord. I ran off to Shenzhen — new place, new opportunities, so many chances right in front of me. In the end I chose to develop two idealistic virtual communities. Only after joining did I discover how many obstacles stand in the way of a team with severely insufficient resources trying to get something done. The lack of manpower stalled every bit of progress. Low-level doers made communicating hard for me and drained enormous energy — even the simplest thing took ages to explain. The lack of funding made the manpower shortage even worse. That’s when I truly understood that everything idealized is just the daydream of school days when you don’t have to worry about food or clothing. In reality, no normal person can pin their future on an idealized product when they can’t even keep themselves fed and clothed. For a while, I lost myself in my work, unable to find my own value. The slow progress on the Shenzhen project has to be reined in somehow. So I’ll leave first. As long as the remaining development follows my original plan, the project will gradually get finished. Let my share of the salary go to more coders. Once again I’m about to set off on a long journey. Even the cat understood my situation and went off early to find herself a new home. She left softly, just as she had come softly, descending from the sky and departing to the sky. The magical cat Wind became a legend. I believe she has a pair of magical wings that carried her to her original longing — a warm, sweet home with an owner who could look after her at every moment. In the blink of an eye, it’s July again. To me, July marks the start of summer, because what I looked forward to most as a kid was summer vacation starting on July 1st — the sign that carefree days had come back. The blazing sun, lively classmates, scorching concrete, badminton downstairs under the broiling sun, drenched in sweat sharing homemade ice cream, hiding in an air-conditioned room wrapped in blankets with a group playing cards… Summer vacation, get-togethers — days like that will never come back, will they. Alone, roaming the world as I please; a thousand sails have passed, and the four seas are my home. I look up and heaven and earth meet — boundless desolation. Suddenly I feel that true freedom is also loneliness. Five years chasing dreams like a moth to the flame. Who in all the land will be crazy with me? This is my 21st summer, still a summer of fighting alone. Who will come to ignite me, grant me warm sunshine and wings, to soar through the blue sky and find the home of my dreams on the other side of the sea?

title: New Opportunities for Flash Mini-Game Developers — Mochi
content: I first crossed paths with Flash years ago, and it was love at first sight. I remember that several years back, small Flash games were hugely popular, and I was blown away by the Xiao Xiao series of Flash animations. Back then I played Xiao Xiao No. 4 over and over, and quietly made up my mind: one day I’d throw myself into the Flash world, build Flash pieces with real visual impact, and create games that are actually fun to play. After I started working, I did Flash website development and Flash virtual community development, and in my spare time I never stopped playing games. Through the day-in, day-out accumulation of work and play, I picked up a lot of inspiration and kept writing it down; some of those ideas gradually grew into a system, and I looked forward to turning them into a series of games and realizing the dream I once had. The reality, though, is no sponsorship and no return. Even though the games I design are ones I’d enjoy playing myself, I can only treat developing these mini-games as a hobby. I always hoped I’d find the spare time to finish them slowly, and hoped that one day my friends could play them and have fun with them. The result? The first few weeks I was full of energy, but then the daily job got busy, my own game inched forward, then stalled. I often felt I had no motivation — the moment I finished my day job, all I wanted was a couple of rounds of StarCraft II and then bed. Time always moves too fast. I watch helplessly as my long-delayed hobby game stays a dream. Among the friends I know, plenty are like me — busy on the career treadmill with an unfulfilled dream. Just counting the people I’ve shared a room with, there’s Proc (Legend of the Star Sea), Halley (MC) and others; of them all, only Huoshan made up his mind to live off his savings and shut himself away at home for six months to focus on developing his own project. As Social Games took off, players idling away their time began buying and selling their friends at will in Social Games, parking cars in front of other people’s doors, and chasing the fun of “stealing crops”… At the same time, Web Games and Flash virtual communities sprang up like bamboo shoots after rain in everyone’s view: Dream Home, Sixth Continent, Seven Dragon Chronicles, Mole’s World, Undersea World, Box World, Hot-Blooded Three Kingdoms, Heroes of Might and Magic, Red Alert, Business Tycoon, Ming Dynasty Era, DDTank and countless more — a new product seemed to pop up almost every day. The huge profit potential of both of those shoved mini-games right out of everyone’s minds. Mini-games gradually lost the luster they once had. It’s not that nobody needs mini-games themselves — so why do mini-game developers keep walking away? I think there are three reasons: first, the profits are small; second, they’re hard to promote; third, you easily end up sewing a wedding dress for someone else. Small profits: The money you can make from a mini-game isn’t as tempting as what Web Games and Social Games offer, and anyone with cash and a team switched direction to Webgames long ago. Once a mini-game is finished, it obviously doesn’t spread as fast as an SNS game, and it has no real profit points either — at best embedded ads, or some company sponsoring it to promote its own brand. With not enough profit, developers naturally lose their drive. You make a mini-game, and you can’t even cover the cost of food, sleep, rent, utilities, rice, oil, salt, and gas — what are you supposed to do? If you’re going to make one, it can only be in these situations: custom work for a client (to promote their own product), public-interest and educational pieces, or a big company sponsoring it (embedding ads) and hiring the developer to build it. Hard to promote: I’m sure every indie developer knows this feeling — unless you’ve got loads of time and energy left after finishing development, it’s very hard to both build and promote. There are certainly great developers who are also publishers, like armorgames, which I’m especially fond of, but for a small team the investment in promotion is still huge. Sewing a wedding dress for someone else: Search Baidu and you’ll find tons of mini-game sites. Most are set up by individuals, and plenty are content alliances. They spend all day downloading every kind of Flash mini-game off the internet, with no awareness of copyright at all, publishing games straight to their sites without the author’s authorization, and the developer’s hard work turns into profit for those publishers. Because of those three reasons, Flash mini-game development isn’t very active. Just as my enthusiasm for Flash mini-game development was about to burn down to ashes, I happened to come across Mochi (https://zh-cn.mochimedia.com/) — the prairie fire that would let Flash mini-games rise again. I’m an indie developer — you could call me a grassroots developer — and I’m also a gamer. My head is full of ideas, but I have neither money nor manpower. Planning and building a mini-game is no problem, but how to make a living from it once it’s finished — that’s a very real question. A single penny can bring a hero to his knees, and with no income, what’s the point of talking about dreams? As the saying goes: only when people have enough food and clothing do they learn honor and shame; only when the granaries are full do they learn propriety. In my frustration, wouldn’t I just follow the crowd and go make Social Games too? After stumbling on Mochi, I found that Mochi was born for exactly this. Through Mochi, both indie developers and small mini-game teams can lower their development costs. Most grassroots developers (especially those with their own ideas but not enough money or people) have no cash to burn at all, but we have the dreams and passion for games, and that shouldn’t be destroyed by reality. The platform Mochi gives us lets us realize our own small creative ideas and earn income once and for all. Mochi has the whole pipeline ready — developer (earns) - advertiser (pays) - publisher (earns) - player (the ad target and the payer). Mochi Ads gives game developers a 50% revenue share and publishers 10%. Users who are both developers and publishers get 60%. Just like the appstore, as a developer you only need to focus on building your game; you don’t have to worry about anything after that. The more fun your game is, the more you earn. It’s a web platform with a pretty long long tail. As this platform grows, it won’t just drive entrepreneurship in the Flash space — it’ll also push more talented indie studios to produce more great original work. Working with Mochi, developers only need to focus on building the product; everything else can be left alone. That not only lowers development costs but also helps improve game quality. Many developers have ideas and the ability to build, but no way to promote and operate — Mochi solves all those thorny problems for them, and all they have to do is give their best to the part they’re best at! A single, narrow responsibility — the optimal setup. On top of that, Mochi also has a developer fund. Mochi’s game developer fund is a $10 million investment, used to help promising Flash and social game developers by supporting their games through sponsorship, licensing partnerships, and publishing. The fund will back small Flash game development studios and indie developers around the world, building world-class games and companies. Open platforms are one of the most important internet advantages right now. Mochi isn’t just a middleman — it also gives developers open APIs to connect with all game users, so you can even build SNS applications. With this platform, development costs are even lower than for a social game. You don’t have to build N versions for different platforms, and the product is the same in nature anyway. Mochi has already handled the social side of things and provides the APIs — user data and online payments all come from Mochi — lowering development difficulty, lowering investment, lowering later maintenance costs… All of that is just fantastic! Being able to turn your interest into your job is a very happy thing, and being able to reclaim the dreams of your youth through that job is about as perfect as it gets. So let’s look now at whether Mochi solves those three problems that decide whether Flash mini-game developers live or die: Small profits? Mochi lets developers embed ads in their games, and when an ad plays, the developer earns income. It works much like Google ads: the developer’s income is determined by the traffic of the game or site and by how much players enjoy the game. A remarkable breakthrough of Mochi Ads is that the developer earns revenue every time a player plays the game. Hard to promote? If one person is both developer and publisher, it’s exhausting. Working with Mochi, developers don’t have to worry about publishing at all — what’s there to worry about when a big platform is doing the promotion? Developers can put everything into their own creative ideas and make games even they love to play, instead of thinking about how to promote them. That improves game quality and brings more original, polished work. Sewing a wedding dress for someone else? This is the beauty of Mochi Ads. It doesn’t matter who downloaded a developer’s game or which page it eventually ends up on — Mochi Ads keeps track of it the whole way and serves the appropriate ads. In fact, Mochi encourages game developers to spread their games across multiple sites to maximize their game’s revenue potential. Every problem is solved, and Mochi won me over effortlessly. I have a lot of faith in it, and I’m really looking forward to picking my dream back up in the days ahead and developing my own games to publish on Mochi. What’s more, I’d be glad to become a Mochi publisher too. Here’s wishing Mochi China growing better and better, creating mutual benefit and a shared future with developers, advertisers, and publishers. If you’re interested in Mochi like I am, head to Mochi’s Chinese official site: https://zh-cn.mochimedia.com/ to find more information. Just watch Flash mini-games set off another wave in China — the new gold rush is right here!

title: Wrote up a bitmap cache rendering optimization
content: Since the project needs to render a large number of characters on the same screen, I needed to improve Flash Player’s rendering performance. This afternoon I ran a rendering performance test and polished up the bitmap optimization library I wrote last year. Screen size 2880*2880500 vector character animation MCs (nested 2 levels deep), looping playbackNone of them removeChild off-screen regionsAll tests run with the Flash Player SA 10.0 debug build No optimization, straight addChild fps4, CPU maxed out, memory 18M~29M Added cacheAsBitmap FPS1, CPU maxed out, memory 156~196M, memory keeps fluctuating Disabled mouse + cacheAsBitmap FPS1, CPU maxed out, memory 156~196M Disabled mouse, no bitmap caching fps4, CPU maxed out, 21M~30M Used the bitmap display object I wrote last year, but without memory reuse for the same object, so every time a new instance was created it would draw the content once from the source MC instance. Script execution was slow and memory usage was high. I’ll optimize a reusable version and test again shortly. fps13, CPU maxed out, memory 476M Used the bitmap display object I wrote last year, with all characters placed within a single screen (scene is still 2880*2880) fps15, CPU maxed out, memory 476M Used the bitmap display object I wrote last year, with all characters placed within a single screen (scene is still 2880*2880), and the character count reduced to 100 fps23, CPU maxed out, memory 186~187M Notes on 1 and 2: The official cacheAsBitmap consumes far too much memory, and it keeps creating bitmap caches while playing. Comparing 3 and 4 against 1 and 2: Disabling the mouse makes little difference in a case like this, where nothing is listening and there are so many objects that it’s already extremely laggy. Notes on 5 and 6: The smaller the region of the bitmap being modified, the higher the fps, but the memory consumed is the same (the whole bitmap). Notes on 6 and 7: Direct bitmap operations aren’t slowed down by a large number of display objects on screen; efficiency depends on the number of pixel copy operations. PS: Just switched to the 10.1 debug SA build — performance dropped by 14. Added a single-frame Image with memory caching (clearing redundant bitmaps), and made the drawing area smaller (800*600) fps30, CPU around 42%, memory 8M~10M New bitmap engine (with a memory resource pool added), 1500 MCs, area 800*600 fps30, CPU around 42%, memory 10M~12M Final result: 1500 MCs playing within the same screen, with a rated frame rate of 30. title: Example of detecting whether a target is reachable by moving in a straight line
content: In my recent project, since the team has quite a few junior ActionScript devs, what was supposed to be pathfinding got cut down to straight-line collision. And the tragic part is, they still tell me the straight-line collision is broken. Yesterday a guy was having the character do a per-pixel collision check after every step to decide whether it could walk. Let me repeat myself one more time: that’s both inaccurate and inefficient. Today I’m posting this example to show the recommended way to do straight-line collision: first draw a line and hit-test it against the walkableblocked model, and only once you’ve confirmed the destination is reachable do you move the character straight there (speed control can come later, it’s unrelated to this example). Demo: the black area is unreachable, and the small red square is the object that needs to move. Document Class : package{import flash.display.SimpleButton;import com.gskinner.motion.GTween;import com.gskinner.motion.easing.Sine; import org.mousebomb.display.RealHitTest; import flash.display.Sprite;import flash.events.MouseEvent; ** * @author Mousebomb (mousebomb@gmail.com) * @date 2010-6-8 *public class HitTestMain extends Sprite{public var pz : Sprite ;public var line : Sprite new Sprite();public var box : Sprite;public var showBtn : SimpleButton;private var boxTween : GTween; private var curX : int 300;private var curY : int 200; public function HitTestMain(){addChild(line);boxTween new GTween(box,.3,null,{ease:Sine.easeOut});curXbox.x;curYbox.y;line.graphics.lineStyle(3, 0xff0000);line.graphics.moveTo(curX, curY);stage.addEventListener(MouseEvent.CLICK, onClick);showBtn.addEventListener(MouseEvent.CLICK, onShowClick);} private function onShowClick(event : MouseEvent) : void{if(pz.parent){removeChild(pz);removeChild(line);}else{addChildAt(pz,0);addChildAt(line,1);}} private function onClick(event : MouseEvent) : void{line.graphics.lineTo(event.stageX, event.stageY);if(RealHitTest.hitTestObj(line, pz)){line.graphics.clear();line.graphics.lineStyle(3, 0xff0000);line.graphics.moveTo(curX, curY);}else{curX event.stageX;curY event.stageY;boxTween.setValues({x:curX,y:curY});}}}} RealHitTest: package org.mousebomb.display{import flash.display.BlendMode;import flash.display.DisplayObjectContainer;import flash.display.Bitmap;import flash.display.BitmapData;import flash.display.DisplayObject;import flash.geom.ColorTransform;import flash.geom.Matrix;import flash.geom.Rectangle; ** * Flash’s built-in HitTestObject is buggy; this class is the real HitTest * @author Mousebomb (mousebomb@gmail.com) * @date 2010-3-14 *public class RealHitTest{private static var bmp : Bitmap new Bitmap(); ** * The idea behind this method comes from ryan-liu * @return Whether they overlap * @param src The object to compare * @param target The object to compare it against * src and target must share the same container, or have their origin coordinates aligned *public static function hitTestObj(src : DisplayObject,target : DisplayObject) : Boolean{Get the region of the object being compared to offset the bitmapvar srcBound : Rectangle src.getBounds(src.parent);var bmd : BitmapData new BitmapData(srcBound.width, srcBound.height, false, 0);bmp.bitmapData bmd;var mtx1 : Matrix new Matrix();var mtx2 : Matrix new Matrix();mtx1.rotate(src.rotation * Math.PI 180);mtx1.tx src.x-srcBound.x;mtx1.ty src.y-srcBound.y;mtx2.rotate(target.rotation * Math.PI 180);mtx2.tx target.x - srcBound.x;mtx2.ty target.y - srcBound.y;bmd.fillRect(bmd.rect, 0);bmd.draw(src, mtx1, new ColorTransform(1, 1, 1, 1, -255, 255, 255, 255));bmd.draw(target, mtx2, new ColorTransform(1, 1, 1, 1, 255, -255, -255, 255), BlendMode.DIFFERENCE);var rect : Rectangle bmd.getColorBoundsRect(0xffffff, 0xffffff);Collision detection doneIf all four Rectangle properties are 0, nothing was foundreturn (rect.x ! 0 rect.y ! 0 rect.width ! 0 rect.height ! 0);} public static function debug(s : DisplayObjectContainer):void{s.addChild(bmp);bmp.x 500;bmp.y 300;}}} Source files click here to download

title: The cat is missing
content: Woke up and the cat wasn’t at my feet. Weird. Come to think of it, I didn’t hear anything getting smashed last night either — could the cat have run off? So I flipped 180 degrees out of my groggy haze and got up to check whether the cat was still around. As usual, I pulled out the ham-sausage-slicing knife and slid it out of its sheath to make a noise. Normally that’s enough to summon the cat, who shows up demanding ham sausage. This time, nothing. What the hell. No way. Then I switched to the cat’s point of view and searched under the bed, under the sofa, under the cabinets — still nothing. Lately the cat likes jumping off the balcony to go play, so it probably slipped out again during the night. I went out and searched the floors, going through all three — 25, 26 and 27 — and still found no trace. Fine. I accept it: it’s gone missing. What grief in coming, what sorrow in going — it’s all fine. Coincidentally, the last image I got in the group chat last night was this one (does it mean something?): The cat lived here for 10 months. Maybe it got bored and wanted a change of scene, or it went off to find itself a husband. Since it isn’t in any of the building’s common areas, it looks like it did what it did when it first came to me: knocked on someone’s door and got them to take it in. I still have an unopened bag of cat food here, and it just up and left like that. A bit of a shame. Last year I was holed up at home all the time, never going out, with no one to hang out with, so I got a cat along the way. But lately the trend is that I often need to go out, and I’ll be traveling far from home for a while. Having no one to look after the cat is a big problem — it would require either me or my mom to always be home, which would seriously tie up both our schedules. Seen that way, the cat’s leaving is one link in the chain of fate. Its original mission is complete, its journey is over, and now the time has come to part ways — without putting anyone out. Thriving in adversity, perishing in comfort. This is an unusual cat. It’s greedy, it’s a glutton, it won’t settle for the status quo, it dares to venture out, its ambitions stretch a thousand miles, and it won’t fritter away its life in comfort at one household. So more thrilling journeys await it. A cat like this — how could it ever stay long in a place like mine? I wish Wind Cat a new, full and happy life, wherever it goes. Years from now, when I’ve made new friends and partners, when everything has changed and nothing is the same, when my career has taken off — will I still remember those once-familiar smiling faces, and every living being along the way that lent me a hand? Friends grown old, family members gone, classmates who vanished into the sea of faces, the cat that companioned my loneliness… A note for my future self, should I read this again someday: every individual, no matter how big or small, is a great existence, and each has contributed its strength to making the unique me in time and space. Without them there is no me. Thank you, every living being!

title: How do you drag objects in the list into the canvas?
content: Question: How do you drag an object from a list onto the canvas? Approach The ability to drag an object from a list straight onto the canvas is something you often need in a scene editor. You put a List on screen, each item corresponds to a building, and the user can drag the building into the scene. It works the same way as dragging things from the Flash library onto the stage. We can store the ClassName corresponding to each item in that item; when dragging starts, we create an instance of it and let it follow the mouse. Only when the mouse is released over a valid area of the canvas do we add it to the new DisplayObjectContainer. I wrote a demo for the details. The List is on the right — try dragging its contents into the box on the left and dropping them to see the effect. Click here to download the source files. Document Class : package org.mousebomb.dragLiToCanvas{import fl.events.ListEvent;import fl.controls.List;import fl.data.DataProvider; import flash.display.Sprite;import flash.events.MouseEvent;import flash.geom.Point;import flash.utils.getDefinitionByName; ** * @author Mousebomb (mousebomb@gmail.com) * @date 2010-4-27 *public class DragListItemToCanvas extends Sprite{public var list : List;public var canvas : Sprite;private var isHoverLi : Boolean false;private var curHoverLi : Object ; public function DragListItemToCanvas(){If you don’t write the following line, flash won’t compile this class in, and you’ll get an error at runtimeClass1;Class2;Create the list contentslist.dataProvider new DataProvider();list.addItem({label:”Drag me if you dare”, data:”org.mousebomb.dragLiToCanvas.Class1”});list.addItem({label:”I’m the same as the guy above”, data:”org.mousebomb.dragLiToCanvas.Class2”});list.addEventListener(MouseEvent.MOUSE_DOWN, onMouseDownH);list.addEventListener(ListEvent.ITEM_ROLL_OVER, onHoverLi);list.addEventListener(ListEvent.ITEM_ROLL_OUT, onOutLi);stage.addEventListener(MouseEvent.MOUSE_UP, onMouseUpH);} private function onOutLi(event : ListEvent) : void{isHoverLi false;curHoverLi null;} private function onHoverLi(event : ListEvent) : void{isHoverLi true;curHoverLi event.item;} Mouse releasedprivate function onMouseUpH(event : MouseEvent) : void{There is a dragged objectif(curDraging){curDraging.stopDrag();removeChild(curDraging);Land on the canvasif(canvas.hitTestPoint(event.stageX, event.stageY)){canvas.addChild(curDraging);curDraging.alpha 1;var localPos : Point canvas.globalToLocal(new Point(event.stageX, event.stageY));curDraging.x localPos.x;curDraging.y localPos.y;}curDraging null;}} Record the current dragprivate var curDraging : Sprite; private function onMouseDownH(event : MouseEvent) : void{if(curHoverLi){var className : String curHoverLi[“data”];curDraging getItemByClassName(className);curDraging.x event.stageX;curDraging.y event.stageY;curDraging.alpha .6;addChild(curDraging);curDraging.startDrag();}} Get the corresponding instanceprivate function getItemByClassName(className : String) : Sprite{var cla : Class getDefinitionByName(className) as Class;return new cla();}}}

title: A Tale of Awkward People and Awkward Moments
content: When you’re in a bind and ask for help, if you’re sincere, the other person will definitely sense it. Don’t expect to get help by using a flattering tone in a moment of crisis. Experienced people all understand: the more unusually ingratiating someone’s tone is, the more that person is a wolf in sheep’s clothing — and the more vicious they turn once the mask drops. Here’s how it went down: at noon today I was playing tai chi on the keyboard with the 26 English letters and a pile of special characters, when suddenly ding-ding-ding — a QQ message came in. Mousebomb 12:31:20 1. Ask your family 2. Ask your client 3. Ask classmates you know well 4. Ask people from your old team X.xiaohui 12:31:03 [ X.xiaohui 12:32:15 All of those you mentioned failed X.xiaohui 12:32:29 That’s why… Mousebomb 12:32:34 Then heaven wants you dead X.xiaohui 12:32:48 [](http://cdn.mousebomb.org/blog/personalblog/wp-content/uploads/2010/04/PVSCAJM1FBYMS2LR5JU1.gif) X.xiaohui 12:33:19 I knew you had no compassion X.xiaohui 12:35:32 I curse you to never find a wife X.xiaohui 12:35:42 Hmph… Mousebomb 12:38:17 I knew you wouldn’t pass the test Mousebomb 12:39:01 One face when you’re asking for help, and the moment you don’t get it you flip. If you keep this up, the one you’re letting down is yourself. Heaven helps those who help themselves. X.xiaohui 12:39:15 I knew you were just messing with me on purpose Mousebomb 12:39:41 If all women were like you, I’d never bother finding a wife. Messing with you? I’m not lending you anything. X.xiaohui 12:40:40 I’m not short of money X.xiaohui 12:40:54 I’ve got plenty X.xiaohui 12:41:58 You piece of garbage, get far away from me After that I just closed the window — I was dead, far, far away. But at that moment I understood: no wonder a girl like her had failed at all of them during her “time of trouble” — 1. Ask your family 2. Ask your client 3. Ask classmates you know well 4. Ask people from your old team. There’s a thing in this world called character, and it works wonders. Deposit a drop of water in ordinary times, and in hard times you’ll have a whole ocean. The reverse is just courting your own destruction… When you’re in a bind and ask for help, if you’re sincere, the other person will definitely sense it. Don’t expect to get help by using a flattering tone in a moment of crisis. Experienced people all understand: the more unusually ingratiating someone’s tone is, the more that person is a wolf in sheep’s clothing — and the more vicious they turn once the mask drops. As someone seeking help, you need to be clear about your own situation, and clear about the other person’s situation too. Nobody owes you anything from birth. Someone’s living their life just fine, and suddenly because they won’t help you, you curse them. Of all things, this kind of hair-trigger hostility toward others hurts you the most — it makes your future life and career go badly, and leaves you annoyed at everyone you meet. Conversely, a person with joy in their heart treats others with generosity and kindness, and they tend to get help from all sides in what they do. If you’re the kind of friend who loves to help others, you also need to be careful of people like this. Many people set out to help others and end up doing thankless work, or even get scammed and lose far more than they gave. Don’t harbor the intent to harm others, but don’t drop your guard either — even a gentleman has principles and limits. Before helping someone, you must understand exactly what’s going on. Take this girl who was chatting with me above — she’s alone in a strange city, has money to get on QQ on her phone and ask someone she’s never met to lend her money, but can’t manage to borrow from the friends and relatives she’s known since childhood, from classmates she’s met face to face, or from colleagues. My guess at the time was that she either ran away from home or she’s a scammer. A person of normal intelligence, taking responsibility for themselves, would never end up in a situation like that. Maybe it’s my ignorance, maybe I’ve never lived through that kind of hardship where she couldn’t even afford a meal, but I believe that a person with good qualities will find helpful people wherever they go. Same as before: you need good character. In hard times you’ve got to keep a broad view — when your heart is at peace, things go smoothly. My wish for everyone who has lost themselves in the city: may you find your innocent heart again, and regain the joy and contentment that were yours from birth.

title: Can't set the size of the Loader?
content: Problem: var loader:Loader = new Loader(); loader.loadBytes(byteArr); return loader; After that, trace(loader.width,loader.height) gives (0,0), and as soon as you change the width and height via loader.width and loader.height, it stops showing up. Cause and solution: Like load, loadBytes is asynchronous. You need to listen for the complete event, and only after complete can you manipulate the content. btw: Starting today, whenever a reader asks me a question — simple or complex — as long as I haven’t written about it before, I’ll record it on the blog.

title: Internal mechanisms of Flash Player 10.1
content: This article was reposted here after I saw it on http://riaoo.com/?p=1658; the original content comes from http://blogs.adobe.com/xwlin/2010/04/flash_player_101_-_adobe_max_2009.html and http://blogs.adobe.com/xwlin/2010/04/flash_player_101_-_adobe_max_2009_1.html Speaker: Lee Thomason (lthomaso@adobe.com) Translator: Lin Xiaowei (xwlin@adobe.com) PrefaceTime: the 21st of this month. Location: Beijing International Convention Center. Adobe is about to hold a two-day Flash Platform technology summit. I’ll have the honor of joining Ely Greenfield as co-speaker for the session, handling both the speaking and the translation. Ely Greenfield is a Senior Principal Scientist in the Apollo Integrated Runtime group, and he gave a superb talk on this topic at Adobe MAX 2007. I googled up a comment from a guy who attended the 2007 MAX conference about Ely himself and his talk: “I think Ely’s topic (Flash Player Internals) was the best of all the topics at MAX…” “Ely is that legendary guy who wrote most of the Flex Charting Framework in three days with his eyes closed”… The 2009 Adobe MAX still has a Flash Player Internals session, but the speaker is Lee Thomason (another hardcore veteran — Flash Player architect, nicknamed Player Guy, said to be the number one Flash Player guy). This is a very in-depth topic, and the talk moves fast: in one hour he covers as many aspects of the player architecture as he possibly can. Here I’ve summarized and translated the gist of his talk for your reference. Building Flash PlayerIn the past, mobile FlashLite and desktop Flash Player were two completely separate products, each developed and maintained by its own independent team. The FlashLite team had its own goals, product positioning and feature set, and decided its own project roadmap. This created a lot of tension and challenges between the two teams. So Adobe decided to merge the two teams — which means the upcoming Flash Player 10.1 for mobile and desktop will be built from the same codebase. At MAX, Lee mentioned that roughly 20% of the Flash Player code is still platform-specific, code that special-cases Palm, ActiveX, OS X, Netscape and so on. There are so many differences between platforms that a 100% shared codebase is impossible, but that still means 80% of the Flash Player codebase is platform-independent. One codebase, more player types.A unified player codebase makes it easier for Adobe to set a consistent strategy across mobile, browser, desktop and other players, but it also brings new challenges for the Flash Player team and the developer community. The first challenge is the processing power (mainly CPU) and memory size across platforms, which differ wildly and the gap keeps widening. An 8-core server CPU and a handheld Palm Pre have vastly different processing power, and a PC browser platform can offer several GB of memory while a handheld has only 20 MB — which pushes developers to build apps in completely different ways. Note: we’re not saying you don’t need to worry about memory usage on a PC browser, only that it matters far more on a handheld. The second issue is the variation in screen size and pixel density that a unified UI has to deal with. Today, more and more applications run across devices, so it’s increasingly important to understand how to lay out pixels on a limited screen and how to use them efficiently. An LCD monitor’s pixel density (pixels per inch) is far lower than a handheld’s, which means a 40-pixel button looks big on your LCD but is too small to use on a Pre. Likewise, even two handhelds with the same resolution can have different pixel densities: the iPhone 3GS has a 3.5-inch screen at 320*480 and 163PPI, while the Palm Pre has the same resolution on a 3.1-inch screen at 186PPI. So if we design our UI purely by resolution, two buttons that the player considers the same size may work fine on the iPhone but be unusable on the Pre. Another challenge comes from the variety of user interaction methods supported by different devices — some devices support keyboard and mouse, some support multitouch, and so on. Flash Player needs to understand different input devices, and we as developers need to understand what that diversity means for the apps we build. When building apps for multitouch devices, we need to remember that a finger is not a pixel-precise input device. The player has to give us the most accurate information possible, from the lowest-level raw data up to high-level user actions like swipes and taps. The last challenge of unifying on a single strategy is that user expectations for an app change from device to device. Expectations around performance and usability shift depending on whether the user is currently on a phone or a desktop browser. On a phone, the moment a call comes in, the current app has to shut down within 10 milliseconds; if the player can’t do that, users will be disappointed. Flash Player itself is not a magic bullet for every challengeThe only conclusion from all this is that we can’t expect Flash Player to solve every problem; in fact, as developers we need to understand deeply the platform our app ships on, and to know that a design that works well for one userdevice combination may not work at all for another. As we start building apps for more and more radically different device platforms, we need to keep these factors in mind. That’s part one of this topic. In part two we’ll look at the execution model and the player architecture, in part three we’ll discuss what improvements ActionScript’s second-generation virtual machine brings, and in part four we’ll dig into Flash video and the rendering system. Understanding the execution modelThe execution model is how Flash Player executes its instructions within each frame cycle. Behind the scenes Flash Player actually runs any number of threads, it’s just that AS doesn’t expose a multithreaded programming model to developers. That means, conceptually, we have to treat Flash Player as a single-threaded entity. The debate over the pros and cons of this single-threaded programming model never stops; I don’t want to say much about such a controversial issue, but please keep this fact in mind. The Elastic RacetrackThe elastic racetrack is Flash Player’s frame execution model. It describes how code execution and frame rendering balance against each other within a single frame’s processing cycle. Flash Player 9 and AVM2 made some improvements to this model; this information is based on research into the event mechanism and the rendering model, and the complete model hasn’t been officially published. The basic racetrack theory hasn’t changed: during the cycle in which Flash Player executes a frame, the first part of the time is used to execute code and the rest is used to render the objects in the display list. Each execution phase can extend its execution time as needed to run more code or do more rendering work, and the total length of the racetrack grows accordingly. What changed from the previous model is what each phase looks like within a micro-cycle and how they add up to a frame. AVM2 is driven by a marshal-level component in Flash Player called Marshal. Marshal is responsible for slicing time into the basic time slices that Flash Player works on. Here I want to clarify that Flash Player’s time slices have nothing to do with the frame rate at which a swf file runs; we’ll ultimately see how Flash Player combines these time slices into a frame. Running a swf compiled by Flex in Firefox on Mac OS, Marshal typically slices time into 19-20 ms slices — the slice size varies by platform and browser. For the sake of our discussion, let’s assume a slice size of 20 ms, meaning Marshal produces no more than 50 slices per second. Within each slice, five possible operations are performed in the following order: 1.Player event dispatch - for example Timer events, mouse events, ENTER_FRAME events, URLLoader events and so on. 2.User code execution - all code listening for the corresponding events from the previous step is executed. 3.RENDER event dispatch - calling stage.invalidate() during user code execution triggers this special event. 4.Final user code execution - user code listening for the special event from step 3 is executed at this point. 5.Player updates the display list. Marshal repeatedly executes 20 ms slices like this, deciding what to do next as it goes. All the operations performed within a slice ultimately boil down to the two-section racetrack described above (code execution, image rendering), which is what we call a frame. User code and invalidate operations fill the code execution section, and render operations fill the rendering section of the racetrack. It’s worth pointing out that these operations can only happen within the time Marshal has allocated; if your user code is short, Marshal will still wait a while after the user code finishes before moving into the rendering phase. To better illustrate which actions are executed how and how the elastic racetrack is created, see the example below, which describes how slices are handled in swfs running at 5fps, 25fps and 50fps respectively. From the example above you can see that at different frame rates, the elastic racetrack in a frame cycle performs different operations — for a 5fps swf, each frame handles 10 user actions, 1 invalidate action and 1 render action; for a 25fps swf, each frame handles 2 user actions, 1 invalidate action and 1 render action; for a 50fps swf, each frame can only handle 1 user action, 1 invalidate action and 1 render action. A very important point to note is that certain events can only occur in certain specific slices — for example, the Event.ENTER_FRAME event can only be dispatched in the initial slice of a frame. Either the code portion or the rendering portion of a slice can run too long, making that slice longer than 20 ms — that’s what “elastic” means. To keep the playback rate close to the frame rate set when the swf was compiled, Marshal will choose to drop some slices. A swf file’s playback rate can’t exceed the rate at which the current Flash Player slices time. You can set a swf file to play at 120fps, but Flash can play it at most at 50 frames per second (the exact number depends on the current system settings). Code can be executed more often than the swf’s frame rate. Play a 1fps swf file: one frame takes 1 second, which is 50 slices, but in every slice mouse or timer events will fire, although only the last slice will render. You can also choose to render early by calling updateAfterEvent(), but only from within mouse, timer and keyboard event handlers. In that case, Marshal considers the current frame finished and moves into the next frame starting from the next slice. Finally, if a Sprite’s visual properties such as width, height change while the mouse passes over that Sprite, Flash will force a render. If the frame rate is not an integer factor of the number of slices per second, the rendering interval on that platform becomes irregular. For example, a swf with a 20fps frame rate running on a system with 50 slices per second: Flash Player’s behavior will be to play two frames every 5 slices, so the swf’s rendering frequency will be 2-3-2-3-2-3 (slices). (This article may be updated as the original author adds more content.)

title: [Repost] StarCraft II: Wings of Liberty Pricing Announced
content: Blizzard Entertainment® Offers Players a Choice of Multiple Payment Models**【April 9, 2010, Taipei】**Blizzard Entertainment® announced today that the highly anticipated real-time strategy game StarCraft II: Wings of Liberty, in its Traditional Chinese version, is coming to Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau, priced at NT$1,950 (HK$488). After purchasing the game, players can join the newly updated Battle.net® for online matches at no additional cost. In addition to buying the product package, Blizzard Entertainment will also offer players a choice of other payment options so they can enjoy StarCraft II, with details of the relevant payment plans to be announced later. Mike Morhaime, CEO and cofounder of Blizzard Entertainment®, said: “One of the goals behind the design of StarCraft II was to attract more players, bringing in both newcomers and seasoned veterans. The same goes for the game’s pricing options — we want to make sure players can have a more flexible experience based on their personal preferences and play style.” StarCraft II: Wings of Liberty is the sequel to Blizzard Entertainment®’s 1998 hit StarCraft, which has long been regarded by players and critics worldwide as one of the best real-time strategy games ever made. StarCraft II once again centers on the conflict among the protoss, terrans, and zerg, deploying beloved units from the original StarCraft while adding many upgraded new units and abilities, letting players experience entirely new missions and strategies. The game uses a new 3D graphics engine that maintains the original’s level of speed and responsiveness while displaying hundreds of units at once in large-scale battles. StarCraft II: Wings of Liberty continues the epic adventure campaign storyline of its predecessor StarCraft: Brood War, depicting the heroic deeds of rebel leader Jim Raynor, and features familiar characters as well as newly born heroes. Players can enjoy a personalized experience across 29 missions, choosing their mission path, the technology they use, and advanced research according to their own play style. The game also includes several mini-challenge modes to help players learn the basic strategies of multiplayer combat. In addition, players can choose from dozens of multiplayer maps on the new Battle.net for online competition; the new Battle.net will launch alongside StarCraft II: Wings of Liberty. The new Battle.net will also offer an unprecedented online gaming experience, with features such as voice communication, character profiles and achievements, stat tracking, ladders and leagues, and cloud file storage. StarCraft II: Wings of Liberty can be installed on Windows® XPWindows Vista®Windows® 7 and Macintosh® systems. More information, including the game’s release date, will be announced soon. About Blizzard EntertainmentBlizzard Entertainment (www.blizzard.com), known for such widely acclaimed series as World of Warcraft®, Warcraft®, StarCraft®, and Diablo®, is a member of Vivendi Games and one of the most important developers and publishers in the global gaming industry. Its track record includes ten number-one-selling single-player and multiplayer games of the year; its Battle.net® service provides an online entertainment platform for players around the world who own Blizzard software, and currently has millions of active members. title: One Slap, One Story - Guoguo and Zhuanzhuan
content: Once upon a time there were two little kids, one named Guoguo and one named Zhuanzhuan. Because of an RP problem, Guoguo had been bitten by a wild dog when he was little, so there was a chunk missing from his face. Zhuanzhuan had been multi-talented since he was small, and since his foundation was rock solid, he lived up to the name “Zhuanzhuan.” Guoguo and Zhuanzhuan went to school together as kids and grew up together. Time flew by, and both Guoguo and Zhuanzhuan grew up. Because of his RP problem, even though his body grew up, the missing chunk of flesh was still gaping right there. By sheer chance, Zhuanzhuan ran into a talented woman named MM. MM worked in the entertainment industry, and before she fell into Zhuanzhuan’s arms she already had countless fans. Everyone who had seen MM’s shows said they were full of love. For a while, everyone took pride in being able to imitate MM’s talent showcases. After MM and Zhuanzhuan met, they not only hit it off but also shared the same lofty ambitions. After they married they fought for supremacy in the dance world together, and even founded their own sect, “Ri Yi Ya.” Every time Zhuanzhuan’s family put on a new show, they performed it on the stage built by the family of Guoguo, the one missing a chunk of his face. The fans at large were also used to watching Zhuanzhuan’s family perform on the stage built by Guoguo’s family. The fans at large preferred to buy the stages Guoguo’s family sold in order to learn Zhuanzhuan’s family’s dance moves and beats. And so the two families worked together for many years. Zhuanzhuan’s family performed on a great many stages, and Guoguo’s family sold a great many stages. Over and over, again and again. The fans had long since gotten used to it. One day, Guoguo’s family invented a new kind of stage. The once-bitten Guoguo felt that he no longer needed Zhuanzhuan’s family’s performances — that without relying on Zhuanzhuan’s family, his own family’s stage could sell just as many, oh so many. Besides, plenty of Zhuanzhuan’s old fans had already learned the kung fu of the “Ri Yi Ya” sect, and there was no shortage of talent in dancing and singing. So he had no intention of letting Zhuanzhuan’s family perform on it — he didn’t even send an invitation. When Zhuanzhuan learned there was a new stage, he assumed Guoguo was simply absorbed in building the most gorgeous stage of all, working for the benefit of song-and-dance and folk-arts lovers the world over and for the cultural needs of the broadest masses of the people, and he didn’t give it a second thought. Zhuanzhuan cheerfully led the whole family in rehearsing a new show, getting ready to perform on Guoguo’s new stage. The Guoguo with a chunk missing from his face threw open training classes far and wide, drawing huge crowds of song-and-dance lovers to lose themselves on his stage; together they founded a new school, “Ai Fen Ya Po Si.” Over the years, countless fans joined the “Ai Fen Ya Po Si” school, and every one of them had more than one “Aifen” stage. For the sake of the new stage, Zhuanzhuan rehearsed new, gorgeous dance steps and harmonious melodies. Zhuanzhuan kept preparing meticulously — for the new stage, and for new fans. So that more people could come up with new tricks. A short while passed. Incredibly, Guoguo once again, with a swiftness that left no time to cover your ears, steal the bell, or jingle all the way, ingeniously rolled out the “Aipade” stage: four “Aifen” stages taped together with adhesive tape. Seen from a distance, the “Aipade” stage was a giant 囧 character — a truly magnificent sight. Guoguo announced: “This is the ultimate misdirection (sorry, wrong word — dancing) experience!” At this point, Zhuanzhuan publicly announced to the fans that he would soon come to perform on Guoguo’s new stage, and that more people would be able to learn to bring out the strengths of “Ri Yi Ya” on Guoguo’s new stage. Fantastic! Fans around the world cheered. Zhuanzhuan even hung a time bomb on the World Wide Fishnet — sorry, my mistake — a countdown clock. Counting down to the moment his glory would return. A group of Zhuanzhuan’s “Ri Yi Ya” fans were having a party, singing “Always waiting, always waiting~ oh oh.” All of a sudden the Guoguo with a chunk missing from his face released his fourth-generation dance training plan. The plan conspicuously declared that Zhuanzhuan’s family’s dances were not allowed on “Aifen.” The plan read: Recently some lawless elements with ulterior motives, in a fit of madness, have raised the reactionary slogan “Zhuanzhuan loves Aifen,” in a vain attempt to use hacking to create a situation in which Zhuanzhuan dances on Aifen, and thereby overturn the indisputable fact that “Aifen loves to the end — living or dead, we don’t want you.” We, the broad ranks of training institutions, express our strong condemnation and deep anger at this. Hereby, on behalf of the broad masses of song-and-dance lovers, we once again reaffirm that our position on the “ultimate dance experience” will never change. There is only one “ultimate dance experience” in the world. Only what Guoguo’s family values is ultimate; only that is rich. Any “Ri Yi Ya” that vainly tries to hack its way onto the “Aifen” stage is stealing resources and will be unstable. Such behavior goes against the will of the people! We will not allow it. We will write it into the training agreement. You are all doomed to fail in the end! The story isn’t over yet… I have absolutely no idea what any of the above means. It’s just that yesterday I dreamed I went climbing, and there on a high mountain peak was a strange stone. I finally scrambled up close and looked carefully, and found that the stone actually had characters on it, so I pulled out my notebook, wrote the text down, and weblogged it. It’s only a dream — don’t take it seriously. Any resemblance is purely a prank. I didn’t understand a word of it. Purely a tragedy. [4.11 update:] Sorry — last night my internet was about to go down, so I didn’t get to the main point. Why did Guoguo decide not to let Zhuanzhuan and the people of the “Ri Yi Ya” school use his stage? The truth is, Guoguo had long been using his stage to attract the elite of song and dance, raking in piles and piles of cash and popularity for himself, and among those elites, of course, plenty had come up through “Ri Yi Ya” and other schools. By now, Guoguo felt his elite was already huge and the world’s profits were rich and plentiful, and he didn’t want to change this money-raking situation. Guoguo understood that he wasn’t just a stage seller — he wanted to take over the entire entertainment industry. In the future, the most famous superstars would all have to be packaged by Guoguo. But the “Ri Yi Ya” school under Zhuanzhuan was growing stronger by the day. Thanks to the foundation MM had laid back then, it had a huge membership spread across all kinds of stages around the world. Watching his stages and his global training institutions grow bigger and bigger, Guoguo worried that if he let the “Ri Yi Ya” crowd in to stir things up, it would eat into his own power. So Guoguo decided to go all the way, to fall out with Zhuanzhuan’s family sooner rather than later, and to demand that the dream-filled members of the “Ri Yi Ya” faction join the official “Ai Fen Ya Po Si” training institution — otherwise they would never get onto Guoguo’s stage. Guoguo — the Guoguo with a chunk missing from his face — pulled out a killer move, claiming that the dance moves of Zhuanzhuan’s “Ri Yi Ya” faction were terribly damaging to the stage, that they would shorten the stage’s service life, and that they could even cause all kinds of problems with the stage. Oh! Now I get it! Guoguo’s stage was indeed gorgeous, but it had a fatal flaw that made it, in some respects, less stable and durable than other stages — because quite a few of Guoguo’s stages were held together with adhesive tape. The “Ri Yi Ya” school had a great many members, with wildly varying levels of skill. Sure, there were quite a few “stage killers” among them, but those were just a minority of beginners. Could Guoguo really be afraid of this small minority? But I really can’t figure it out — Guoguo’s stage may be taped together, but it has its own protection mechanism — when a dancer uses too much force, the stage automatically catapults the unlucky guy off to Mars. So why, with that mechanism in place, is Guoguo still not reassured? More and more voices of doubt. Later Guoguo added: “The old model is already OUT!” “Even if you show up in hazmat suits, you’re not welcome on my stage. What you’re doing is simply breaking the standard.” I think I get it now. Guoguo — the Guoguo with a chunk missing from his face — go screw yourself!

title: [Repost] Apple Slaps Developers In The Face
content: This article is reprinted from http://theflashblog.com/?p=1888 [Adobe would like me to make it clear that the opinions below are not the official views of the company and are entirely my own.] By now you have surely heard about the new iPhone 4.0 SDK language that appears to make creating applications in any non-Apple-approved languages a violation of terms. Obviously Adobe is looking into this wording carefully so I will not comment any further until there is an official conclusion. [Sentence regarding Apple’s intentions redacted at request from Adobe]. This has nothing to do whatsoever with bringing the Flash player to Apple’s devices. That is a separate discussion entirely. What they are saying is that they won’t allow applications onto their marketplace solely because of what language was originally used to create them. This is a frightening move that has no rational defense other than wanting tyrannical control over developers and more importantly, wanting to use developers as pawns in their crusade against Adobe. This does not just affect Adobe but also other technologies like Unity3D. I am positive that there are a large number of Apple employees that strongly disagree with this latest move. Any real developer would not in good conscience be able to support this. The trouble is that we will never hear their discontent because Apple employees are forbidden from blogging, posting to social networks, or other things that we at companies with an open culture take for granted. Adobe and Apple has had a long relationship and each has helped the other get where they are today. The fact that Apple would make such a hostile and despicable move like this clearly shows the difference between our two companies. All we want is to provide creative professionals an avenue to deploy their work to as many devices as possible. We are not looking to kill anything or anyone. This would be like us putting something in our SDK to make it impossible for 3rd-party editors like FDT to work with our platform. I can tell you that we wouldn’t even think or consider something like that. Many of Adobe’s supporters have mentioned that we should discontinue the Creative Suite products on OS X as a form of retaliation. Again, this is something that Adobe would never consider in a million years. We are not looking to abuse our loyal users and make them pawns for the sake of trying to hurt another company. What is clear is that Apple most definitely would do that sort of thing as is evidenced by their recent behavior. Personally I will not be giving Apple another cent of my money until there is a leadership change over there. I’ve already moved most of my book, music, and video purchases to Amazon and I will continue to look elsewhere. Now, I want to be clear that I am not suggesting you do the same and I’m also not trying to organize some kind of boycott. Me deciding not to give money to Apple is not going to do anything to their bottom line. But this is equivalent to me walking into Macy’s to buy a new wallet and the salesperson spits in my face. Chances are I won’t be buying my wallets at Macy’s anymore, no matter how much I like them. Now let me put aside my role as an official representative of Adobe for a moment as Speaking purely for myself, I would look to make it clear what is going through my mind at the moment. Go screw yourself Apple.

Flash SEO Tool
content: I stumbled on Flash SEO tool — an SEO tool for Flash sites that helps get your Flash site crawled by web spiders. The project will soon be available for download on Google Code http://code.google.com/p/flashseotool/. Current features: HTML menus and submenus for web spiders Title, meta, keywords and description Friendly URLs Simple, automatic updates straight from your AS3 code Features coming later: Generating a Google sitemap Deep linking integration support Integration with Delicious, Twitter and friends Generating RSS How it works:Google has actually been exploring how to index Flash sites for a long time, and it made progress early on (there’s an article http://googlechinablog.com/2008/07/flash.html). Google’s crawler can index content compiled into the SWF, but dynamically loaded text or images are still a pain. Flash SEO tool’s solution is to automatically generate a fully functional HTML counterpart to your Flash content. Flash SEO tool takes care of it without you writing a single line of server-side code. The simplest way to update your SEO info with this tool is this — show the content to your users, and it updates itself. There’s an official example: First, add some AS3 code to your site. var seoSite:SeoSite new SeoSite(“someflashsection”);seoSite.title “Some title”;seoSite.keywords “Some, keywords, here”;seoSite.description “Provide some description too see it in google results.”;seoSite.htmlContent “Put content of the site here. You can use HTML tags here.”;SeoTool.updateSite(seoSite); Once the code is in place: Create some new site content Run the site in update mode (e.g. http://site.com/index.html?updateFlashSEO=myOwnUpdateKey) Click through the links on your site and browse every subpage, and the database gets updated. Then browse http://site.com/some/flash/section.html (that’s normal mode, so SeoTool.updateSite() in the code has no effect). The site you just optimized now shows content matching your Flash, and you can inspect it with http://site.com/some/flash/section.html?noflash. Heh, looks good. Once it’s downloadable I’ll try it out on my own site. For more on Flash and SEO issues and discussion, you can also check out this site http://www.flashnseo.com/ and http://www.flashseo.com/. [Addendum]: Its SEO approach is actually similar to my personal site. After looking at their site, I added a noflash parameter to my own site too: http://www.mousebomb.org/2009/?noflash. Either way, the static HTML content is visible to search engines, while people who open the page without the parameter see the Flash.

title: With HTML5 here, flash won't get far?
content: Ever since news of HTML5 got out, the new waves have been pushing the old ones forward, and more and more people have started paying attention to HTML5. From last September until now, I’ve read quite a few articles arguing that Flash will be replaced by HTML5. Recently I came across another one, “With HTML5, How Much Farther Can Flash Go?”, and it struck a nerve: http://blog.csdn.net/cping1982/archive/2010/02/23/5321010.aspx Thanks to the author Pengling Sanqian for sharing these valuable thoughts — the article is well reasoned and well supported. Having read it, I’d like to add a few personal points. 1. Times Have Changed — Flash Won’t Necessarily Repeat Applet’s FateWhether Flash lives or dies depends on many factors, and there’s no need to compare it to Applet. The historical context and user demands have all changed, so the old lessons no longer apply. True, Flash’s shortcomings have always been there (not long ago, even the iPad — touted as offering the “best web experience” — stubbornly refused to install Flash because of performance issues, leaving many web pages unable to display fully). But whether a product is good or bad is only part of the odds of winning; operations, promotion, and user demand matter just as much. A bad product doesn’t necessarily fail to make money, and a good product doesn’t necessarily make money either — there’s a certain fate in it all, and whoever wins the hearts of users wins the world. The author has already pointed out that Sun’s top brass at the time lacked foresight, retreated without a fight, and handed the web front end and desktop market over to others. Nowadays, though, Adobe is going all out with the Flash platform. It’s already a powerful software galaxy, with its parts echoing one another, its user base still growing, and developers fighting tooth and nail to get into the Flash development circle. Adobe has been laying out its pieces and building momentum all along, playing a game of Go over the future RIA lifestyle ecosystem. Right now it’s still on the upswing, with a long way to go before it heads downhill. 2. It’s Still EarlyThe author says: In the new era, as HTML5 gradually becomes widespread, a great reshuffling of web technology will arrive once again. I agree strongly with this. But our country has always been slow when it comes to reshuffling civilian IT technology. If a major tech reshuffle centered on HTML5 begins abroad, how much resistance would there be for our motherland to change its technology all at once? I think you can see it clearly just by looking at the fact that the MIIT’s website-filing sites still only support IE6 to this day. Doing technology here is subject to “macro-control.” The author says: Just take a quick look at recent update trends for Chrome and FireFox, or even the future plans for IE9, and you’ll immediately realize: will they wait for you until 2022? Absolutely not! Before 2015, HTML5 will already be the de facto standard across all browsers. I think it’s just a shame that the proportion of users in China using these two browsers is still far too small — the customer is king, so there’s nothing you can do. The number of the unenlightened masses still surfing the web on a ten-year-old IE6 is just massive… Tell them to switch browsers and they’ll drown you in a vast ocean of the masses’ spittle and saliva. Just to wait for this crowd to upgrade their equipment, I figure HTML5 would already be in its adolescence. 3. HTML5 Has Been Deified — Flash and HTML5 Don’t Conflict“Engineer Zhang, have you started using HTML5 lately?” “Not yet — everyone keeps telling me that once you use HTML5, your back stops aching, your legs stop hurting, and you can run up five flights of stairs in one breath! I’m just about to give it a try!” “Yes, yes, come try it right away — HTML5 is really badass, it has all of Flash’s common features!” The author says: Just imagine: as HTML5 gradually becomes widespread, when you can play HD online video through a single tag, when you can render quite dazzling web animations through a single tag, when WebGL lets you hardware-accelerate your web pages to run 3D effects no worse than World of Warcraft, when WebSQL lets you save data in the browser as easily as using a desktop app, when WebSocket effortlessly enables communication between browser and server — who will still care about swf, who will still remember Flash? I agree with everything said above, but I don’t agree with that last line — “who will still care about swf, who will still remember Flash?” The original author is a clear-headed person, but readers often take things one-sidedly. Today in a chat group I heard quite a few people conclude, after reading the author’s article, that Flash has no future. So let me give some examples to show that HTML5 and Flash focus on different areas: HTML5 is really badass — it has all of Flash’s common features. 1. Web games. If someone makes web games with HTML5, I’ll play them the same way. This one is quite reliable! 2. Making cartoons. In the future someone will make cartoons like Pleasant Goat and Big Big Wolf with HTML5, and I’ll definitely watch them. 3. Cross-platform desktop apps. In the future someone will make desktop software with HTML5, and I’ll try it out too. 4. Multimedia courseware. In the future someone will make courseware on trigonometric functions, or even science-education shorts, with HTML5, and I’ll definitely recommend it to teachers and classmates. 5. Designing UIs with gfx. Hmm, in the future let StarCraft 3 or whatever else design its UI with HTML5, why use swf, who’ll still remember Flash? My examples aren’t meant to exaggerate Flash, but to show that there are areas where Flash needn’t be compared with HTML5 at all. As a user, I applaud the arrival of HTML5, but HTML5 is, after all, a markup language and shouldn’t be deified. A ruler has its strengths and a foot has its weaknesses; technology is just a means, and it’s fine as long as it’s used where it should be. The future is an era of cultural convergence, and technology has reached an era of learning from each other’s strengths and joining two swords into one. The application scopes of HTML5 and Flash are more about differences than similarities, and the two are more complementary than conflicting. In Summary, My Point of ViewWhether Flash lives or dies depends on many factors. There’s no need to draw an analogy with Applet — the historical context has all changed, and change makes prediction impossible. Please don’t exaggerate the role of a still-gestating HTML5 while belittling FLASH, and don’t compare HTML5’s strengths with FLASH’s weaknesses; the overlap between the two is far smaller than their differences. There is no eternal way in the world. Every era comes to an end someday, and Flash is no exception. Those of us working in Flash development should indeed be on guard — technology is only a means, not an end, and constantly keeping up with the times is the best course. When Flash technology finally retires to its hometown, there’s no need to feel reluctant to let it go. Flash’s glory days will be inscribed on the monument of history in every developer’s heart — a sacred and inviolable classic era. PS: Friends who aren’t familiar with HTML5 can refer to html5, the rising star of rich internet

title: The Ordeal of Downloading the StarCraft 2 Beta [Updated: Download and Crack]
content: StarCraft 2 is the RTS game I’ve been looking forward to most this year. Recent news says the open beta will be downloadable this month — I’m thrilled. Then I saw this: RT @StarCraft: #StarCraft2 beta will be released later this month! #SCUpdate I checked the official docs (http://us.blizzard.com/support/index.xml?locale=en_USgameId13), and indeed this round of open testing is open to all players — with one catch: you need a BN account and you have to create a StarCraft 2 BETA profile (you’ll need to submit your system info and such so BLZ can analyze it). Once the beta profile is created, you can reach the download page (though of course, I figure the beta download isn’t out yet, so after submitting your system info you’ll have to wait a few days to get to the download page). But when I logged into BLZ’s Battle.net, it actually redirected me to the Korean BN! I was baffled — is NetEase’s China Battle.net just for show? Why redirect to kr? So I had to manually go to the North American Battle.net and log in with my old account (last time when NetEase WOW launched, I was forced to change that account’s bound email, because the China Battle.net and NA Battle.net login emails can’t be the same!). After logging in, right where you create the beta profile, I got this blunt message: “You must have at least one full version of a BLZ game attached to this BN account in order to set up your beta profile.” True enough, I hadn’t added any games on the NA Battle.net; I’d only played wow on the China Battle.net. So I tried logging in with my China Battle.net account, and it told me the password was wrong. This shows BLZ requires that a NetEase Battle.net account can’t duplicate an existing BN account — maybe as prep for future data merging or cross-region play — but the NA Battle.net currently doesn’t recognize China Battle.net accounts. So then I went back to log in on the China Battle.net, and it actually told me “this service is unavailable.” Even if I could get in, I’d probably just see a world of boxes (World of Boxes, that is). Ma de in China, I say — StarCraft 2 is such a badass game, how long do players have to wait? I figure it’s got to be 8 months, right? 8 months?? 8 months is “especially late”! StarCraft 2 is a year minimum, don’t complain it’s long, and no discounts! You have to study the current state of the economic crisis — “especially late” already held you up nearly a year, and StarCraft 2 couldn’t care less about holding you up another two. Alright, this means that a CWOW user like me can’t join the StarCraft 2 beta through official channels. I’m hoping friends who have a NA Battle.net with a game account activated will share the StarCraft 2 beta after downloading it — I can’t wait for NetEase’s StarCraft 2. 2.13 update: Thanks to kain for providing a NA Battle.net account — I’ve filled in the beta profile and am waiting for BLZ to release it. Oh yeah, I might get to play this month! 2.20 update: The good news is Blizzard started the open beta the day before yesterday, handed out the first batch of beta keys, and the client can be downloaded from BN. The bad news is this batch had a limited number of accounts with open beta access; most players have to wait for the next batch of keys. The exact number for the next batch depends on research data like server load from recent testing. The StarCraft 2 client requires players to log in with a BN account; all in-game matchmaking features need you to be logged in to use, and even maps have to be downloaded after logging into Battle.net. Clearly, StarCraft 2 is no longer a single-player game but an online competitive client. Impatient players like me won’t just sit and watch, of course. If you want to experience StarCraft 2 early, you can follow these steps: Download the StarCraft 2 client (1.64G) with rayfile, and install it: StarCraft 2 beta client installer Download http://www9.zippyshare.com/v/36162268/file.html and extract it. Open the folder where you installed the StarCraft 2 BETA, and go into the Battle.net folder (e.g. C:\Program Files (x86)\StarCraft II Beta\Battle.net) Extract the archive you just downloaded to get the Battle.net.gfx file, and put it in the Battle.net folder Once you reach the StarCraft 2 BETA main screen, you’ll see the offline client mode up in the options [2.21 morning] I just finished downloading last night before I lost my connection, applied the patch and went in to take a look. Login screen: you can see the Guest login mode After logging in as Guest Clearly StarCraft 2 was born for online competition; it’s no longer that single-player game. You can imagine how booming Blizzard’s Battle.net map business will be in the future. Related resources A StarCraft 2 map download site: http://www.nibbits.com/sc2/ An open-source StarCraft 2 Battle.net emulator project Starcraft-2-Battle.Net-Wrapper http://sc2.uuu9.com/ all the Chinese resources are up to date here Bonus — how to crack it to play single-player and AI matches: On top of the previous client, download Duowan StarCraft 2 Box or U9 StarCraft 2 Super Assistant, extract it to any directory (just put it in the StarCraft 2 directory), and it will automatically create a desktop shortcut. Open it, pick a map, and start playing. The 5.5AI I’ve been using lately (the computer cheats). Yesterday, after I rushed down one computer with z and s, I ran into another computer that had two squads of carriers, a squad of archons… Fortunately the 5.5AI is still pretty lame, and I pulled off a successful transition. I originally thought that since the Protoss Phoenix could only attack air, it should be the most specialized anti-air — who knew that although it’s anti-air, it gets sliced up by heavy warships and is only good against mutalisk-level units…
