title: I got called out (does that even mean anything?)
content: Tagging: Junghae Tagged by: Mousebomb Rules: 1. The person who gets tagged must write their answers on their own blog Qzone. Then add 1 question of your own and pass it on to 10 other people. List the names of the 10 people who have to answer the questions, and let them know they’ve been tagged. The tagged person may not refuse to answer, and whoever finishes the game will forever receive everyone’s blessings. 2. These 10 people must note on their own blog QQ Zone where they got the questions from. And they must think up one more question to pass on to 10 other people, so this happy game keeps going. 3. No passing it back, or you’re cheating! 4. The people whose names are called will receive everyone’s blessings, and all their beautiful wishes will come true before long. 01: Who occupies the biggest place in your heart right now? Given the principle of reader supremacy, the one occupying the biggest place in my heart right now is of course you. 02: If time could flow backwards, which day would you want to return to? Year One of the Cosmic Era. 03 Whose messages do you keep on your phone? Apart from ads, I keep them all. 04: What’s the dumbest, silliest, most regrettable thing you’ve ever done? Answering this question. 05: What’s the most romantic thing you’ve ever experienced? My life. 06: Who is the person you love most? Earthlings. 07: If your beloved were going abroad to study or for further training (at least two years), would you wait for them or break up — what would you choose? Can’t I go abroad too? 08: What were you just doing? Thinking about how boring the next question might be. 09: Any plans for the next holiday? I’m on holiday right now, designing and building my new site. 10: What do you want most right now? MacBook Pro 11: Would you confess to the person you like? I’m afraid I’d have to learn how to turn people down… 12: Do you prefer amusement parks or entertainment venues? I have no real concept of either — homebody here. I don’t like traffic jams and shoulder-to-shoulder crowds. 13: Your own nicknames — list as many as you can. Ovaltine, Dede (dě dé), Mouse, Bomb, Mousebomb, Kangaroo… 14: Who do you feel most grateful to, from birth until now? My family — though really the answer could be everyone. 15: In your next life, would you rather be a human or a small animal? Why can’t I exist in some other form? 16: Do you think friendship is forever? It both is and isn’t — it’s a long story. Why not think about it (idealist angle): suppose in your last life you were very close to a friend, but in this life you meet like strangers — would you say that friendship is forever? Or think about it (materialist angle): your friendship for a friend arises at a point in time and space — is that point eternal? 17: Which part of your looks are you most happy with? How come I can’t understand this question… What class is “looks”, what class is “part”? They’re different types. 18: You have to say one sentence to the person you love most! Just one sentence? Then I’ll say: “Great, you’ve shown up. Time is tight, I can only trust you — please remember to check what goes wrong with my mouth-centered audio output system after I finish this sentence.” 19: Do you often feel like a failure? I think the bro who asked this question probably often feels like a failure, haha. That’s a good thing. If you feel like a failure, just go create success. I often feel like a failure… 20: When do you want to get married? Huh? I’ll tell you when I figure it out… This question is like asking when the universe will be destroyed. 21: The most failed moment of your life? Answering this question. 22: Who is the person you most want to marry? This question is ungrammatical! Well said upstairs! Thinking about it, I’m speechless — beyond the grammatical error, on closer reflection this question has terrible user experience… 23: If you had to pick a character from a movie, who would you be? Huh? None of the characters in movies are anything like my style. I don’t want to pick a single one — I’m just me. This one gets me fired up: when I was a kid, parents were always saying to their kids, “Why can’t you be more like so-and-so, look how good they are…” — ugh, if that’s the logic, let’s all just go clone ourselves. 24: Your beloved can’t keep you company when you ask — what do you do? After a hundred days of rain, sunshine must come one day. As long as the green hills are there, there’s no fear of no firewood. 25: Would you rather be a wise person or a beautiful person? Wise. 26: To be together in the future, would you wait 5 years for the person you love? In that situation there’s usually no guarantee the other person won’t fall for someone else… Only if both sides can withstand the test, then… If it were me, I’d definitely take the long view and spend some time doing a full assessment of the situation… 27: Do you think your so-called love is the happiness of a whole lifetime? What meaning does a lifetime have? Is it really that long? What about the next life? Let me hit you once more: where’s your lover from your past life? Found them yet? 28: What kind of life would satisfy you? To be happy only after everyone else is happy — looks like I’ll never be satisfied in this lifetime. 29: The thing that has moved you most, from birth until now? The creation of heaven and earth. 30: When are you very confident? After surpassing the person I used to be. 31: In your eyes, the most beautiful scenery is What? The order of all things in heaven and earth. 32: Which song makes you cry when you hear it? Quite a few, it seems; most recently the Olympic theme song “You and Me”. 33: What do you hope the person you love is like? It’s a long story… 24: What are you like now, or what were you like last time — describe it in four characters. Sweating buckets. 34: Do you prefer mature or naive? Naive in how I treat people, mature in how I handle things. 35: Do you think that when you like someone you’re falling in love with their soul? Or is appearance more important? What use is loving a soul? What use is appearance? Is there anything eternal? 36: When you can’t forget someone, what do you do? After you die, will you still remember that in a past life I was your best friend? 37: American, European, Japanese, Korean or domestic dramas — which do you like best? Recommend one. X FILES, American. 38: Family, friendship, love — rank them and explain. Just order them randomly. What a mystical question… You rank the chicken and the egg for me and let’s see. 39: When are you most conflicted? I haven’t thought of a more conflicted moment yet; I’ll tell you when I do. 40: What do you do when your inner self and reality can’t be reconciled? Same as 34. 41: Would you allow yourself to be hurt twice by the person you love most? It depends how badly. As long as I don’t take a major loss myself, better to be tolerant (watch your master go enlighten them…). Actually, so what? Humans go around hurting each other all the time, don’t they? Yet as a whole we’re still pretty united. 42: A woman who’s even less driven career-wise than you — would you still accept her? There are plenty of people less driven than me; that’s completely normal. If someone were more driven than me, that’s when I’d pay serious attention. PS: this question seems to assume I’m rather lacking in drive? 43: Can you forget your first love? Probably not… but what’s the point? It all passes in an instant. 44: What makes you the very saddest? People have joys and sorrows, partings and reunions, and the moon waxes and wanes. Birth, aging, sickness, death — cycling endlessly. 45: Do you like the Alps or a diamond ring? I’m neutral on both. 46: One day you have to travel alone to a faraway place and can only bring three things — what would you bring? Laptop, credit card, bag. 47: What were your dreams as a kid? What are your dreams now? As a kid: build airplanes, writer, painter, Minister of Defense, company boss, hermit. Now: if not building a hut in the mountains, then roaming the four seas. 48: How do you feel? This game eats up a lot of time… 49: After finishing the questions, do you blame me in your heart? I’m a bit unhappy with the quality of the questions, but I still thank you for the self-assessment review you gave me… 50: Where do you want to live with your beloved, and in what kind of house? Scenic places, buildings of different styles. Chinese coastal cities, the Irish countryside, Hokkaido in Japan… Chinese neoclassical architecture, and so on. 51: What do you do when you’re heartbroken? Work, study, keep busy waiting to die. 52: Do you avoid making promises because you’re afraid of breaking them? Only promise what your abilities allow. If you shoot your mouth off, you’re doomed. Once you promise, do your best — even if you break the promise, as long as you did your best you have nothing to be ashamed of before heaven and earth. 53: Now that you’ve finished the questions, tell a joke (since you’re done, this shouldn’t count as giving people a hard time). Too bad I’m not done yet… 54: Will you always remember me? “Me” is ambiguous — the original author, or the previous baton-holder? 55: Is being fat a crime? No. 56: When was your first love? During my first love, of course. 57: Use one thing to describe “happiness”. Wholeness. 58: What’s your reaction when you see a handsome guy (or a beauty)? Adjusting my focal length… 59: How do you grind out MONEY? What does the question even mean? Is it a dialect? I don’t get it. 60: If you had to pick a man or woman from Laos or Myanmar as your partner, which would you pick? What if it were an alien? The question I’m adding: 61. Do you think this snowballing game is meaningful? How is the “no passing it back” rule actually enforced? Who’s responsible for bubbling up and listing everyone it’s been passed to? An appeal: whoever starts this game first in the future, please keep a list of everyone who’s taken part as the questions snowball, to avoid recursion… I’m not tagging anyone… I’m exhausted. Whoever wants to pick it up, just Trackback.

title: Fixing the error when Flash reads a ByteArray from amfphp
content: Who will save me? Error reading ByteArray from amfphp in Flash Related search phrases: Sending a ByteArray from AMFPHP to Flash fails AMF can’t send a ByteArray to AS3 ByteArray can’t be remoted to Flash TypeError: Error #1034: Type Coercion failed: cannot convert Object@******* to flash.utils.ByteArray. TypeError: Error #1034: 强制转换类型失败:无法将 Object@*******转换为 flash.utils.ByteArray It happens with AS3 Flash remoting, not with Flex remoting. Problem description:I keep files on the server and want to return them as a ByteArray through amfphp. Something like this:PHP part AS part package { import flash.net.NetConnection; import flash.display.Sprite; import flash.utils.ByteArray; import flash.net.ObjectEncoding; import flash.events.*; import flash.net.Responder; public class Test extends Sprite{ private var __netConn:NetConnection new NetConnection(); private var __gateWay:String; public function Test():void { var gw:String”http://Universe.mousebomb/amf/gateway.php;//修改地址测试 __netConn.objectEncodingObjectEncoding.AMF3; __netConn.connect(gw); __netConn.call(“mousebomb.Test.a”, new Responder(onCallResult,onCallFault)); } private function onCallResult(re:ByteArray):void { trace(re);输出: TypeError: Error #1034: 强制转换类型失败:无法将 Object@3046179 转换为 flash.utils.ByteArray。 } private function onCallFault(re:Object):void { for (var i in re) { trace(i+””+re[i]); } } } } The result returned by AMF shows up in the AMFPHP browser as type ByteArray: (flash.utils::ByteArray)#0 bytesAvailable 124118 endian “bigEndian” length 124118 objectEncoding 3 position 0 But in the Flash I’m testing with it outputs: TypeError: Error #1034: 强制转换类型失败:无法将 Object@3046179 转换为 flash.utils.ByteArray。 So where’s the problem? Solutions:Solution 1:PHP code: … $contents base64_encode(file_get_contents(“$文件路径”)); return $contents; AS code: protected function onCallResult(re:String):void { var fileBytes:ByteArray Base64.decodeToByteArray(re); fileBytes已获得. 可以有很多用途,比如,用Loader载入一幅图片… … } This approach returns the file as a base64 string and decodes it back into a ByteArray in Flash. To pull this off you need the class provided by import [http://dynamicflash.com/goodies/base64/(http://dynamicflash.com/goodies/base64/)If you can’t be bothered to go there, you can download it here. Solution 2:This is the real key, actually. You can’t just assume that setting NetConnection.objectEncoding ObjectEncoding.AMF3 on the Flash side is enough — what matters more is setting AMFPHP itself to AMF3 encoding. Add $GLOBALS[‘amfphp’][‘encoding’] ‘amf3’; to the PHP code AS code, for example you can write it like this protected function onCallResult(re:ByteArray):void { ….直接用re喽 } And the problem solves itself… Writing this down, even though it really shouldn’t have been a problem in the first place… I hope this article is useful to you, so that if you run into the same situation you don’t have to take as many detours as I did. This problem had been bugging me since last night. After more than 20 hours of fighting, the search-and-rescue operation finally made progress, and I ended up with two solutions. Even though I got the effect I needed, I’m still puzzled: it seems this problem only exists in Flash, Flex is fine with it. Someone says the same. A lament: there’s way too little technical writing in Chinese, so searches keep coming up empty. I had really bad luck this time — I almost couldn’t find it even in English… Thanks to AuZn, 杜增强, Y-boy, Lonely Volcano for the leads… References:http://forum.sephiroth.it/showthread.php?t=10194 A guy on this forum asks “Blob field not casted to ByteArray upon sending to AS3“http://www.astorm.ch/blog/index.php?post/2008/04/01/Remoting-et-ByteArray-avec-Flash-et-AS3 Remoting et ByteArray avec Flash et AS3

title: SGA5 Episode 4, Aerial Combat
content: The first 3 episodes of this season were all pretty boring, but episode 4 showed up with a time-hopping Daedalus that drew them aboard and took them on a tour of a few parallel universes. Along the way they ran into aliens and had a bit of a space battle — space battles still have some appeal for me… even though the effects aren’t as good as Sins of a Solar Empire‘s effects, it’s rare to see a TV show pull this off. Overall, I still haven’t come across any genuinely gripping plot this season — feels like SGA is starting to drift toward soap opera territory. I really miss season 2; the storylines were so good! Looking forward to what’s next.

title: China in Its Bones — The 2008 Olympic Opening Ceremony
content: I’m very much behind this Beijing Olympics opening ceremony. It didn’t just embody the spirit of these Games and show off the depth and breadth of Chinese culture — it also showed China’s peace and friendship toward the people of the world. The ceremony was steeped in cultural heritage. When that enormous scroll appeared as if by magic amid the heavy tones of the guqin, and unrolled before everyone’s eyes, the whole stadium was stunned. This giant LED screen — 147 meters long and 27 meters wide — was the scroll that would unfold five thousand years of Chinese history, and the opening ceremony’s performance began from it. The “Ancient Echoes,” the Four Great Inventions, Chinese characters and opera, the Silk Road — China’s splendid culture was displayed as if by magic. The presentation was freehand and romantic, yet also concrete: symbols like the Four Great Inventions were woven throughout, letting Chinese and foreign audiences alike take in the essence of Chinese civilization directly. More than the brilliant creativity and high technology of the artistic program, what I appreciate is the unity, fraternity, generosity and benevolence of the Chinese people that it implies. China’s strength was not built in a day. The powerful Qin, the great Han, Tang, Yuan, Ming, Qing, and down to today’s People’s Republic of China — this unity of many ethnic groups is China’s great trend and the source of China’s strength. Since ancient times, China has treated others with courtesy and won people over with virtue, making outstanding contributions to world peace and shared prosperity. Since Zhang Qian of the Western Han was sent as an envoy to the Western Regions, exchanges between China and Central Asia were very frequent. Central Asian Ferghana horses were highly prized by Han emperors, and Central Asian crops such as alfalfa were introduced to China. Over 2,000 years ago, China was already trading goods with Central Asia and Europe along the Silk Road, exporting silk, tea and other goods. From the Han dynasty onward, the Korean peninsula and Japan had trade and exchanges with China. Starting in the Eastern Han, Indian Buddhist culture began to spread to China, eventually taking root there and then traveling via China to the Korean peninsula and Japan. During the prosperous Tang dynasty, Chang’an became one of the world’s most important cities, tolerantly embracing cultures from all over. With Tang support, Silla unified the Korean peninsula and maintained very close ties with China. Japan repeatedly sent envoys to Tang, wholly learning and adopting Tang politics, economics, society and culture, even modeling Japanese characters on Chinese ones and building its capital in imitation of Chang’an. In the Song dynasty, shipbuilding and maritime trade flourished, and the compass was already in use for navigation, pushing foreign trade beyond any previous level. The Yuan dynasty had a vast territory and great national power, and China had extensive exchanges with European countries as well as the Ilkhanate, the Golden Horde and many others. Marco Polo is the most famous representative of this. In the Ming dynasty, Zheng He’s voyages to the Western Seas were a feat in the history of navigation; the treasure ships of the eunuch Zheng He were far sturdier and more massive than Columbus’s ocean-going vessels. China’s policy at the time was to proclaim national prestige, not to plunder and colonize, so from nearby Southeast Asia to distant Somalia in East Africa and the Arabian peninsula, everyone welcomed them with joy. … Napoleon once said, do not wake the sleeping giant. But more than 100 years ago, Western bandits ignored that advice, came to the giant’s home, and not only stole things but killed people and set fires. From then on, of course, the giant was awakened. Later, the giant treated this band of bandits with forbearance. This is exactly the generosity and benevolence bred by our great China’s ancient, radiant civilization. The Chinese people are great in their tolerance, embracing all rivers and seas, benefiting all things without contending. A strong nation, but one that does not bully the weak; many inventions and creations, but no willingness to do evil. Since ancient times we have been a nation in pursuit of a harmonious society. Dynasty after dynasty has demonstrated the pursuit of peace and love. (Think of gunpowder — invented by the Chinese, used by the Chinese for entertainment, while Westerners used it for war…) That is the China in the bones! Peace and love are the eternal theme, our dream, and the dream of the whole world. The theme song of this Olympics, “You and Me,” took everyone by surprise — no one expected it to be so tender, not swallowing mountains and rivers, not surging and magnificent, but carrying the tenderness of moonlight, reaching straight to the softest place in people’s hearts. The lyrics are only 12 short lines, the melody simple and beautiful, using plainness to highlight greatness, conveying big emotions through a small perspective, with a strong human touch. Understand? My friend, that is the tender side of us Chinese, the benevolence bred over thousands of years of civilization. The Chinese people welcome guests from all sides with a brand-new bearing. At the very moment the main torch was lit, the giant seemed to bow and salute the whole world, interpreting love and peace to the world, interpreting the Olympic spirit to the world. World, did you see? Beijing welcomes you! Sharing: 2008 Olympics Opening Ceremony Beijing Olympics theme song MV “You and Me” (FF not supported…)

title: Still a classic: Beautiful Genesis 2
content: Remember this beautiful game? 美丽创世纪2 Gold Edition (simulation + strategy). It’s an old game, but its gorgeous art style still captivates plenty of players to this day (according to completely non-existent statistics -_-!). The delicate, finely wrought visuals and the lively, adorable character designs — this game made me feel just how warm and cozy a simulation game can be. I first played it by pure chance back in middle school, and I could never get it out of my head afterward. Early this year I was really looking forward to exploring that gorgeous fairy-tale world again, but times have changed: the domestic publisher 世纪雷神 is no longer with us. I searched high and low with no luck, and it took a lot of effort before I managed to get a secondhand copy on Taobao from a veteran gamer — what a collector’s item! Sigh, 世纪雷神 has faded from the stage. A moment of silence for them, and thanks to 世纪雷神 for bringing us the Chinese version. Heh, I still remember that endearingly goofy Pimon (who always makes me think of 3DsMAX) — all he cares about is eating; a UFO could land right in front of him and he wouldn’t even notice. Then there’s the drop-dead handsome Sajiki, whose fad is “spitting” (sort of like a water-splashing festival), and the sexy, gorgeous Amazons, where everything is turned upside down — a matriarchal society of women farming and men weaving. So this year I started playing this classic again. I’d play over LAN in the dorm with Xiong and Niu. Back when their towns were at level 2, people would move out every few days, and at the time I’d secretly congratulate myself on how wonderful my ideal rural kingdom was — everyone living in perfect comfort. But what I could never wrap my head around was that by the very late stage of level 3, once the number of houses hit its cap and no more could be built, my people started getting unhappy across the board, and crime exploded! Xiong, on the other hand, could basically keep having a batch of citizens leave every few days and never had a mass riot. Was I playing the game wrong? The most intense run I ever had: early on the town was totally comfortable, no resource ever ran seriously short, and mining, iron, and stone were all coming in fast enough. The people were content — farming, ranching, blacksmithing… Vast territory, expanding borders, everyone mobilized, trudging long distances to build the Great Wall. To build the Wall, those foremen often couldn’t make it back to town for lunch at noon, so I built a hotel and a warehouse out in the wild. That’s where the bad luck started… I guess I was only thinking about military expansion and wasn’t paying attention to my people’s happiness every day. In hindsight, that move was a total failure. Military expansion, patrols. The army attacks. Shit — this Amazon town is solid as a rock! It took a whole day and I still couldn’t take it; my soldiers were cut down in droves and I was getting ready to retreat. It got dark, then it got light again — shit! I’d been so focused on the expedition that I hadn’t noticed: back home my people had rioted! Bandits were running wild, and not a single citizen was left. Failure taught me: 1. Good fortune hides disaster within it. Everyone being happy is only skin deep; if you don’t constantly remind yourself to pay attention to your people’s lives, national decline is lurking… 2. War brings your own destruction. If you try to invade others, it won’t end well for you. Sigh, I’m not that good at the game. If you’re reading this and you play 美丽创世纪2, why not teach me a few tricks? 《美丽创世纪2》ISO image download: Download page (shared by StG) Download page (shared by 众人是孤独的)

title: The Chinese Wikipedia site is now accessible!
content: I’m behind the times again, aren’t I? If you’re even more behind than me, come on in and take a look—makes me feel a bit better about myself. I stumbled across it in a search today: the Chinese Wikipedia is accessible again. Turns out that back on July 31, 2008, a little after 3 p.m., word was already out that mainland China had lifted its block on the Chinese Wikipedia… From around 3 p.m. on July 31, 2008 (UTC+8), based on confirmed status reports, mainland China has lifted its block on the Chinese Wikipedia (both the encrypted and unencrypted versions). title: Google Music Search is here
content: Just noticed that Google’s music search has gone live (am I living under a rock again?) [caption id”attachment_89” align”aligncenter” width”500” caption”The preview player is pretty slick too, wow”][caption] Unlike Baidu, Google requires you to manually agree to a provider’s terms before you can preview a track in search results (currently it’s mostly an integration through a partnership with 巨鲸音乐网?). That’s a bit more rigorous — nice. Google takes copyright very seriously: any music you can find is licensed and cleared to be indexed (how nice is that). It’s comfortable to use, too. The most obvious feature: Google lets you select multiple tracks right in the search results and play them. Actually, I think that since GOOGLE cares so much about copyright and still offers this search service, why not add a payment platform and sell low-priced, legit online MP3 purchases? For more fun, go give it a try at http://www.google.cn/music/

title: Keep your mind wide open——Bridge to Terabithia
content: I took some time this afternoon to watch Bridge to Terabithia (aka The Bridge to Terabithia). After Howl’s Moving Castle, this is the fairy-tale fable film I’ve liked most. The film opens with a boy scribbling and running — art and dreams on one side, a hint at the rush of reality on the other.We live, we hustle, we run. From a certain angle you could say that the teeming crowds, bustling to and fro, are still muddling along, numbly living lives that make no sense at all. For money, for power, we scurry around all day long, forgetting the fantasies of childhood, giving up our ideals, our interests and our gifts, losing who we really are. Open your heart and keep your mind infinitely open, and you can create a brand-new world that belongs to you.The boy comes from a family that’s in the red. He loves to draw and to run, but because of his family situation he doesn’t seem to fit in. The girl who moves in next door and transfers into his class doesn’t fit in either (my guess: because she’s too good). Both of them get picked on by the school bullies, so they decide to go looking together for a secret territory of their own, one with none of those obnoxious classmates.You run a stretch into the forest, reach the creek, swing across on the rope over it to the far bank, and arrive at an idealized “land of kings.” Soon they’ve founded a kingdom here — Terabithia. They fend off the attacks of the Dark Lord’s minions — pine trees, porcupines, vultures — build a castle on the foundations of an abandoned tree house, free the Dark Lord’s prisoners, rule over Terabithia, and defend the castle from dark monsters and giant beasts…I think everyone has a kingdom of their own in childhood. When I was little, a few classmates and I once occupied the abandoned camper downstairs and turned it into a haunted castle — and even then outsiders were always stirring up trouble. Later I built models of warships, fighter jets and civic buildings at home and put together a simulated city…Oh, right — I also drew skulls and treasure maps. The skulls hung in the castle to scare off invaders; the treasure maps were handed out in limited quantities…What classic years those were. Hidden away in them are countless beautiful memories beyond counting or remembering.Living in reality, hustling about, in the end it comes to nothing — you’re a loser whether you win or lose. What matters is that you don’t forget the pure, beautiful fantasies of childhood, those incredible, dreamlike-yet-not-dreamlike, elusive fantasies.Friend, open your heart and keep your mind infinitely open. You can create a brand-new world of your own. On the girl Leslie’s****death (a “dictatorial” personal opinion; ignore it if you don’t like it):I’d assumed the film’s point was to reawaken the child in people, that it was a warm, My Neighbor Totoro–style story. I never imagined it would use “death” to elevate things — isn’t that superfluous? It was fine without the death; by the two-thirds mark I was already ready to give the film full marks, and then the plot hit me with a bolt from the blue. And now look — the American My Neighbor Totoro has turned into the American Pan’s Labyrinth. Through the whole last stretch I kept waiting for a miracle, thinking this was a fairy tale and it would surely have a happy ending, but by the end the die was cast… It sure earned a lot of audience tears.Still, at least they didn’t make the audience look at the body, and there’s no heart-rending wailing. The film still expresses the belief that people must live on bravely in this lonely, absurd, inexplicable world.(A pessimistic reading: the film is really suggesting that no matter how strong your imagination and how pure and lovely your dreams, they’re pale and powerless before reality — death! Read that way, I think the film is superfluous: it sabotages the very atmosphere of spiritual homecoming it built up in the earlier part.)Could pressure from Christians in the West be the reason they killed off this girl who doesn’t believe in Christ — to vent their spite?If they’d swapped in that actress from The Chronicles of Narnia to die, I bet there’d be a lot fewer tears (-_-!). To watch this film you should also watch a few related ones — My Neighbor Totoro, Pan’s Labyrinth, Howl’s Moving Castle. Comments from other viewers on Douban: 端午: (1) Fairy tales, presumably, are mostly written by adults, and presumably besides children, adults read them too. The adult world contains too many impurities; colorful as they are, they’re no longer the many-colored splendor of childhood. People will still say you haven’t grown up whenever you mention fairy tales. Just know this in your heart: a wounded heart and a masked face still having the courage to stand open and honest before pure fairy tales — that is probably exactly what lets you taste a sweetness in life that others can’t, rather than only rushing about and helplessness. (2) The authors of fairy tales aren’t ignorant of life’s cruelty, aren’t avoiding it. It’s precisely because they understand it that they understand life’s beauty even more, and that’s why the world in their writing is so pure, so illusory. (3) But is there such a thing as a fairy tale in reality? (4) But what if the fairy tale were very realistic, and the story in the fairy-tale world were no longer pure, no longer illusory? (5) A path opens in the labyrinth wall, yet the bullet strikes Ofelia; bright red blood runs down her arm, yet where it drips at the center of the altar, it opens the door to the underworld; Ofelia sees the king, her father in the underground kingdom, while everyone else sees her cold corpse. Illusion, or reality? Is this the illusion she imagined, or a real fairy tale? Or is this, too, a labyrinth — inside our minds. In the dark, rainy weather, the flitting fairy is no longer a winged creature with cicada wings; its exterior is blue-black, its face hideous; Ofelia wants to go back to the underground kingdom and become a princess again, but the one guiding her is Pan, god of beasts, embodiment of nightmares. How we wish this were a fairy tale, so Ofelia could happily turn back into a princess. Even though her kind heart could give up returning for the sake of the little brother in her arms, she dies anyway, at the hands of a cruel dictator. In the end, in that golden, glittering hall, she returns to the underground world and becomes a princess again — yet how do we know this isn’t just her fantasy? We hope it isn’t, and yet we feel it is. We’re still in reality; we don’t know whether Ofelia made it to that beautiful fairy-tale world. (6) Terabithia is a wonderful fairyland. With a magnificent castle, a winding river, a Dark Lord who has the people of Terabithia besieged, whose evil minions try to destroy freak and leslia, and a giant whose weakness, it turns out, is that grass growing between her toes tickles. And all of this is imagined by freak and leslia. After school they swing across the creek to this forest that belongs only to them, bringing along that puppy which is the giant’s dog, and the tree giant who follows them is modeled on the schoolyard bully girl, the monsters running on the ground are really little squirrels that can throw pinecones, and their cries are the boys in class who always bully freak; the things flying in the sky are eagles. Who says childhood is all happiness — an ordinary family, loneliness, a somewhat timid freak; only the fantasy world under his pen is beautiful, plus a beautiful, kind music teacher. Only together with leslia, who loves fantasy just as much, in their fairy-tale world, do they get to have a beautiful, happy childhood. A boy who draws especially well; a girl who does woodwork especially well; a wonderful fairyland reached by imagination alone. Let’s all sink quietly into this happiness and illusion. Yet that morning, the music teacher took freak into the city to visit a museum and didn’t invite Leslie to come along. That afternoon the sunlight was the same as ever, but freak and the rest of us were told that when leslia went into the forest alone, the rope snapped, and she who smiled like an angel had left. We cried. I always thought that in this story, freak and leslia would walk out of loneliness together, grow strong together, and the story would end there. If so, the story would be very ordinary — so ordinary it would soon be forgotten. But even so, I’d rather — I’d rather not remember this beautiful little girl than have her leave this world. (7) leslia’s death is more natural, more lifelike; and so, all the more tearful — because of that smile of hers, like a cool breeze, like warm sunshine. At least, through freak’s final care for his little sister jesse, we see redemption and hope, perhaps. ofelia’s death, though, is darker; even though the scene of her turning back into a princess appears, we still feel it’s the hallucination of her dying moments, that near-despair darkness, that darkness which mocks our wishful thinking about fairy tales. (Postscript one) I’d rather live in the house beside that nanmu tree. When I first moved in, if I’d met a black spirit, I’d probably have opened my eyes wide just like Mei, and been more surprised than frightened. Suddenly I think of my own home, and the creek by the road. Does the hill behind our house have a cute, chubby Totoro in it too! nettv: I just finished The Bridge to Terabithia — a work that touches the heart. Only after reading about it did I learn that it’s adapted from a novel, and a novel with profound influence in the US. Since I haven’t read the original, I’ll just talk about my own feelings about the film: 1. Life can be happy and simple, but it’s also full of unknown troubles and disasters. Through abstract fantasy, the work tells us to face everything bravely and open our hearts. 2. As the plot unfolds step by step, I gradually came to like so much of it and to recall bits and pieces of my own childhood. The melancholy boy, the dull chores, the bland schoolwork, the sudden turns into wonder, Leslie’s idiosyncratic personality, her rich imagination, the childlike innocence and enthusiasm she can’t hide — all of it instantly infected the boy, and infected me. Sadly, beautiful things are always fleeting; Leslie disappears, and the world of the two of them turns lonely again. Pain, repression, regret, all mixed together. When he finally realizes that nothing can be changed or undone, he picks himself up again and lets everything carry on its beauty and magic. All of this happens to a boy — how could it not stir you deeply. 3. The work has a strong Western flavor. Running through it from start to finish are encouragement, tolerance and the pursuit of ideals, and the plot is natural and engaging. I truly hope we can have works that teach us these ways of encouraging and educating children. Finally, I recommend it to all my friends. May every child grow up smoothly. 月华清影: Tonight I finished watching Bridge to Terabithia (bridge to terabithia) alone, and I was a complete mess of emotion. In the related forums on Baidu and Douban, the posts are also one long chorus of lament. Come to think of it, this film suits my taste especially well, because in it I vaguely see my own childhood. I had a similar feeling before, when I read The Green-Haired Water Monster. I was a freshman then, and one line has stayed with me ever since: “Not everyone gets to meet their Yao Yao.” The stages of life aren’t like a fairy tale, full of chance encounters. Most people have also grown used to mediocrity and triviality. Only after you meet “himher” do you discover how unbearable your life was all along. If she had never appeared, that country boy’s life would have been like most people’s — bland and boring. His parents, struggling to feed five children, wear sour faces and have short tempers. His sisters mock him and keep their distance. He sleeps in a small, dirty bed, has no new sneakers, and can only go to school in his sisters’ hand-me-down shoes, enduring his classmates’ jeers. His teacher is a stern, boring old woman. At school the boys tease him, making a “beep beep” sound whenever he comes close. That fat girl from the upper grades bullies him openly. Even the school bus driver, when he’s framed, throws him off the bus without asking any questions. After school he still has to help his always-busy father. A childhood like that plays out for countless people — luckily, that transfer student changed everything. The moment Leslie appeared, her striking presence knocked me sideways. I marveled that such a girl could exist — so full of spirit and yet so sweet. Leslie has an extraordinary imagination. Together with him, on the far side of the bridge to Terabithia, she builds an imagined country: Terabithia. There are magnificent castles, giant tree trolls, evil pine-tree monsters, sword-bearing dragonfly knights… Everything is real, and everything is fake. Magic and reality interweave; Terabithia is the paradise children build in their minds. The ending is impossible to accept. But compared with most people, the boy is still lucky. If he had never met her, how could he have shaken off all the trivial fetters of reality and enjoyed the wonderful world of fairy tales? Not everyone gets to meet their Yao Yao… 墨墨:收到明信片要吱声 It’s not fantasy — it’s the story of a boy growing up, and of his spiritual mentor, the girl next door. Growing up, and the troubles of growing up, is an eternal topic. Little Jesse has clean eyes and a sensitive soul. The troubles he runs into: 1. Not fitting in. He’s quiet by nature and loves running and drawing. 2. Being bullied. By classmates and by older kids. 3. A poor family. He can only wear his sister’s running shoes. 4. Craving a father’s love. Wishing his father would value him, even if it’s just a hug. 5. A secret crush on the beautiful music teacher. Just as he was sinking into these worries day after day, a girl named Leslie transferred into his class. Jesse’s life had always been closed up in a narrow environment and a stuffy atmosphere. Leslie’s arrival was like a key given by an angel; she opened the door to another world and led Jesse to see a broader world — and, more importantly, a broader soul. Leslie’s thinking is far more mature than Jesse’s; she has her own little philosophical system. She tells Jesse that a person’s growth has nothing to do with their parents. (My parents are writers — that’s got nothing to do with me having an imagination. Your father works at a hardware store — are your hardware skills that good?) She appreciates Jesse’s drawings. She gives him expensive watercolor paints. She keenly notices Jesse’s admiration for the music teacher and encourages him to help her carry heavy things. She creates the wonderful world of Terabithia and encourages Jesse to imagine, to build this world. We can see very clearly that Terabithia exists entirely inside the children’s heads, but we can also see the journey to Terabithia as the boy’s journey of growth and tempering. Accept the challenge, exercise your courage, and put it to use in your life. Rather than a private space belonging to two children, it’s a training ground Leslie created for Jesse. After all this, Jesse’s life changes. He gradually stops being timid, and he dares to say out loud to his father what he’s unhappy about. When the music teacher takes him to the museum, his eyes shine, and we can foresee that in the life ahead, Jesse will move toward a broader world, and he’ll always keep his love of drawing and his joy in imagining. We can guess at his profession: illustrator, advertising man, writer, picture-book author, film director. We can even imagine that when he grows up he’ll write, draw and film the Terabithia he can never forget. (Just musing… please don’t argue with me.) The boy has grown up. And his mentor Leslie, on the day he went to the museum, fell into the creek and lost her life. Or we could say that when the angel finished her task, she left this world; Leslie vanished forever into the creek that lies between the farm and Terabithia. In a sense, Leslie is the Bridge to Terabithia — she is what connects reality and imagination. At the end of the film, Jesse builds a bridge over the creek and leads his little sister to Terabithia. Jesse takes over Leslie’s role and becomes his little sister’s mentor. When the little sister grows up, there will surely be another mentee (I’d guess the baby in their family), and Terabithia will welcome generation after generation of princes and princesses. The fuel is used up, yet the fire is passed on, and no one knows its end. This is the best annotation of Leslie.

title: Enjoyed Legend of the Great Tang Rangers
content: Just finished the finale today. I’d actually written a whole lot… and then deleted all of it. Let’s not say any more. Each to their own view, each to their own wisdom; different perspectives, different takeaways.The world’s quarrels never cease, love and hate never pause, and no one can judge right and wrong, gain and loss.Hatred only breeds more curses; it takes universal love to save all living beings.Those who reach the summit will in the end vanish beyond the mortal world.Build a hut on Buguishan — or just roam the four seas. That ending where the four Great Tang rangers set off as a party was good — a new day begins again!Watching it, I suddenly thought of how many heroes fell along the way (the waves wash away all heroes)…The show tells us at the end: the true great hero is the one who takes peace under heaven as the highest ideal.Oh come on — if that’s all it takes, wouldn’t the world’s great heroes work themselves to death!The real great hero is every person themselves; only the innate universal love of humanity can truly bring peace to the world. Peace under heaven isn’t up to a handful of people — it depends on the awakening of all humanity. Attaching the theme song: Theme song “True Love” lyrics: For you I’d cross ten thousand miles of mountains and rivers, roaming to the ends of the earth. Through ten thousand zhang of wind and rain I’d stay by your side, making home wherever I go. Ten thousand pursuits, all for a love from a dream. Ten thousand times crying, crying, only waiting for you to open your mouth and answer, answer. Through ten thousand hardships we walked through autumn, winter, spring and summer. For ten thousand reasons I’d keep you in my heart for life. Ten thousand ways to say it, no need for vows of sea and mountain. Ten thousand times moved, moved, only for that one word in your heart.

title: A Somewhat Awkward Review of Kung Fu Panda
content: It really is a big world full of wonders, and hidden masters just keep coming out of the woodwork! I came across this badass review over on Douban, -_- Is the author a huge detective mystery fan or what? They actually worked out a hidden plotline. I can’t track down the author’s site for now — I’d really love to go pay my respects. What follows is the original text: I watched the movie twice more from the beginning and picked out a few details here and there, and I found that Tai Lung isn’t actually bad — he was most likely framed. On the contrary, Tortoise may be the real mastermind behind it all. I roughly pieced together the outline of what happened: the Dragon Scroll was actually brought up the mountain together with Tai Lung. Tai Lung was destined from birth to be the Dragon Warrior, and the Dragon Scroll isn’t a martial arts manual but a scripture for cultivating immortality. But Tortoise secretly swapped out the real Dragon Scroll and put an empty one back in its place. So when Tai Lung came of age and wanted to take back the Dragon Scroll, Tortoise stopped him, and came up with a way to lure Tai Lung into seizing the scroll, then framed him and had him thrown in prison. Over the next twenty years, Tortoise kept studying the contents of the real scroll and made some modest progress. He had a premonition that Tai Lung was about to return, so he hoped Badger would take some action — but Badger was scared witless. With no other option, Tortoise had to say they should open the Dragon Scroll. When it came to choosing the heir of the Dragon Scroll, Tortoise originally wanted to give it to the tiger, because the tiger is stubborn and fiercely competitive — even if she found out it was an empty scroll, she’d just study it herself and wouldn’t be exposed for a while. But when he saw the panda, who knows zero martial arts, he chose the dopey panda, figuring that would buy even more time (or maybe he thought it was almost a good thing?). Later, when he heard that Tai Lung had really broken out, he got scared again, so he pretended he had reached the end of his life — but in fact he just used the immortal arts he’d learned from the scroll to fly away. That’s why his departure was so sudden. Later still, on his way back, Tai Lung ran into the Furious Five, beat them, but didn’t kill them — instead he let them go back to the mountain. And when he himself returned to the mountain, he called himself a disciple, and when Badger said he wanted to fight him, he initially meant to turn and leave. There are also a few details worth special attention. First, Tai Lung appeared at the very instant the lightning flashed in Badger’s eyes, but he didn’t take the opportunity to launch a surprise attack. Second, when Tai Lung saw the staff the old Tortoise had left behind, he went silent all at once, because he thought the old Tortoise was dead and he’d never be able to take revenge on him — which was exactly the point of leaving the staff behind. What a scheme. Third, when his master said “I’m sorry,” Tai Lung’s expression changed immediately, which shows those words hit him hard; but in order to take back the scroll that was rightfully his, he hardened his heart and kept demanding the scroll. Yet during his fight with his master he actually held back his strength considerably, as you can tell from how his master was still full of fight a moment later (and he knows the Wuxi Finger Hold too — if he’d wanted to kill his master, he’d have used it long ago). So really, Tai Lung isn’t bad by nature at all. Think about it: he was framed and locked up for 20 years, so a little bit of retaliation on his part is honestly nothing. Tortoise is the true culprit — everyone has been played right into his hands. A few more details: 1, The Furious Five probably don’t even know for sure what happened 20 years ago, because they only joined after Tai Lung was imprisoned. And Badger would most likely avoid mentioning what happened to his most prized disciple, so the story of Tai Lung slaughtering the valley could very well have been told to the Five by Tortoise with plenty of embellishment. And with even a little thought, you can see it’s unlikely to be true: Tai Lung even let the Five go, which shows he isn’t someone who kills the innocent. How could he possibly slaughter ordinary folk? Besides, his goal was the scroll — sneaking in to grab it would be far easier than stirring up trouble in the valley first so that Tortoise and Badger were on their guard and then having to fight his way in. Tai Lung had no reason to do that. The only one he hated was Tortoise. 2, About Tortoise: he first began his cultivation on that very mountain, yet he rarely returns to the Jade Palace. Why? Because he needs to secretly practice the immortal arts — otherwise, no matter how powerful his martial arts, there’d be no reason for him to be able to foresee the future. Of course, his so-called “passing” was also faked, because the timing was just too convenient: if Badger hadn’t come up at that moment, he would have just ascended on his own — wouldn’t that mean nobody would even know? And even if his body turned into a sky full of peach blossoms, his clothes can’t have dissolved along with it, so the peach blossoms were just an illusion. That’s a very common spell in traditional Chinese novels. 3, About the scroll: it definitely wasn’t placed there long ago, because when the panda couldn’t get it open no matter what, Badger took it and opened it in one go — he even knew which end the opening was on (only now as I write this do I remember that Tai Lung knew too…). That shows he had opened the scroll before, or at least seen someone else open it, though he hadn’t seen what was inside. So it’s possible it was brought up together with Tai Lung, and he opened it back then; at the time there may have been something inside besides the scroll — something about Tai Lung’s identity. Also, I don’t think the real Dragon Scroll could be blank, because if it really were blank, then what you could attain from it wouldn’t just be “martial arts” — it would be more like “Zen.” And would someone who can grasp Zen still do evil? So what reason would Tortoise have to deny Tai Lung the scroll? And in fact, Fat Po didn’t really gain any insight from the scroll at all — the only reason he could beat Tai Lung is that his fur (or fat?) is too thick for pressure points to work… 4, About Tai Lung: his origins are a mystery. When Badger opened the door and saw Tai Lung, it was nighttime (there’s a lantern behind him), so there’d be no reason to open the door and go outside in the middle of the night unless someone knocked. And whoever brought Tai Lung there would have had to run down that long mountain path in just that brief moment (note the part where the panda can’t get in the door — you can tell there’s nowhere to hide on the mountaintop), so their kung fu couldn’t have been too shabby either. That suggests Tai Lung may have come from a martial arts family, and his later extraordinary talent for learning kung fu seems to confirm it. Tai Lung grew up strong under Master Badger’s tutelage, learning every one of his master’s countless skills. But my guess is that, having lived so long with a master as kind as a loving father, Tai Lung’s personality may have come to resemble Master Badger’s in some ways: stubborn to a fault and, being so straightforward, easy to trick — yet under Master Badger’s guidance, Tai Lung’s nature could never be too bad. Tai Lung’s growth did not escape old Tortoise’s eye. When Tai Lung came of age and was about to take back the Dragon Scroll, old Tortoise set a trap for him: he tricked Tai Lung into trying to seize the scroll to prove he was worthy of being the Dragon Warrior, and sent his men disguised as Tai Lung to go on a killing spree in the Valley of Peace and frame him (this part is pure speculation), making Master Badger believe Tai Lung had turned evil. Then, during the “trial,” he suddenly struck and hit Tai Lung’s pressure points, giving him no chance to explain, and had him thrown into a prison prepared in advance — locked up for 20 years. So Tai Lung was framed by Tortoise, not only failing to get the scroll but also being locked up in a heavily guarded dungeon. And to be precise, it was a very, very, very heavily guarded dungeon — so heavily guarded it was almost overkill: a thousand-plus guards, a dungeon dug hundreds of zhang deep, sturdy walls and fortresses and all kinds of deadly traps, and even heavy siege equipment of the kind you’d only see in large-scale warfare. But the most over-the-top things were Tai Lung’s shackles and the final go-down-with-everything scorched-earth move. Speaking of the shackles, we have to talk about old Tortoise. This dungeon was clearly set up by Tortoise, because the shackle that locked Tai Lung up was a tortoise shell! Even if Tai Lung had committed the most heinous crime, locking him up would be enough — did you have to chain him up so tightly that he couldn’t even scratch an itch? As the saying goes, the worst you can do to a man is kill him; old Tortoise didn’t kill Tai Lung but arranged things this way, which must have had a purpose. Then there’s the prison’s last line of defense: lighting the explosives and blowing up the whole prison. Don’t forget there were still plenty of rhino guards alive down there — why would their commander order the explosives lit (or rather, why set up such a twisted mechanism at all)? Sacrificing hundreds of his own men just to keep Tai Lung in? That can only mean there’s some great secret about Tai Lung worth far more than those men’s lives! My guess is it definitely has to do with the Dragon Scroll. Also worth noting: those rhino guards don’t look like good guys at all — doesn’t that also reveal the true character of the sanctimonious old Tortoise? So Tai Lung narrowly escaped the prison with his life and headed straight for the Jade Palace. Along the way he ran into the Furious Five, who had come to stop him. From what we see in the film, against Tai Lung and his pressure points, dealing with the Five was a piece of cake — so why didn’t he use a pressure point in that first fight on the bridge? I think it’s because anyone hit with one can’t move, and if Tai Lung had hit them on the bridge, the Five would likely have fallen to their deaths — something Tai Lung, as their senior brother, didn’t want to see. In fact, Tai Lung didn’t even want to fight them at all; he just wanted to defeat the so-called “Dragon Warrior,” reclaim his honor and win his master’s approval. This respect for life made the Five doubt — even waver over — the rumors they’d heard before. They didn’t know whose side to take, which is why they left before the final battle; otherwise, given their bravery and their personalities, there’s no way they’d have left their master alone on the mountain to face a powerful enemy by himself. Later still, when Tai Lung returned to the mountain, he found himself facing his master rather than old Tortoise or the so-called “Dragon Warrior,” and his master refused to forgive him no matter what — that’s when he said those sour words (listen closely and there’s almost a sob in his voice…). Deep down he was jealous of Fat Po. Then, out of respect for his master, he didn’t want to fight him and meant to turn and leave, but his master insisted on fighting, so he had no choice but to strike (though this part is a bit of a stretch). After defeating his master, what Badger said moved him deeply, but the Dragon Scroll might be hugely important to him and his family, so he had to harden his heart and press for the scroll’s whereabouts. Yet even though he wanted the scroll badly, the kind-hearted Tai Lung still refused to hurt his beloved master too much — otherwise he could easily have struck a few pressure points that would have caused his master excruciating pain to force the scroll’s location out of him. But he didn’t do that (though I can’t rule out the possibility that foreigners don’t know pressure points can be used that way…). And when he saw Fat Po, he only hit his master’s pressure point so he couldn’t interfere in his fight with the so-called “Dragon Warrior” — he didn’t want to hurt him; otherwise, in that situation, a casual toss into the water might well have drowned Badger… Then he fought the panda. Though he didn’t like this junior brother, he’d learned from the Five that their master wouldn’t teach the panda and the others the pressure-point technique, so, being a seeker of the martial way, he held to the principle of fairness and never used pressure points. And he didn’t really fight the panda much at all — on the contrary, the panda kept beating on him… Until he actually got the scroll, only to find it was a fake (only a simpleton like Fat Po would believe the Dragon Scroll was blank). Being clever, he knew Tortoise had pulled a trick — but since he thought Tortoise was dead, there was probably no one left who knew where the real scroll was. Decades of effort down the drain; his spirit broke, and he struck the panda hard. Unfortunately for him, the panda was immune to pressure points, and Tai Lung, reeling from the blow, had no heart for the fight, while the panda, heartless thing that he is, hit especially hard — so in the end he was defeated and killed by the panda (or was his kung fu stripped?), truly a case of a tiger fallen to the plains being bullied by dogs. 5, About the panda: dopey as he is, you have to admit he’s also a martial arts prodigy. And since he’s an orphan too, I suspect he’s connected to Tai Lung and the Dragon Scroll. Maybe both the panda and Tai Lung are the orphaned survivors of the clans that guarded the scroll. Of course, Tai Lung is probably a generation older than Fat Po. Fat Po’s dad might be a polar bear (Tai Lung is a snow leopard; their home base could be an ice field, maybe even the model for the Peach Ridge Prison), and his mom a black bear from the Valley of Peace (obviously a panda can’t actually be born from that — I’m just making this up). As for why he wasn’t with Fat Po, I’m not sure — maybe it’s connected to Tortoise sending men disguised as Tai Lung to massacre people in the Valley of Peace 20 years ago, and his parents died fighting to the last. Tortoise might well have known about this too, which is why he chose Fat Po as the Dragon Warrior — maybe he thought it’d be fun to have the descendants of the two guardian clans kill each other~ What an evil old man~ 6, About the Wuxi Finger Hold: this probably isn’t martial arts at all — it’s most likely an immortal art Tortoise learned from the real Dragon Scroll. Tortoise told Badger about it so he could defend against Tai Lung, and Fat Po, being a descendant of the guardians, figured it out on his own. = Most of the above is well-grounded — it’s pieced together from details in the film plus guesswork and association, not just talk. But what follows is pure nonsense, purely my own speculation… Long ago, at the end of the Third Dynasty, the Sorcerer King’s rule was about to be brought to an end. The last of the Sorcerer royal family ordered the imperial guards — the snow leopard warriors and the ice bear strongmen clans — to migrate with their entire clans to the kingdom’s treasury, the Peach Ridge Vault, to guard the last treasures of the Sorcerer Kingdom: the Dragon Scroll and the Phoenix Scroll, until they were once again summoned by the Sorcerer King. In exchange, the strongest members of the two clans could study the contents of the scrolls and share in their powerful and mysterious force. Time passed; centuries went by and dynasties rose and fell. Over those centuries the warriors of the two clans multiplied and prospered, still keeping their oath, guarding the two scrolls in that ice-bound land unknown to anyone. Until one day a man appeared who changed the fate of both clans: the son of the chieftain of the polar bear clan, and Fat Po’s biological father, Whitewave. One day, while out hunting, young Whitewave was caught in a powerful blizzard. He risked his life pulling a companion who’d been blown away by the storm back into a sheltered cave, but was himself blown off a cliff. After days of unconsciousness, he was — how soap-opera is this — rescued and taken home by a beautiful young woman of the black bear clan who was up the mountain gathering herbs, Blackie (yes, I’m being way too silly…). And even more soap-opera: they fell in love just like that… And the most soap-opera part needs no explanation: the fair maiden (fair bear?) Blackie was, of course, the adopted daughter of the big villain old Tortoise. And Whitewave, being naive, carelessly let slip quite a few of the scrolls’ secrets to his future father-in-law. Old Tortoise, who had already cultivated his kung fu to its peak and could scarcely advance further in his own practice, naturally turned his greedy eyes toward the Dragon and Phoenix Scrolls. So, following the standard soap-opera script, Whitewave and Blackie innocently returned to Peach Ridge with the fine wine old Tortoise had given them — doctored, of course. The two clans, seeing the young chieftain they’d thought dead return safe and sound, and having brought back a petite dark beauty to boot, joyfully threw a grand banquet, and even the guards drank a lot. Then old Tortoise charged into the vault with a band of wicked rhino bandits. The warriors of both clans, having drunk the poisoned wine, were too weak to fight back. Only Whitewave and Blackie, along with the snow leopard chieftain’s young son Tai Lung, managed to fight their way out; every other clan member was killed. But apart from a great hoard of gold and silver treasures, old Tortoise searched the entire vault and could not find the two legendary mystic scrolls. Whitewave and Blackie, both wounded and with young Tai Lung in tow, fled in a panic and ended up near the Jade Palace, intending to ask Master Badger — one of Blackie’s former suitors (I first thought he was a red panda; a badger chasing a bear is a bit weird, heh~) — for help. But at the foot of the mountain they were caught up by Tortoise and his crew (don’t ask me why a tortoise can run that fast…). With no way out, Whitewave and his wife threatened to carry the scrolls’ secret to their graves, making the scrolls’ whereabouts an eternal mystery. Old Tortoise had no choice but to strike a deal with them: Tai Lung would be raised by Badger until he came of age and would inherit the power of the Dragon Scroll, and in return Whitewave would hand the Phoenix Scroll over to Tortoise. So Whitewave left Tai Lung outside the gates of the Jade Palace and gave the Dragon Scroll to Master Badger for safekeeping, asking him to bestow it on Tai Lung when he came of age. Whitewave and Blackie then settled down in the Valley of Peace. In the blink of an eye, 19 years passed. Tai Lung grew up strong under Master Badger’s guidance (and with the love of Whitewave and Blackie, of course — though they never told Tai Lung about the clan’s massacre, and Master Badger didn’t know either). His martial arts progressed at astonishing speed: sparring bare-handed with Master Badger, who was in the prime of his life, he could hold his own for hundreds of moves without giving ground. So in no time the day came for Master Badger to bestow the Dragon Scroll on Tai Lung — but the cunning old Tortoise had plans of his own. On the morning of the ceremony day, Tortoise told Master Badger that etiquette required the ceremony be held at night, but he told Tai Lung that Master Badger didn’t think his character was upright enough and would no longer choose him as the Dragon Warrior. Dejected, Tai Lung went down the mountain to find Uncle Whitewave, who had always doted on him, only to find Whitewave and his wife lying in a pool of blood. It turned out old Tortoise knew Whitewave was going to retrieve the hidden Phoenix Scroll that day and had been following him, then caught him off guard and struck, wounding Whitewave and his wife. With his dying breath, Whitewave told Tai Lung about the clan massacre and his feud with old Tortoise, then breathed his last. Enraged, Tai Lung rushed back up the mountain to challenge Tortoise, but was defeated by him, framed for killing Whitewave and his wife, thrown into the Peach Ridge Vault, and secretly had the real scroll swapped out for a blank one. Meanwhile, though Whitewave and his wife were dead, they had left behind a son not yet a year old — Fat Po (what a prescient name!). After their death he was taken in by a kind-hearted neighbor who ran a noodle shop. Another 20 years flew by, and so the movie begins… The author is truly unbeatable. My admiration for him… flows on and on like an endless river, and to quote the old saying, “hearing is false, seeing is true” — this is the real deal, I’m genuinely impressed… Never mind saying the author is nitpicking or overthinking things with too many twists and turns of the mind — after all, there are plenty of BUGs in this film (and many of those BUGs exist because the gags try to be too clever by half, which is how others spot the holes). Everyone has a different level of sensitivity, and highly sensitive people, in order to explain those BUGs to themselves, will naturally go to great lengths with all sorts of logical deductions and assumptions. The result is that they’ve reworked this film into a hidden plot in the style of a Chinese wuxia story — and that research spirit deserves praise. Even though the plot isn’t really this complicated, and I prefer the simple original story, this guy’s analysis makes a lot of sense too. Upvoted. I learned something!

title: SGA5 Episode 2 Torrent
content: SGA Season 5Episode 1 had already aired, and after a long 13-day wait I finally caught a glimpse of Episode 2. Just found the time to watch it Boss Whoosey has arrived in City A… His “inaugural address” really didn’t waste a single word. Watching the first half, I kept finding more to like about Whoosey. He’s a rigorous, cautious, rational guy who values efficiency. When he deals with something, he always thinks it through, rationally weighs the pros and cons, and quickly settles on the best decision. Sure, that makes him seem a bit old-fashioned, but it’s exactly what you’d expect from the head of an interstellar expedition. As the first male commander-in-chief, I’m backing him too. Support. This episode’s crisis comes from the alien pathogen contracted during the last break-in at Micle’s lab. The main plot: the pathogen inside Kelly flares up, her body is gradually assimilated, and at breakneck speed it grows into a Hive ship! Luckily, before she collapsed she had freed Carson; at the critical moment Carson develops a countermeasure, and in the end Sheppard flies a Jumper straight into the isolation room and uses a syringe to defuse the crisis. Several moments this episode show how much Rodney cares about Kelly. (omitted) Whoosey may be a rational guy who firmly enforces the rulebook, but once he got to City A he still dared to take a gamble at a life-or-death moment. Haha, I did say so last time, right? Didn’t expect it so soon. Yep, good comrade. A person needs to be rigorous, cautious, rational and efficiency-minded — but also flexible.The rules we make are distilled from the laws of how things develop, a set of guidelines for the relatively optimal way to keep people acting correctly. But they don’t apply at all times. The key is that people must act according to the laws of how things develop, not according to man-made rules. (The laws of development never change, but the rules we make keep being refined and revised along with human experience.)Whoosey is a smart guy; he knows that following nature is a higher level. Hehe, Sheppard goes off on his own again — to save Kelly, he actually flies a Jumper straight into the isolation room to inject the antidote. Ugh! One move and it’s done. A real pro, and his RP is just great. American TV shows always embody this kind of humanitarian spirit: life over material wealth, saving people over protecting property. (Whereas what we’ve been fed is: for public property, you may sacrifice your life.) Whoosey didn’t go after Sheppard either… Sigh, this kid changes fast. Whoosey himself said: “I violated at least half a dozen basic safety protocols” “Rules exist for a reason.”

title: Badass 3D engine! newX3D
content: China’s first Flash 10 3D engine is now open source Thanks to the author machaoii for the painstaking, day-and-night grind. Work on the Flash 3D engine officially kicked off in early July, and yesterday it finally took shape. The project has now been renamed NewX3D — China’s first Flash 10-based 3D engine After several months of late-night coding by the author, this Flash 3D engine — with all the basic features you’d expect from a 3D engine — is finally done. Project codename: NewX3D[caption id”attachment_81” align”alignnone” width”250” caption”Awesome 3D Engine”][caption] What the project is:A Flash 3D engine built on Flash 10 Astro. Its architecture and algorithms are unlike those of any mainstream 3D engine today. The hope is to approach 3D from a different angle and deliver features other engines simply can’t (no pervy stuff, mind you). Project strengths: Clear architecture, built on polygon and vertex operations, easy to extend. Developed by a Chinese author, with tutorials published continuously to guide developers in maintaining and extending the engine together. Foreign engines usually only give you tutorials on how to use their API rather than how to extend it, so you end up boxed in by whatever features they happen to ship — and they don’t document their workflows or algorithms either, so extending them yourself is pure wishful thinking. Documentation entirely in Chinese, so a shaky grasp of English no longer keeps you away from 3D work. The project still has plenty of rough edges, and it needs enthusiastic people like you to join in — let’s build an engine that’s high-performance and full-featured together. More importantly, this is an engine of our own. If you’d like to join the project or just keep an eye on it, get in touch with the author and do your small part for the open source cause.
